Charles de Bernard's novel continues in its second volume with a friend's sharp reproach. Marillac learns that Gerfaut led him off their agreed route at Strasbourg, through the Vosges, for a reason Gerfaut had kept hidden: the Baroness de Bergenheim.

The volume turns on trust between friends and the pull of a forbidden love. Marillac feels his confidence abused, while Gerfaut must own the detour and its motive. Bernard keeps the quarrel civil and pointed, letting honor, friendship, and desire argue in plain speech. Readers see how one secret journey can strain even a long bond.
39841-the-esperantist-vol-2-no-2:
The Esperantist for February 1905 is volume two, number two of a London gazette for the spread of the planned world tongue. One copy cost fourpence, and a year cost three shillings. All letters went to the editor in Kensington Gardens Square.

The list holds a verse scene of Henry the Seventh entering Shrewsbury, and a Gautier poem turned into Esperanto. A month by month part tracks the cause, and a serial tale called Vivien runs on from the last issue. Other pieces give a cat nest tale, a visit to the Chinese court, and a fable in verse by Clarence Bicknell. Lists of local societies close the issue, from Acton to Brighton. Tongue fans see the young Esperanto world at work.
3987-conscience-volume-2:
Hector Malot's novel of guilt and crime continues in its second volume with a night watch outside a door. A man waits near a porte-cochere across the street, hoping to watch the concierge without being seen by passersby.

The crucial moment turns on watching, waiting, and fear of notice, as the watcher weighs a safer plan against the risk of being marked. Malot keeps the tension close and plain, letting streets, doorways, and small choices carry the dread. Readers follow a man whose conscience has become his jailer, long before any court or judge takes up his case.
3992-madame-chrysantheme-volume-2:
Pierre Loti's Japan novel continues in its second volume among the officers' households on the suburban slopes. By July, four officers of the ship live in like fashion, married through the same agent, Kangourou, and on visiting terms with each other's wives.

The merry neighbor Madame Campanule leads a round of calls, small talk, and household scenes. Loti keeps his sailor's eye on gardens, rooms, and daily custom, showing how a set of brief marriages forms a small foreign colony. Readers get a warm, close view of port life, where charm and distance sit side by side in every visit.
39961-the-works-of-sir-thomas-browne-vol:
Volume two of The Works of Sir Thomas Browne holds his great error hunt. Charles Sayle shaped the book for Grant Richards in London in nineteen hundred four. Browne’s own skull, in a photograph, fronts the grave volume. The Constables of Edinburgh printed the English Library set.

Pseudodoxia Epidemica, the third book, runs on from the first part. Griffins and the phoenix lead its bestiary of fond false tales. Frogs, toads, and the toad stone take their turns in the dock. The salamander in fire and the two headed snake stand tried here. Hares, moles, lampreys, snails, and the chameleon fill the mid list. Unicorn’s horn and spermaceti get their cold tests of truth. The fourth book turns to man: his upright frame and his heart. Browne’s calm prose weighs each old saw and finds most wanting.
3997-an-attic-philosopher-in-paris-volum:
Emile Souvestre's Paris journal continues in its second volume with dated notes from a top-floor room. On the first of July the writer marks the end of June, the month the Romans gave to Juno, and notes how Numa's reform kept old month names alive.

The volume mixes sky, season, and city life with short moral notes on power, fame, and daily conduct. Souvestre writes as a quiet watcher from the roofs, finding lessons in small sights. Readers get a gentle, thoughtful book, part diary and part essay, that invites slow reading and a second look at ordinary days.
39979-audubon-and-his-journals-volume-2:
Audubon and His Journals, in its second volume, presents the travel journals of John James Audubon, edited by his granddaughter Maria R Audubon. Elliott Coues supplied zoological and other notes. Charles Scribner's Sons of New York published the work in 1897. A frontispiece reproduces Audubon's unfinished drawing of Townsend's bunting.

That bird is known from a single specimen, shot in Chester County, Pennsylvania, in May 1833. The volume continues the Missouri River journals from the first volume. Episodes from Audubon's earlier travels fill out the record. Maria Audubon shaped her grandfather's papers for a public that knew him through his great bird plates. Coues, the leading American ornithologist of the day, checked the science. The journals show the artist naturalist in the field: shooting, sketching, and naming the birds of a vanishing frontier.
39983-the-weird-of-the-wentworths-a-tale:
The Weird of the Wentworths, volume two, is a tale of George the Fourth's time by Johannes Scotus. Saunders and Otley published it in London in eighteen sixty two. The motto, Sans Changer, stands on the title page with a Scott epigraph. Volume two drops the reader straight into a prison cell at midnight.

L'Estrange, a condemned murderer, weighs escape against staying to face his doom. A rope and a file lie ready for flight through the barred window. He lingers because escape means never seeing Ellen again in his life. The captain who slipped him the tools may force him to flee anyway. Rain and lightning split the night as that captain walks home whistling. The tale mixes Scots scenes, Arthur's Seat among them, with high romance.
40022-the-history-of-chivalry-or-knighth:
The History of Chivalry, or knighthood and its times, is a history by Charles Mills, issued at London in 1825. Mills had also written a history of the Crusades. This second of two volumes opens with the state of chivalry in England under Edward the Third. Its contents range over tournaments and the founding of the Order of the Garter.

The chapter heads praise the courtesy of Edward and the spread of chivalric taste among all classes. English archers and the Black Prince stand beside tales of the king's own chivalry. Long space goes to a famed knight whose deeds fill many heads: his vows, his fights for his lady, and his rescue of two brother knights. The volume treats England of that reign as the very seat of honour.
40042-the-deserted-yacht-madge-sterling-:
The Deserted Yacht, by Ann Wirt, is the second book in the Madge Sterling series for young readers. The Goldsmith Publishing Company of Chicago copyrighted it in 1932. The series list also names The Missing Formula and The Secret of the Sundial.

Madge Sterling arrives by train at Cheltham Bay in a neat dark blue travelling suit, expecting friends to meet her. None appear, and the porter sets her suitcase down while she waits in puzzlement. A letter had promised they would go straight to the yacht Flora, anchored in the harbour, with everything ready for the trip. The chapters ahead promise an abandoned yacht, Enid's story, a midnight visitor, a motor boat chase and a rescue. Wirt wrote brisk mystery adventures for girls, and the puzzle here begins with an empty platform.
40057-the-life-of-florence-nightingale-v:
Sir Edward Cook wrote this great life of Florence Nightingale in two volumes. Macmillan printed the first at London in 1913. It runs from 1820 to 1861, from her birth to her work after the Crimea. A water-colour of her mother and the girls in 1828 heads the plates.

Aspiration is the first part's name, for the years 1820 to 1854. Childhood and schooling fill its start: Lea Hurst in Derbyshire and Embley Park in Hampshire. Her father taught his girls history, the classics, and deep thought. Tales of a young call to service stand in the list. Cook, her chosen life writer, had her papers in his hands.
40058-the-life-of-florence-nightingale-v:
Volume two of Edward Cook's Life of Florence Nightingale was published by Macmillan in London in 1913, covering the years 1862 to 1910. A portrait of Nightingale in 1887, from the picture by Richmond at Claydon, fronts the volume. Part five, For the Health of the Army in India, opens the book, and its contents are a detailed map of her desk-bound campaigns.

The first chapter begins in loss: despondency after Sidney Herbert's death, the Herbert Hospital at Woolwich, and work carried on as in his times. Then the Indian army, whose high death rate made her, in the contents' phrase, its saviour. She pressed for a royal commission for India on the lines of the home commission of 1857. She worked for it through 1862 and 1863, gathering evidence by a circular of inquiry sent to India.
40100-life-histories-of-north-american-w:
Life Histories of North American Wood Warblers, part one of two, is a work of ornithology by Arthur Cleveland Bent. Dover Publications reissued the work at New York in 1963 in this edition. It is an unabridged reprint of the edition of 1953 from the Government Printing Office. That edition was Bulletin 203 of the United States National Museum of the Smithsonian.

Bent life histories gather, species by species, what was known of each bird habits. The wood warblers, small bright birds of the American woods, fill two parts in his scheme. Part one stands here as the first half of that treatment for the family. Bent volumes, built from his own field work and a wide correspondence of observers, remain standard sources. Bird men still cite them for nesting dates and habits recorded before the great changes in American woodlands of the later century.
40101-popular-technology-or-professions-:
Popular Technology, or Professions and Trades, by Edward Hazen, fills two volumes; the second was printed in New York in 1870 by Harper, from an 1841 copyright. Eighty-one engravings show the trades at work. Hazen also wrote spelling books and a practical grammar. This volume runs from the musician and the musical instrument maker through the fine arts to the heavy crafts.

Chapters treat the sculptor, painter, engraver, lithographer, author, printer, type-founder, and paper-maker. Then come the architect, carpenter, mason, potter, glass-blower, optician, jeweller, silversmith, blacksmith, cutler, and gunsmith. Each trade gets its tools, materials, and steps explained in plain terms. The book opens with music itself, defined as the science of combining sounds, each passion having its own tone.
40144-a-history-of-art-in-ancient-egypt-:
A History of Art in Ancient Egypt, volume one of two, comes from the French of Perrot and Chipiez. Armstrong turned it into English and edited it for Chapman and Hall. Five hundred ninety eight engravings and fourteen plates fill the two volumes. The London and New York printing is dated eighteen eighty three.

Perrot was a Paris professor and Chipiez a sharp critic of building art. Their aim is a history of antique art from the Pharaohs to the Roman emperors. Egypt comes first as the seed of that long growth toward Pericles. Armstrong kept close to the French, cutting only one repeated stretch in full. The authors chose to trace each art alone from birth to decay. That plan forced some going back over ground, owned in the preface.
40149-a-history-of-art-in-ancient-egypt-:
A History of Art in Ancient Egypt, volume two, comes from the French of Georges Perrot and Charles Chipiez. Walter Armstrong translated and edited it, and Chapman and Hall of London with A C Armstrong and Son of New York published it in 1883. Five hundred and ninety-eight engravings fill the text, with fourteen steel and coloured plates.

The volume opens with civil and military architecture: palaces, houses, and forts. A long chapter on building methods follows, covering materials, the arch, columns and the Egyptian orders, doors, windows, temple lighting, and obelisks. Sculpture then runs from its origins through the ancient empire and the Theban ages to the Saite period. Painting, caricature, and ornament come next, then the trades: glass, pottery, metal-work, jewelry, and woodwork. A closing chapter weighs the character of Egyptian art and its place in art history.
40159-manners-a-novel-vol-2:
An anonymous novel in three volumes reaches its second volume in a London edition of 1817, with mottoes from Juvenal and Frederick the Great. Chapter one heads a Spanish verse from Cervantes, footnoted in English: I know, Olalla, that thou lovest me. Selina's agitated spirits are long in composing, the text begins. When she sinks to rest at last, the story proceeds.

Printed for Baldwin, Cradock, and Joy at Paternoster Row, the volume belongs to the Regency novel trade. Its manners are those of courtship and society in the Austen decade. Selina's love, confessed only by guarded eyes, drives the plot. Three volume publication let circulating libraries lend the tale in parts.
40259-charles-auchester-volume-2-of-2:
Elizabeth Sheppard continues a music tale in Charles Auchester, volume 2 of 2, printed at Chicago in 1891. McClurg made the book, with a first word and notes by George Upton. Upton had writ books on the standard operas and on woman in music. A sketch of Mendelssohn in his youth fronts the volume.

Chapter one looks back on a start in Germany. The teller recalls the morning he set out from Lorbeerstadt for Cecilia. He had no friends yet on the new ground and went alone. A vague sadness sat on him, the sun being under cloud. He had not wished Aronach good day, for Aronach was out on school duties. His violin and his certificate went with him on the road.
40280-retrospect-of-western-travel-volum: Volume one of a two volume retrospect of western travel, issued by Harper and Brothers of New York in the late 1830s. The surviving head is publisher's matter: a long Harper list of important works just published. It offers the works of Charles Lamb, Wilbur Fisk's travels in Europe during 1835 and 1836, memoirs of Aaron Burr, and Poe's Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket. The travel narrative itself lies beyond this advertising front matter.
40281-retrospect-of-western-travel-volum:
Harriet Martineau looks back on her American tour in volume two of a two-volume travel book. Saunders and Otley issued it at London in 1838. Harper and Brothers sold it at New York.

The volume starts with a Mississippi voyage. Her party boards the Henry Clay, a boat with ninety-six trips and no accident. A judge warns them, half in earnest, to bring life preservers. Later chapters take in Cincinnati, the Natural Bridge, and Colonel Burr. She visits the White Mountains and Lake George. She writes on Channing, on schools for the deaf and blind, and on cemeteries. Martineau watched the young republic with a reformer's eye. Her travel books rank among the sharpest foreign reports of the 1830s.
40324-true-to-a-type-vol-1-of-2:
Cleland wrote a novel in two volumes, with volume one printed in Edinburgh and London in 1887. The prologue opens on an evening in New Orleans. The brief swift evening of the South links the sultry glare of day to the cool of night with imperceptible graduation. Narrow old streets grow dim in the transparent dusk.

Houses sealed all afternoon against the heated air throw wide their doors and casements to the breeze. Inhabitants come forth from their siesta. A young man of twenty one, browned and sharpened by climate and vicissitude, stands among them. Clam Beach, surf bathing perils, Rose and Lettice, and a mother's cares fill the contents. A tableau, an omnibus ride, and a storm stayed close round out volume one.
40340-beaumarchais-and-the-war-of-americ:
Elizabeth S Kite wrote the second volume of Beaumarchais and the War of American Independence. Richard G Badger issued the book in Boston in nineteen hundred eighteen. James M Beck lent the work a warm foreword of praise. Secret French aid to America fills this half of the tale.

The Chevalier d’Eon, a sly spy who feigned a woman’s life, opens it. Beaumarchais won the spy’s famed chest of state papers for France. His memoirs then urged the king to back the rebels’ just cause. Arthur Lee met him in London and wrote home to Congress of hope. His trade house, Roderigue Hortales and Company, masked the aid. Silas Deane signed the pact that sent arms across the wide sea. Franklin’s coming and ten ships’ sailing mark the tale’s high tide. Vergennes cleared the playwright when blame fell thick on his name.
40384-musical-myths-and-facts-volume-2-o:
Carl Engel wrote Musical Myths and Facts, and this file holds the second of its two volumes, issued at London by Novello, Ewer and Company in 1876. The volume opens with Mattheson on Handel, drawing on the scanty notices of Handel's youth that survive. A set of diabolic music tales follows: the indefatigable fiddler, the haunted mansion, witches, the changeling, and the rat catcher of Hameln.

Royal musicians, composers as practical men, and music and medicine take the middle of the book. Popular stories with musical traditions gather the handsome minstrel, the invisible flute player, and the plague in Goldberg. A short survey of the history of music, a dated chronology, and the musical scales in use at the present day close the volume.
40436-plato-and-the-other-companions-of-:
Plato, and the Other Companions of Sokrates, volume two of four, is a work of philosophy by George Grote, author of the History of Greece. A new edition was printed at London by John Murray in 1888. The volume's twelfth chapter treats the dialogues Alkibiades the First and the Second. Its contents lay out the talks step by step.

Sokrates questions the young Alkibiades, who means to advise the Athenians on war and peace. Asked what standard he will use, Alkibiades answers: just and unjust. Pressed on where he learnt to tell them apart, he owns he never learnt it from anyone. He learnt it from the multitude, as he learnt Greek. Sokrates shows the multitude cannot teach it, since they disagree among themselves. Alkibiades is brought to admit that whatever is just, is good. Grote's book walks through the dialogues with close summaries for the student.
4058-marius-the-epicurean-volume-2:
Walter Pater's philosophical romance continues in its second volume among the Stoics of Marcus Aurelius. The emperor's ideas of large generalization could chill the heart, yet Aurelius joined them to kindness, humor, and the popular religion with its many gods.

A chapter called The Ceremony of the Dart marks the volume's ritual and reflective pace. Marius tests Stoic calm against Epicurean pleasure and the pull of early Christian faith, in prose of great beauty. Readers who stayed with the first volume will find the second deeper and graver, as Marius nears his life's turning point.
40615-a-history-of-the-reformation-vol-1:
A History of the Reformation, volume one, is a church history by Thomas Lindsay. Lindsay was principal of the United Free Church College at Glasgow. Clark of Edinburgh brought the two volumes out in the year 1906. This first volume treats the Reformation in Germany alone of lands. Its span runs to the Religious Peace of Augsburg at the close.

Book one paints the eve of the Reformation across western Europe. The papacy's claims to world rule open the survey of that age. Chapters weigh the political map, the Renaissance, and social conditions next. Towns, trade, peasant revolts, and home religious life fill that picture. Humanism and its circles lead at last to Luther's own story. His youth, convent years, and first lectures stand in the contents. The indulgence controversy opens the clash that changed the church.
40634-in-northern-mists-arctic-explorati:
In Northern Mists, volume two, is a history of Arctic exploration in early times by Fridtjof Nansen. Nansen was professor of oceanography at the university in Christiania. The work was translated by Arthur Chater and published in London in 1911, with illustrations. This second volume carries the story from the Norse voyages toward early modern discovery.

Its contents open with Wineland the Good and the discovery of America, then turn to the Eskimo and the Skraeling. The decline of the Norse settlements in Greenland follows. Later chapters treat Norwegian expeditions to the White Sea, voyages in the polar sea, and whaling and sealing. The north in the maps and geography of the middle ages gets a long chapter. The book closes with John Cabot and the English discovery of North America, and with the Portuguese discoveries in the north-west.
40643-the-life-of-johannes-brahms-vol-1-:
Florence May wrote a life of Johannes Brahms in two volumes, printed in London in 1905. A picture shows Brahms at the age of twenty. May opens with her own recollections of the composer. She thanks the kind friends whose sympathy helped her through the writing of the books.

Volume one runs from 1760 to the mid 1850s. It tells of Johann Jakob Brahms, of his son's birth and childhood in Hamburg, and of first teachers such as Cossel and Marxsen. The boy gives concerts, struggles for work, and meets Remenyi, Joachim, and Liszt. His first meeting with Schumann closes the span, the turn that made his name known in the music world.
40644-the-life-of-johannes-brahms-vol-2-:
Florence May wrote a life of Johannes Brahms in two volumes, with volume two printed at London in 1905. Chapter twelve covers 1862 to 1864: Vienna, its music societies and leading men, the Prater, and Brahms at a Hellmesberger Quartet concert. His first Vienna concert, hopes of the Hamburg Philharmonic conductorship, and the First Serenade follow.

Brahms is elected conductor of the Vienna Singakademie and settles in the city. Chapter thirteen moves to Baden Baden with Frau Schumann's circle, Hermann Levi, and Pauline Viardot Garcia. The Horn Trio, the first cello sonata, and the German Requiem rise in these years. May knew the world she writes, and her life stands full of dates, letters, and first hearings.
40667-the-mystery-of-jockey-hollow-arden:
The Mystery of Jockey Hollow is a girls' mystery novel by Cleo Garis, the second book in the Arden Blake Mystery Series. The Burt Company of New York copyrighted it in 1934. The series list also names The Orchard Secret and Missing at Marshlands.

The frontispiece catches the tone: a girl screams that something terrible is down in the cellar. The chapters promise a ghost mansion, the sight of the dead, the ghost of Patience, and a trial by jury of sorts. A missing man, a figure in red, and two ghosts follow. Arden and her friends Terry Landry and Sim investigate, with a Christmas party, mistletoe and frightened screams along the way. Garis wrote brisk haunted-house mysteries for schoolgirls, in which the heroine's idea, as one chapter title boasts, does the real investigating.
40798-a-history-of-the-reformation-vol-2:
Thomas Lindsay wrote a history of the Reformation in two volumes, with volume two printed at Edinburgh in 1907 in the International Theological Library. It treats the Reformation in Switzerland, France, the Netherlands, Scotland, and England. The Anabaptist and Socinian movements and the Counter Reformation go with it. A map of the Reformation and Counter Reformation from 1520 to 1580 is bound in.

In this volume I have fulfilled the promise made in the former one, Lindsay writes, to describe the Reformed churches and the movements named. It rests on a careful study of sources of the time, he says. No important fact is recorded without evidence from the time itself. Lindsay, principal of the United Free Church College at Glasgow, writes church history with a scholar's care.
40955-the-brownie-of-bodsbeck-and-other-:
James Hogg wrote this set of Scots tales, first printed in Edinburgh in 1818. Volume one holds the title tale and verse for a kind patron. Hogg was known for tales of farm folk and strange sights. He wrote in both prose and song.

A verse note thanks Lady Anne Scott for her care of poor folk. Hogg says the tales grew from long winter nights of talk. The mood is wild, sad, and full of old Scots lore. Readers meet a voice rooted in Yarrow vale and its hills. The book runs to two volumes in all.
41018-john-leech-his-life-and-work-vol-2:
John Leech, His Life and Work is the next part of a two part life of the famed draw man of a great jest sheet. William Powell Frith, a paint man of rank, wrote the life. It came out at London in eighteen ninety-one, with a face plate and a score of cuts. The first part of this book treats Leech and that sheet.

Parts treat his jest cuts, his love of field sport, the tale men he drew for, and his kin with the two great tale men of the age. A comic past of Rome, sport tales, and folk types each take parts. Late parts give tales of the man from his friends, his show of works, and his ties with a famed paint man of the day. Cut names at the front show hunts, courts, and school scenes.
4102-the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1:
Azel Ames's Mayflower history continues in its second volume with the ship herself. Early chroniclers left neither picture nor general description of the Mayflower, and few data from which to rebuild her lines and details.

Tradition places her among the merchant craft of her day, and Ames works from that tradition with care, weighing tonnage, rig, and build. The volume suits readers who love ships, as it rebuilds a famous vessel from scraps. It gives the Pilgrim story its wooden stage, plank by plank. Ship lovers will linger over every guess and measure.
41218-the-diary-of-john-evelyn-volume-1-:
The first volume of John Evelyn's diary, edited by William Bray. M Walter Dunne published this edition at Washington and London in 1901. Richard Garnett of the British Museum adds a special introduction. Photogravures illustrate the volume, starting with Charles the First in prison. Other plates show Cromwell dictating to Milton. Lord William Russell taking leave of his children also appears.

The introduction contrasts Evelyn with Pepys at once. Pepys is the zoological garden, Evelyn the museum. Decorum rules Evelyn's pages where garrulity rules the other's. Yet Evelyn draws one portrait admirably: his own. The diary covers the civil war, the Restoration court, and the plague and fire years. It remains a prime source for seventeenth-century England. Evelyn's interests ran to gardens, science, and fine buildings.
41229-guy-deverell-v-2-of-2:
J S Le Fanu wrote Guy Deverell, here in the second of two volumes. Bernhard Tauchnitz issued this copyright edition at Leipzig in 1865, as volume 803 of his Collection of British Authors. Le Fanu was the author of Uncle Silas. The volume opens with Lady Alice and Varbarriere together in the library. Varbarriere orders his wings and talks with Donica Gwynn. A story of a magician and a vampire stands early.

Guy Deverell at Slowton, an uncle and nephew scene, and the guests together follow. The Green Chamber holds two chapters and a morning. A doctor's visit and an interrogated patient raise the mystery. General Lennox appears, and the bishop sees the patient. Guy arrives late, under a chapter line of surrender: I am thine and thou art mine, body and soul, for ever.
41275-miles-tremenhere-a-novel-vol-1-of-:
Annette Marie Maillard wrote Miles Tremenhere, in two volumes; this is the first. G Routledge and Company published it at London in 1853. A line from Lopez de Vega heads the title. She dedicated the book to Erasmus Wilson, friend of the poor. The first chapter opens in a girl's voice.

Tick tack, for ever goes the large hall clock, the narrator says. The clock began the day she was born, seventeen years ago, and has not paused an hour since. They say it stopped once, the day her mother died, for its ticking recalled her birth-day. Her aunts and uncle Juvenal are kind and loving, she owns. Still, it is not a mother's love, and she yearns for that unknown thing.
41309-love-letters-of-nathaniel-hawthorn:
Love Letters of Nathaniel Hawthorne, volume one, was privately printed at Chicago in nineteen seven for members of a society. William K Bixby held the rights and owned the first letters. The letters were written to Sophia Peabody during their courtship.

Julian Hawthorne and Rose Hawthorne Lathrop had quoted the letters in part before. Their cuts, the editors note, broke the flow and served set points. Read whole, the letters show ease, beauty, humour, and tenderness. The editors say almost nothing needed cutting, beyond light banter in good taste. Care was taken that no private matter should wound the living. Two volumes hold the set.
41332-ten-thousand-a-year-volume-2:
Ten Thousand a Year, volume two, is a novel by Samuel Warren, in a Boston edition of 1900. Little, Brown and Company published the volume, printed at the University Press at Cambridge. A plate shows the crest and coat of arms of Tittlebat Titmouse, the hero of the tale. The arms are given as described by Sir Gorgeous Tintack, Garter King at Arms, in the jest.

Contents of volume two open after the battle, with the behaviour of the belligerents in the suit. Mr Aubrey surrenders at discretion, and the opposing generals hold a council of war in the third chapter. Warren novel of a draper clerk raised to a fortune by a will was a sensation of the 1840s. Its law scenes, drawn by a barrister author, made the long Chancery fight at its centre famous on both sides of the Atlantic.
41359-the-golden-bough-a-study-in-compar:
The Golden Bough, volume two, is the second half of James George Frazer's study in comparative religion. Frazer was a fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge. This two-volume edition was printed by Macmillan in 1894. Later editions grew to twelve volumes, but this early form already holds the core of his argument.

The contents continue the third chapter, on the corn-spirit. The corn-spirit appears as an animal: a gander, a goat, a hare, a cat, a fox. Then come eating the god, killing the divine animal, the transfer of evil, scapegoats, and the killing of the god in Mexico. The fourth chapter, on the golden bough itself, treats Balder and the external soul in tales and customs. Few books shaped the study of myth and ritual as this one did.
41368-love-letters-of-nathaniel-hawthorn:
Love Letters of Nathaniel Hawthorne, volume two of two, was privately printed at Chicago in nineteen oh seven by the Society of the Dofobs. William K Bixby held the copyright. The letters are addressed to Miss Peabody: Sophia Peabody, Hawthorne's wife. Volume two covers the courtship's later stage, from eighteen forty-one.

The first letter here is dated at Oak Hill on April thirteenth, eighteen forty-one. Hawthorne calls himself her poor husband in a polar paradise of snow. He compares their venture to the Plymouth pilgrims, who landed in storm and prospered. He is glad she will not see their future home first on such a day. The private printing kept the letters to a circle of collectors. They show the romancer of gloom writing as a lover in bright, plain earnest.
41436-the-sportswoman-s-library-vol-1-of:
The Sportswoman Library, volume one, was shaped by Frances E Slaughter and printed at Westminster by Archibald Constable in 1898. Plates come from photos and old prints. The book is given, by permission, to the Marchioness of Worcester, a keen sportswoman and wife of one of the foremost sportsmen of the age.

The contents open with Englishwomen and Sport, by the editor. Fox Hunting by Mrs Burn and Hare Hunting by the editor follow. Shooting by the Honorable Mrs Lancelot Lowther and Fishing for Tarpon by Mrs Murphy Grimshaw stand next. Archery, skating, golf, and croquet fill the rest, with rules for golf and croquet at the back. In her preface Slaughter thanks the many good sportswomen who aided her. They brought great stores of working knowledge to their subjects. Sport fans get lady experts on field games.
41470-history-of-the-reformation-in-the-:
History of the Reformation in the Sixteenth Century, volume two, by J H Merle d'Aubigné, came out in a new translation by Henry Beveridge from William Collins in 1846. The translation carries the author's latest improvements. The volume takes the story into the year 1519 and the debates that spread Luther's cause.

Book Five opens with the discussion at Leipzig. It traces how the papal chamberlain Miltitz pressed Luther to recant, and how Luther refused yet offered silence. Later chapters stage the contest between Eck and Carlstadt on the question of the pope. Portraits of Luther, Carlstadt, and Eck enliven the account. D'Aubigné writes from a firm Protestant faith, set out in his motto from Theodore de Beze.
41735-the-girl-of-the-period-and-other-s:
Lynn Linton wrote The Girl of the Period and the social essays bound with it, first printed in the Saturday Review. Richard Bentley and Son of London gathered them in two volumes in 1883, and this is the first. She dedicated the book to all good girls and true women.

In the preface Linton tells the price of fame. The title essay drew anger from readers who held women above all blame, and strangers began to claim they had written it. She was twice introduced to the supposed author, once a clergyman and once a lady of rank. The essays take sharp aim at the manners and morals of young women of the day. Readers get Victorian social criticism at its most combative, under the author's own name at last.
41736-the-girl-of-the-period-and-other-s:
The Girl of the Period and Other Social Essays, volume two, gathers short pieces by Lynn Linton first printed in the Saturday Review. The London edition came from Richard Bentley and Son in 1883. The essays take up manners, types, and frictions of Victorian social life. Their titles map the ground: Gushing Men, Sweet Seventeen, The Habit of Fear, and Old Ladies.

The volume runs to more than forty essays. Later pieces treat voices, burnt fingers, the art of reticence, men's favourites, and womanliness. Others look at the sweets of married life, social nomads, great girls, and shunted dowagers. Church strangers, hotel life in England, heroes at home, and modern man-haters get their turn. The pieces are brief, pointed, and written from close watching of drawing-room life. They form a sharp portrait of the period by one of its best-known women essayists.
41747-the-real-shelley-new-views-of-the-:
John Cordy Jeaffreson wrote The Real Shelley, new views of the poet's life, in two volumes printed in London in 1885. This is the first volume. Contents open with the Shelley of fancy life-writing. That chapter treats the makers of the fanciful Shelley and the poet's looks: his little turn-up nose, his speech, and his striking untruthfulness.

His temperance and its lack, and his treatment as a victim of home persecution, stand in the head. The chapter asks whether the Necessity of Atheism was a mere squib, and treats Lord Eldon's decree and the slaughter of good names. The Shelleys of Sussex take the second chapter, with the Michelgrove and Castle Goring lines. Shelley's childhood, his birth and the likenesses of him, fills the third. The Brentford schoolboy follows, with the character of Dr Greenlaw and tales told to his blame.
41748-the-real-shelley-new-views-of-the-:
The Real Shelley: New Views of the Poet's Life, volume 2, is a biography by John Cordy Jeaffreson. Hurst and Blackett published the two volumes in London in 1885. Jeaffreson had already written The Real Lord Byron. This second volume turns from the poet to the circle that formed him. Its first three chapters belong to William Godwin and his wives.

Chapter one follows Godwin from Socinianism to hack-work and Political Justice. Chapter two gives Mary Wollstonecraft's story in blunt detail. Her years in Paris, her union with Imlay, and her death all appear. Chapter three takes up the second Mrs Godwin, Mary Jane Clairmont. Throughout, Jeaffreson attacks Kegan Paul's earlier account of the family. He convicts Paul of inaccuracies from Paul's own evidence. The tone is prosecutorial: this Shelley biography is also a brief against rival biographers.
41796-the-brownie-of-bodsbeck-and-other-:
Brownie of Bodsbeck and Other Tales is a set of tales by James Hogg, author of The Queen's Wake. The hosted text is volume two of two, issued at Edinburgh in eighteen eighteen. Contents of this volume give the continuation of the title tale first. The Wool Gatherer follows, then The Hunt of Eildon. A transcriber's note warns that the title tale has no chapter four and two chapters three.

Chapter one of the continuation opens next morning with Davie Tait astir early. He takes his plaid and staff and sets out to see what became of his ewes. Five score of them are the poor remains of a good stock, the tale says. The events of last night are fresh in his mind as he climbs. He is conning a new prayer for some great emergency.
41914-the-stones-of-paris-in-history-and:
The Stones of Paris in History and Letters, volume one of two, is a city past by Benjamin Ellis Martin and Charlotte Martin. It came out at New York in eighteen ninety-nine, with plates from draws by a named hand. A plate of the great stage bard of France heads the book. Parts treat three worn stairs, the school mens camp of the old age, and the bard and his friends.

A part runs from a famed wise wit to a stage man of the next age. The Paris of the great revolt closes the list of this book. Plates show an old house of a queen, a church of the camp, and the doors and wells of the bards homes. The book is writ to a man of note in thanks for his own book on the traits of that land.
41918-the-philippines-past-and-present-v:
The Philippines Past and Present, volume two of two, is a survey of the islands under American rule. Dean Worcester wrote the work from long service in the island government. He was secretary of the interior from 1901 to 1913 and sat on the Philippine Commission. The Macmillan Company published the book in New York in 1914, with many plates.

The contents run from schooling to the rule of the non Christian tribes. Chapters treat slavery and peonage, the island legislature, and the land and forests of the group. Later parts weigh trade prospects and the results of American rule. The closing chapters ask whether independence is now possible and what should follow. An appendix prints the orders given to the first commissions. Pictures show Igorot life, schools, trails, and constabulary soldiers.
42013-salem-chapel-v-1-2:
Salem Chapel, by Mrs Oliphant, appears here in the Tauchnitz edition, volume one of two. Tauchnitz issued it at Leipzig in 1870 as volume 1091 of British authors. The Last of the Mortimers and Margaret Maitland stand in her list in the front. Chapter one opens toward the west end of Grove Street in Carlingford.

On the shabby side of that street stood a red brick building, the tale begins. A pinched gable and a curious little belfry, not meant for any bell, mark it. It looks not unlike a handle to lift the edifice by, the narrator jokes. This was Salem Chapel, the only dissenting place of worship in Carlingford then. A young minister travails in a small town chapel drive the Chronicles of Carlingford tale.
42044-salem-chapel-v-2-2:
Salem Chapel, in its second part, is a novel by Oliphant, of the Chronicles of Carlingford. This form is a cheap print for the trade of the continent, in a run of British authors books. It came out at Leipzig in eighteen seventy, with the right to turn it into other tongues kept back.

Its first page is a dread Sunday dawn. A mother rises from a bed where she has not slept, worn by an awful night. Snatches of sleep more dread than wake had fell on her, and she starts up sure she hears her girl call. Had the lost Susan called, had she come home in any plight, the mother feels she could bear it. What she could not bear, yet did bear, was the hush.
42081-the-diary-of-john-evelyn-volume-2-:
The Diary of John Evelyn, volume two, continues the famous seventeenth-century journal. Bray edited it from the original manuscripts. Walter Dunne published this edition in 1901. Garnett of the British Museum wrote a special introduction. The volume spans the years 1665 to 1706. Photogravure portraits illustrate it. Charles the First in prison fronts the set.

The entries open on January 2, 1665. Evelyn records publishing a translation that day. Sharp frost and snow mark the week. He rides toward Dover on a commission. Wounded and sick sailors set ashore need care. Port officers from Kent to Portsmouth fall under his charge. Nell Gwynne's portrait appears among the plates. Cromwell dictating to Milton is pictured too. Court, war, and plague fill the diary's daily round.
42215-a-pilgrimage-to-nejd-the-cradle-of:
A Pilgrimage to Nejd, volume one, is Lady Anne Blunt's account of her journey into central Arabia, published by John Murray in London in 1881. Blunt had already written of the Bedouin tribes of the Euphrates. This expedition, made with her husband, aimed at Jebel Shammar and the court of the Arab emir, and her drawings illustrate the book.

The editor's preface explains the title. To the northern Bedouin, Nejd is the cradle of their race and of the chivalry they still live by, as Palestine is to the Jews. Antar did his labours there, and Hatim Tai entertained his guests there. Few northern Arabs have ever crossed the great Nefud desert to reach it. To the Blunts, steeped in desert romance, the journey felt like a pilgrimage to a holy land, and the book keeps that tone: travel narrative as an act of reverence.
42217-a-pilgrimage-to-nejd-the-cradle-of:
Lady Anne Blunt wrote A Pilgrimage to Nejd, the Cradle of the Arab Race, and here is volume two of two. John Murray published the second edition in London in eighteen eighty one. Blunt had earlier written The Bedouin Tribes of the Euphrates. The contents open with a long chapter on Nejd horses.

That chapter treats the rarity of the horses, Ibn Saoud's stud, and the stables at Hail. Later chapters ride with the Emir, leave Hail, and join the Persian Haj. A hyena hunt, hawking, and tales and legends follow. The party is adopted by a tribe, makes a forced march, and reaches Nejef with a terrible loss of camels. The shrines of the Shias and Bagdad close the travel part. A section called Our Persian Campaign follows. Travel readers get an English lady's ride through Arabia.
42303-the-expositor-s-bible-the-acts-of-:
The Acts of the Apostles, volume two, is a commentary by Stokes in the Expositor's Bible series. Nicoll edited the series, and Armstrong printed this volume at New York in 1892. A long front list maps all six series of the set, each volume at a dollar fifty. Stokes closes his survey of Acts with this book.

In a closing note he explains his plan. He discussed the latter portion of Acts more briefly than its earlier chapters, and he did so on purpose. His reasons stand explained in the body of the work. The commentary follows the apostles' story to its end, treating Paul and the road to Rome. Preachers and teachers were its intended readers, as with all the Expositor's Bible volumes.
42313-the-life-and-letters-of-lafcadio-h:
A second volume of the life and letters of Lafcadio Hearn gathers his correspondence, with photographs and his own small sketches noted where they fall. The transcriber explains that Hearn's Japanese script in letters cannot be reproduced here. Its positions are marked as illustrations instead. No translations were made, since the text usually supplies them. Hearn wrote from Japan to friends in America and Europe.

Elizabeth Bisland edited the life and letters after Hearn's death in 1904. His letters chart the making of his Japanese books, from Glimpses of Unfamiliar Japan to Kwaidan. Volume two carries the later Matsue, Kumamoto, and Tokyo years. The sketches show his eye at work.
4234-correspondence-of-wagner-and-liszt-:
The second volume of the Wagner-Liszt correspondence carries the two composers' letters through triumphs and quarrels. One letter notes that a call to Berlin for Tannhauser has by no means been frustrated, though the theater intendant cannot decide the matter.

The king alone can suspend the usual order, and his decision stands independent of the intendant's authority. Wagner argues his case with passion and pride, while Liszt answers as friend, champion, and critic. Readers who love music history will find genius and ego in every letter. Genius, pride, and friendship sound through every page.
4236-dynevor-terrace-or-the-clue-of-life:
The second volume of Dynevor Terrace, a Victorian domestic novel, opens its fifth chapter on a new world of emigration. Prayers for emigrants sing of southern skies, new stars, and fresh hues where pearl and coral hide, tokens of grace ever fresh and new.

Early-year days, devoid of spring brilliance but full of soft, heavy fragrance, foster tender growth in grey air. The novel follows a family through separation, faith, and the clue of life itself. Readers who enjoy Yonge-era domestic fiction will find a gentle, earnest continuation.
42492-lady-eureka-or-the-mystery-a-proph:
A nameless scribe wrote a future tale of Lady Eureka in three books. Volume two came out in London in 1840. He wrote Mephistopheles in England in his past strange works. A talk on past, now, and days to come leads this book. Australian new life and Posthumous's case room fill the front list.

A gay meet, a do good man in a bind, and China stand there. A Chinese bard, the great rains, and game laws in India come next. The harm of good aims is drawn in a bold late part. Athenia closes this book's list of wild future scenes. Zabra tells his hid tale to his cure man in page one. Keep it close, he begs.
42578-private-letters-of-edward-gibbon-1:
Rowland Prothero edited the Private Letters of Edward Gibbon, published by John Murray in London in 1896. This first volume covers letters from 1753 toward the historian's death in 1794. The Earl of Sheffield wrote the introduction. His grandfather had been Gibbon's intimate friend, host, devisee, and literary executor.

The Sheffield family kept Gibbon's portraits, manuscripts, letters, and relics at Sheffield Park for a century. A commemoration in November 1894, a hundred years after Gibbon's death, revived interest in the remains. Readers asked that the manuscripts be collated again and the unpublished matter given to the world. These letters show the author of The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire in private: his friendships, his Lausanne years, and his work, in his own polished hand.
4258-andersonville-a-story-of-rebel-mili:
The second volume of John McElroy's prison narrative opens in the spring of 1864. New prisoners began to reach Andersonville after a quiet winter. A first lot of about seven hundred men had been captured at Olustee in Florida. They joined older prisoners taken at Gettysburg, Chickamauga, and Mine Run.

McElroy records the arrival of Black soldiers and harsh treatment of officers of colored regiments. He records the killing of a sergeant of a Negro squad, and the rough justice of the camp. The volume keeps the private soldier's viewpoint of the first volume. Names, regiments, and small scenes make the prison's growth concrete.
4263-the-golden-bowl-volume-2:
Henry James published The Golden Bowl in 1904, and this second volume carries the second half of the novel, Book Second: The Princess. The story centers on Maggie Verver, her father Adam, her husband the Prince, and Charlotte, whose close ties and hidden pasts create a quiet crisis inside a wealthy, polished marriage.

James tells the tale largely through Maggie's slowly widening awareness, as she begins to accept what she has sensed and to act on it. The famous golden bowl itself, a flawed object bought in a London shop, becomes the emblem of a marriage that looks perfect and is not. This volume completes the arc begun in Volume I.
42632-private-letters-of-edward-gibbon-1:
Private Letters of Edward Gibbon, volume two, gathers the letters of the great historian from 1753 to 1794. The Earl of Sheffield wrote the introduction, and Prothero edited the set, printed at London in 1896. A silhouette portrait of Gibbon stands at the front of this volume, and the letters run on from number 418.

The first letter here, to his stepmother in July 1781, reports his election for Lymington in his absence. Gibbon jokes that he is already so old a member that he complains of the heat and length of the session. He tells of hiring a small pleasant house at Brighthelmstone for the summer, hoping sea air, light study, and good company will roll the season away.
42732-the-englishman-in-china-during-the:
The Englishman in China during the Victorian Era, by Alexander Michie, tells the age through the career of Sir Rutherford Alcock. A saying of Confucius on reciprocity heads the first chapter shown here. A portrait of Alcock at the age of thirty four fronts the passage. The golden rule quoted is the measure of the whole study.

Michie uses one consul’s life to frame the British place in China. Trade, treaties, and the clash of customs fill the background. Alcock stood at the heart of that world for decades. The book asks what Englishmen did in China, and how the Chinese bore it. Reciprocity, doing not to others what you hate done to you, is set as the test. The work is history with a moral edge.
42844-life-and-correspondence-of-david-h:
Life and Correspondence of David Hume, volume two, was printed in 1846. William Tait issued it at Edinburgh. John Hill Burton wrote the life, an advocate by profession. His sources were papers bequeathed by Hume's nephew to the Royal Society of Edinburgh, and other originals. A portrait from a bust fronts the volume. Facsimiles show a page of the History of England and a letter from Rousseau. Chapter ten covers 1756 to 1759. Contents promise the second Stuart volume and Hume's apologies on religion. The Four Dissertations and two suppressed ones follow.

Home's Douglas, the History of the Tudors, and Smith's Theory of Moral Sentiments fill the same chapter. Chapter eleven, 1760 to 1762, treats Ossian's poems and Madame de Boufflers. Burton prints letters beside the narrative, letting Hume speak in his own hand.
42857-journals-of-dorothy-wordsworth-vol:
William Knight edited the Journals of Dorothy Wordsworth, and this second volume was printed in London in 1897. A portrait of William Wordsworth fronts the book, with Grasmere Church and churchyard on the title page. The contents open with the Recollections of a Tour Made in Scotland in 1803, carried on from the first volume. A journal of a mountain ramble by Dorothy and William in November 1805 follows.

Extracts from her journal of a tour on the continent in 1820 and from a Scottish tour of 1822 come next. Mary Wordsworth's journal of a tour in Belgium in 1823 and Dorothy's tour in the Isle of Man in 1828 close the list. The Scottish pages name Loch Katrine, the Highland girl of the poem, and the parting with Coleridge. Glen Coe, Loch Awe, Killin, and the falls of Moness fill the day-by-day heads.
42906-great-porter-square-a-mystery-v-2:
Farjeon wrote Great Porter Square: A Mystery, a novel in three volumes printed at London in eighteen eighty-five, and this is volume two. It opens at chapter twenty, deep in the tale. A newspaper, the Evening Moon, ends its account of a London murder. Talk turns to Lydia Holdfast, a childlike and flighty young wife.

Much of the volume is given to statements by the Holdfast family. Frederick Holdfast sets out his side at length, part after part, and Becky answers her lover's statement in turn. Richard Manx courts Becky, and a writer who signs as Justice writes to the Evening Moon. At the core sits a wife who waits for a husband who does not come home, and fears some harm has met him far away.
43261-the-broken-font-a-story-of-the-civ:
The Broken Font is a story of the English Civil War, printed in London in 1836. This text is volume one of two. The author, unnamed on the title page, also wrote Tales of the Wars of Our Times. His preface says no one can study that period without feeling for both parties in the great quarrel.

Until the sword was drawn, he writes, generous Royalists stood a faint line apart from the best men of the Parliament party. His tale dwells on the miseries and persecutions the war brought on private families. The clergy and their households suffer most in his pages. The novel looks back at the seventeenth century with a healer's temper.
43262-the-broken-font-a-story-of-the-civ:
A tale of the Civil War in England fills volume two of The Broken Font. The book came out in London in 1836. Its author had wrote Tales of the Wars of Our Times. The tale turns on Katharine Heywood and Jane Lambert. Donne's verse heads the first part here.

Jane has borne risk and shame for a task Katharine asked of her. Katharine sees she must clear Jane's name with Juxon. She hopes to join two fine hearts made for each other. Her own grief and pride must yield to that duty. Court life, love, and war press on each choice in the tale.
43271-the-works-of-alexander-pope-volume:
Alexander Pope's works fill this second volume of a new edition in ten volumes, printed in London in 1871. Whitwell Elwin adds introductions and notes. The set holds several hundred letters never printed before and other new materials, gathered in part by John Wilson Croker. This volume is the second of the poetry, with portraits and other pictures.

The volume opens with An Essay on Criticism, written in the year 1709. Notes trace its first printing in 1711, when a thousand copies were made. The publisher Lewis was a Roman Catholic and an old schoolfellow of the poet. Second, third, and fourth editions all came within two years, and the rights changed hands in 1716.
43317-lord-lyons-a-record-of-british-dip:
Newton wrote the life of Lord Lyons as a record of British diplomacy, and Edward Arnold of London published the first volume in 1913. Lyons entered the service in 1839 as an unpaid attaché at Athens. Posts at Rome and Florence followed, and in 1858 he went as minister to Washington.

The heart of the volume is the American Civil War. Then came the crisis of the Trent. Two envoys of the South were seized from a British ship, and war between the two lands hung in the air. Lyons kept a complete reserve and urged the defence of Canada. The men were set free, and the American secretary owned his care. Later chapters treat consuls, cruisers, and the strain of the war years.
43498-flora-adair-or-love-works-wonders-:
The first volume of a novel by A M Donelan. Chapman and Hall published it at London in 1867. Its subtitle promises that love works wonders. A Latin tag from Hosea heads the title page. It speaks of drawing men with cords of charity. Rome supplies the opening scene.

A March morning on the Corso starts the story. Mrs Adair sits working in a sunlit drawing room. Sorrow has marked her once-beautiful face deeply. Devotedness, the narrator says, sums up her whole character. Her youngest daughter Flora is her remaining treasure. The elder children married and drifted from her daily life. Flora herself is no conventional beauty, the narrator confesses. Good figure, broad forehead, and dark blue eyes must serve.
43499-flora-adair-or-love-works-wonders-:
Flora Adair; or, Love Works Wonders is a novel by Donelan, of which this file holds the second volume of two. Chapman and Hall published it in London in 1867. A Latin motto from the prophet Osee stands on the title page: I will draw them with cords of Adam, with the bands of love.

The volume opens in Venice, inside the mind of Earnscliffe. Would Flora have spoken so, he wonders, had she known that, although he was in Venice, all his thoughts were occupied about her? The morning after their starlight walk finds him depressed in proportion to his happiness. But he reminds himself that he knew such an evening long ago. The woman he loved and trusted then brought him only misery. Life, hope and faith were blighted by her, and he asks whether it is not worse than folly to believe in a woman again.
43589-the-life-of-isaac-ingalls-stevens-:
A biography of Isaac Ingalls Stevens by his son Hazard Stevens. Houghton, Mifflin and Company published it in 1900. Maps and illustrations fill the two volumes. The son dedicates the record to the young men of America. His sources include family papers, diaries, and letters. Army and Indian affairs reports add official detail. The elder Stevens was soldier, engineer, and surveyor. He also became the first governor of Washington Territory.

This volume covers the early life first. Mexican War service and Coast Survey years follow. The great Pacific railroad survey takes up the later chapters. A second volume stands on Project Gutenberg as well. It carries the story through the governorship. The Civil War, where Stevens died a general, closes it.
43678-anne-of-geierstein-or-the-maiden-o:
Anne of Geierstein, or The Maiden of the Mist, is a late novel by Sir Walter Scott, set in Switzerland and Burgundy in the days of Charles the Bold. This first volume belongs to the Border Edition of the Waverley Novels, with an opening essay and notes by Andrew Lang, published in London in 1894.

Lang is frank about the book's standing. He writes that with The Fair Maid of Perth readers take leave of Scott at his best, and that Anne of Geierstein was no favourite of the author's own. The edition carries ten etchings and is dedicated to Scott's great-granddaughter and her children at Abbotsford. The tale itself follows young Arthur de Vere among the Swiss cantons, the secret courts of Westphalia, and the court of the Duke of Burgundy.
43893-my-miscellanies-vol-1-of-2:
Wilkie Collins gathered his short pieces in My Miscellanies, in two volumes from a London house in 1863. Collins was then famed for The Woman in White and No Name. Most of these papers first ran in Household Words and in the early years of All the Year Round, the journals led by Dickens.

Collins says he picked and revised the best of them, and set them in contrast so the book shows all his short forms. Groups bear heads such as Sketches of Character and Social Grievances. His aim was a light, plain touch, like a letter or friendly talk, not a lay sermon from a crowded pulpit. He left out many more pieces than he kept, by his own count.
43991-a-hand-book-to-the-primates-volume:
Henry Forbes's A Hand-Book to the Primates, volume one, was published by Allen at London in 1894 in Allen's Naturalist's Library. Bowdler Sharpe edited the series and wrote the preface. Sharpe notes that knowledge of the animals has grown so much since Jardine's monkey volume of sixty years before that Forbes could not compress it into one volume. Forbes had years of study and had seen many species in a state of nature.

The old Jardine plates were mere caricatures of monkeys, Sharpe says, so a new set was drawn by Keulemans. Volume one covers the lemurs and the monkeys as far as the macaques; volume two continues with the rest of the monkeys and the apes, plus the order's geographical distribution. Forbes directed the Liverpool museums and wrote A Naturalist's Wanderings in the Eastern Archipelago.
43992-a-hand-book-to-the-primates-volume:
Henry Forbes wrote A Hand-book to the Primates, volume two, in 1897. Forbes directed Liverpool's museums then. Lloyd's Natural History, edited by Sharpe, carries the book. Edward Lloyd at London put out this second volume. A macaque plate stands near its front.

The preface hopes the distribution part interests readers. Museum material is meagre for habitats, he owns. The introduction turns to extinct forms beside the living ones. Forbes reviews known monkeys as fully as he can. Enormous work remains on the primates, he says. Sportsmen shrink from collecting monkeys, he notes. To shoot one feels like killing a sort of relation, he writes. Old naturalists spoke loosely of ranges, he complains. Brazil might mean any of South America to them. Forbes gives the order a handbook of ranges and kinds.
4402-the-shaving-of-shagpat-an-arabian-e:
George Meredith wrote this Arabian entertainment around Shibli Bagarag, nephew of a barber, whose task is to shave the enchanted Shagpat. This second volume opens with the betrothal of Shibli to Noorna bin Noorka, daughter of the vizier Feshnavat, who smiles gravely at the bargain. Noorna declares herself content with her fair youth of flowing speech.

Later tales in the volume include the punishment of Shahpesh the Persian, the genie Karaz, the well of Paravid, the horse Garraveen, and the talking hawk. Meredith tells the whole in a rich, mock-oriental prose, full of nested stories. The volume carries the quest forward, with magic, wit, and betrothal at its heart.
44060-the-mystery-of-carlitos-mexican-my:
Helen Randolph wrote The Mystery of Carlitos for young readers. The Saalfield Publishing Company issued it in 1936. The book stands second in her Mexican Mystery Series. The Secret of Casa Grande came first in that line. Crossed Trails in Mexico followed it. Twenty chapters carry this tale.

The Mysterious Blue-Eyed Boy opens the action. Neighbors in the Cave and an unwelcome visitor follow. Footprints and a mysterious light build the hunt. Jo Ann watches a man and Carlitos by a fire. That scene forms the book's frontispiece. A soiled, yellowed envelope turns the plot mid-book. The pinata party and a dangerous trail come late. Prisoners and a daring plan raise the stakes. The New Hope Mine closes the case. Cheerful border mystery fare gave girl readers caves, mines, and a lost boy south of the line.
4407-the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-volum:
Book Two of George Meredith's Ordeal of Richard Feverel opens with a public duty: the laying of ghosts. The mystery of the apparition that frightened little Clare was never solved at Raynham, where dread walked the abbey. Meredith takes up the ghost as a figure for the fears haunting his hero's youth.

The book's chapters run from the blossoming season and the magnetic age through an attraction, Ferdinand and Miranda, and the unmasking of Master Ripton Thompson. Good wine and good blood follow, with the system encountering the wild oats. Richard's boyhood ends here, and the ordeal of love begins.
4414-sandra-belloni-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Sandra Belloni opens on a memorable evening at half past nine, when five-and-twenty stout young fellows of the Hillford Club march to Ipley Common. Prize-winners, wrestlers, boxers, and topers set out together, and the scene gives Meredith's comedy its rough, male chorus.

The book's chapters promise the magnanimity in beer, sentiment and passion taking the disease of love, a short discourse on puppets, the Besworth question, and Wilfrid's exhibition of treachery. Emilia, the singer at the novel's heart, moves among the ladies of Brookfield toward resolve. This volume deepens the love plot and the social satire.
44143-lord-lyons-a-record-of-british-dip:
Lord Lyons: A Record of British Diplomacy, volume two, by Lord Newton, was published by Edward Arnold in London in 1913, with portraits. Lyons was Britain's ambassador in Paris through the early Third Republic. This volume's contents open in 1871 with Thiers as chief of the executive. Negotiations for a new Anglo-French commercial treaty head the chapter.

The following chapters treat Marshal MacMahon's presidency from 1873 to 1875, and then the Eastern Question of 1876 to 1878. Franco-German relations, the war scare of 1875, and Bismarck's confidences to Lord Odo Russell fill the pages. The rumoured sale of the Khedive's Suez Canal shares appears, and their purchase by the British government. The contents run on to the Congress of Berlin: Lord Derby's resignation, Lord Salisbury's appointment, and his circular of April 1878. An Anglo-Turkish convention and the inquiry about French designs on Tunis close the story.
44205-gregg-s-commerce-of-the-prairies-1:
Josiah Gregg's Commerce of the Prairies appears here as Part Two. The Arthur H Clark Company issued it at Cleveland in 1905. Reuben Gold Thwaites edited the Early Western Travels line. Gregg's book forms Volume Twenty of that line. Its full tale tells of a Santa Fe trader. Eight trips across the great western prairies fill it.

Gregg spent near nine years in northern Mexico. Part Two holds chapters twelve to sixteen of volume one. All of the first book's second volume joins them. A front plate shows an Indian alarm on the Cimarron River. A map of inner northern Mexico faces the text. Camp Comanche and a prairie dog town get cuts. A medal of Our Lady of Guadalupe shows too. A trader's own journal, the book maps the Santa Fe road as men lived it in the 1830s.
4422-rhoda-fleming-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Rhoda Fleming opens at the theatre, where Edward's club engagement that evening was with his unlucky cousin Algernon. He wants a dinner and five pounds or so, a hazy margin that shows a borrower dancing on fortune's edge. The scene sets the novel's money worries in motion.

The book's chapters follow the farmer speaking, Rhoda and Robert, a visit to Wrexby Hall, Fairly Park, and a yeoman of the old breed. An assembly at the Pilot Inn and Robert smitten low follow, with Mrs. Lovell showing a tame brute. Rhoda's steadfastness anchors a story of sisters, seduction, and the price of honor.
44247-anne-of-geierstein-or-the-maiden-o:
Anne of Geierstein, or The Maiden of the Mist, volume two, is a Waverley novel by Sir Walter Scott, in the Border Edition printed in London by John C Nimmo in 1894. The set runs to forty eight volumes, and this is volume forty four. Andrew Lang wrote the opening essays and notes, with rights held. Ten etchings fill the volume, drawn and etched by R de Los Rios.

The plate list names King Rene at the front, then The Secret Tribunal, Arthur Before the Queen, and The Defiance. The Funeral of the Queen closes the set. The tale stands in the Swiss wars of the fourteen hundreds, with Anne and young Arthur de Vere amid courts and secret courts. Lang notes guide the reader through Scott history and romance. Scott fans get a rich late novel.
4428-evan-harrington-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Evan Harrington opens at the Aurora, a rare old tavern with the smell of good food and long custom. The house, born when taverns served as clubs for steady men, has lived on its bachelor regulars. For a month it has known dismay and sorrow over its most constant patron.

The book's chapters introduce an eccentric, place the countess in low society, and send the gentleman on the road again. Doings at an inn, ale shown to have one quality of wine, and the match of Fallowfield against Beckley follow. Evan, son of a tailor, moves among gentry who do not know his birth, and comedy follows.
44280-the-life-of-the-rev-george-whitefi:
The Life of George Whitefield, volume one of two, is a biography by Tyerman. Whitefield, of Pembroke College, Oxford, was the great evangelist of his age. An engraving by Cochran shows him aged twenty four at his prime youth. Ads for Tyerman life of Wesley front this cheaper edition of the work.

Tyerman had written lives of Samuel Wesley and of John Wesley in full. Review quotes praise his Wesley volumes as painstaking, veracious, and trustworthy records. The same hand now traces Whitefield preaching career and times in two volumes. Portraits in cloth binding at seven shillings sixpence a volume sold the set. Methodist and evangelical readers were its clear intended buyers.
4436-vittoria-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Vittoria opens in Verona, where a lieutenant reads a letter as he clatters through quiet streets toward the Porta Tosa. The writer is glad their old affection is not dead, yet she cannot consent to meet him yet. She would rather they should not meet, and the letter breaks into reproach.

The book's chapters follow the Pope's mouth, Laura Piaveni, the bronze butterfly, and the plot of Signor Antonio. Vittoria, singer and patriot in the Italian revolt against Austria, moves between love and conspiracy. This volume carries her from Verona's streets toward the larger drama of revolution.
44437-the-war-with-mexico-volume-1-of-2:
Justin H Smith writes the standard history in The War with Mexico, volume one of two, from the Macmillan Company of New York in 1919. Smith was formerly professor of modern history at Dartmouth College. He had written The Annexation of Texas, Our Struggle for the Fourteenth Colony, and Arnold's March from Cambridge to Quebec.

A publisher's card for the Texas book fronts this one, calling it the only work attempting to deal thoroughly with that affair. The war volume itself rests on the same deep digging in records. Two volumes carry the conflict; this first sets the stage and opens the campaigns.
44438-the-war-with-mexico-volume-2-of-2:
A past of the war with Mexico fills two books, this being the last. Its back notes are vast, and three kinds of notes crowd the text. Star notes first sat as page foot notes in the print form. Those now stand just past the words they gloss in this text. Count notes point to a great notes part at the book's back.

Those back notes bear part counts set by the part they serve. A war of march, siege, and hard field work fills the tale. Treaties and grub, chiefs and ranks, fill its long claim lists. Maps and files ground the grave work of the past man. War past fans get a full, sourced store in two books. Each claim bears its proof.
4445-the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-vo:
Book Two of George Meredith's Adventures of Harry Richmond opens with a free life on the road. Harry wakes very early, kindly taken to his pillow, with an arm round his rest. The boy's adventures widen from Dipwell Farm to the highway. Janet Ilchester and an evening with Captain Bulsted come along the way.

An expedition follows, with the great fog and the fire at midnight. A voyage bound on the Priscilla follows that. Harry conducts learned arguments with the captain and meets old friends. His father, the adventurer, draws nearer through these chapters, and the novel's comedy of fortune gathers speed.
44486-dodo-a-detail-of-the-day-volumes-1:
Dodo, a Detail of the Day, by E F Benson, was printed in London by Methuen in 1893, in two volumes, and the hosted text holds the fourth edition. A grim quote on truth and falsehood as boats on a sea heads the first chapter.

Benson opens with poets who swear there was once a Golden Age of fine weather. He doubts the age can come back till the weather stays golden for good. He notes that fine days lift body, mind, and spirit in London as much as in any old tale. The novel then turns to its heroine and her set, with cool rides in the Row and chairs under park trees. Readers meet a smart, sly tale of high society in the 1890s.
44517-points-of-humour-part-1-of-2:
Points of Humour, part one, was published in London in 1823 by Baldwin of Newgate Street. The writer stays anonymous; the designs are George Cruikshank's, ten engravings on copper and twelve wood cuts. A speech from Shakespeare, let me play the fool, heads the title page, and the preface is disarmingly plain about the book's making.

The literary part, it says, is of humble pretensions. Its one object was to select or invent incidents amusing in themselves that also gave scope to the artist, and such subjects are rarer than they look. A point of wit cannot be pictured, and the humour of many a laughable story vanishes under the pencil. Only humour of situation holds. All the effect, the writer insists, belongs to Cruikshank; the writer merely suggested the materials.
44518-points-of-humour-part-2-of-2:
George Cruikshank drew the designs for this second set of humorous points, published in 1824. Ten engravings on copper and twelve wood cuts fill the part, the title page states. A merry speech from Shakespeare, urging mirth and laughter on old wrinkles, stands as the book's motto.

The best preface to this set is the former set, the preface jokes at the start. That set disposed readers' muscles for a cackling sound, heart-food to Cruikshank, it says. One worthy gentleman in Newgate Street has laughed over the points already, we are told, wedged among piles of books opposite the prison.
4454-beauchamp-s-career-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career opens with Captain Baskelett, while England bustles over an extinguished war and counts its cost. Nevil Beauchamp, naval officer turned radical, moves through a country arguing about empire, honor, and the price of glory. His career will test every loyalty he holds.

The book's chapters bring an interview with the infamous Dr. Shrapnel, a superfine conscience, and the leading article of Mr. Timothy Turbot. Cecilia Halkett appears, with a partial display of Beauchamp in his colours, his friend and foe, and the act of canvassing. Politics, love, and principle collide in Meredith's most political novel.
44553-letters-of-samuel-taylor-coleridge:
Volume one of the Letters of Samuel Taylor Coleridge gathers the poet's correspondence, edited by his grandson Ernest Hartley Coleridge. It was published in London by William Heinemann in 1895. A portrait stands at the front. The editor thanks a roll of helpers in his preface. Leslie Stephen and Dr Garnett of the British Museum stand in the list. Of Dykes Campbell he says no praise is too high. Campbell knew the tale of Coleridge and his friends past any man then living.

The letters run from the poet's youth toward his great years of work and friendship. They show the mind that made the Ancient Mariner and Kubla Khan at its daily tasks. Plans, debts, opium, and high talk of poetry fill the pages in their turns. The notes place each letter in its setting. The set is a chief source for the life of Coleridge.
44554-letters-of-samuel-taylor-coleridge:
Ernest Hartley Coleridge edited the Letters of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, published by Heinemann in London in 1895. This file holds the second volume. It opens with a long absence, the years 1804 to 1806, when Coleridge travelled in Malta and Italy in failing health. The letters run in numbered order, each with its date and recipient. Thomas Poole, Robert Southey, and the Wordsworth family receive the first letters of the volume.

Coleridge writes to his wife, to Daniel Stuart of the Morning Post, to Richard Sharp, and to many others. The editor's notes give the sources, since many letters had appeared in print before, in lives of Wordsworth and in memoirs of Poole. The correspondence of these years shows the poet as journalist, critic, and friend, struggling with illness and opium while his mind worked at full stretch. Together the two volumes form the standard Victorian edition of Coleridge's letters.
44571-points-of-humour-part-1-of-2:
Points of Humour is a comic picture book with designs by George Cruikshank, published in London in 1823. This text is part one of two. It holds ten engravings on copper and twelve woodcuts. The title page quotes Shakespeare on playing the fool with mirth and laughter. The book sold for eight shillings.

The preface admits the literary part has humble pretensions. Its one aim, it says, was to choose or invent incidents that amuse in themselves. They also had to give scope to the artist's peculiar talents. Cruikshank's plates of comic scenes were the real draw. Such books of humour, pairing short tales with caricature plates, were a staple of Regency London.
44572-points-of-humour-part-2-of-2:
Points of Humour, part two of two, is a collection of pieces illustrated from designs by George Cruikshank: ten engravings on copper and twelve wood cuts. Robins and Baldwyn published it in London in 1824. A Shakespeare motto heads it: let me play the fool, and let my liver rather heat with wine than my heart cool with groans.

The preface declines argument. The best preface to this set, it says, is the former set, which disposed readers' muscles for a cackling sound that is heart food to Cruikshank. One gentleman, the bookseller opposite Newgate prison, has laughed over the points since, his face lit with sunshine in a dark shop. The compiler adds that he followed a critic's hint and drew part of his material from the author richest in the humour of situation. Fielding, he judges, is less suited to Cruikshank's pencil than his successor in that walk.
44588-john-inglesant-a-romance-volume-2-:
John Inglesant, volume two, was written by John Henry Shorthouse. Macmillan published the romance in London in 1881. A Greek text from the epistles heads the title page. Chapter one opens abroad: Inglesant travels to Marseilles, then by packet boat to Genoa. The approach by sea delights him. Marble palace streets, thronged squares, and picture galleries fill his mind with astonishment. He stays some time, with letters to Jesuit fathers there. Under their guidance he begins an education in art.

Church music at London and Oxford had been but a prelude, he finds. For whole hours he kneels at mass, lost in its variety. He improves fast on the violin and masters the viola d'amore, a wire-strung viol of soft tone. From Genoa he goes to Sienna, where the dialect was held pure for foreigners to learn.
4462-the-tragic-comedians-a-study-in-a-w:
Book Two of George Meredith's Tragic Comedians opens on the plains, where the hero comes down to his love on the second day. As usual when they meet, it seems they have not parted, and his animation makes it so. His warmth, like summer morning sunlight, strikes through her blood and disperses her hesitating strangeness.

The novel studies a well-known story, the love of Ferdinand Lassalle and Helene von Donniges, retold as comedy and tragedy together. Meredith watches two strong wills, girlish dread, and the steps taken and regretted. This volume deepens the courtship, as messages from a distance give way to meetings that thrill and unsettle.
4466-diana-of-the-crossways-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Diana of the Crossways opens with Redworth laughing for gladness of heart. A position of delicacy for a lady and gentleman is met in simple fashion, without hurt to either. The conflict of the night follows, with a journey in a chariot. Dialogue and a small incident on the road fill the ride.

Between Emma and Diana, the first days of her probation follow. Glimpses of Diana under her cloud before the world follow those. Percy Dacier is introduced, with a midnight bell and a scene of early morning. The Princess Egeria closes the book. Diana, witty heroine and novelist, moves through London society toward scandal and survival.
4472-one-of-our-conquerors-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's One of Our Conquerors opens on the dumbness possible in a household with one heart. Two who live in union are expected to share everything, Meredith notes, especially when they love one another and share a cause. Yet reserves on important matters persist, and the chapter probes that silence.

Later chapters bring the latest of Mrs. Burman, a stage on the drive to Paris, and a patriot abroad. Skepsey's misconduct and its effect on Nataly follow, with a young maid's imaginings and suitors for the hand of Nesta Victoria. Victor Radnor, the conqueror of the title, and Nataly move through London toward a reckoning.
44721-the-pillars-of-the-house-or-under-:
Charlotte Yonge ends a family tale in The Pillars of the House, or Under Wode, Under Rode, volume 2 of 2. Macmillan of London prints the book in 1875. Yonge had writ The Heir of Redclyffe. Chapters run from 24 to the conclusion.

The heads keep her fond, allusive style. Family Ghools leads, then Don Giovanni and Transmutation. Stars Gratis, Brynhild, and The Sculptor stand in the run. The Vicar of Vale Leston and The Old Squire and the New ground the tale in parish life. Possession, invasions, and four years of change build to Shattered Pillars near the end. Chapter 24 opens with a verse on Love as a careless child.
