44741-the-life-of-george-cruikshank-in-t:
Blanchard Jerrold's Life of George Cruikshank, in two epochs, appeared in two volumes in 1882; this is volume one. Tributes from Ruskin, Rossetti, and Sala front the book, Ruskin praising the Grimm etchings next to Rembrandt. The dedication to Gustave Dore recalls an evening at Boulogne some twenty-five years earlier. Waiting for the Queen with Herbert Ingram of the Illustrated London News, Dore filled a vast sheet with fancies, squibs, and caricatures. Ingram carried the sheet off the next morning before they were up.

Jerrold links Dore's genius to Cruikshank's, the illustrator of Grimm, of Oliver Twist, and of Falstaff. The preface promises Cruikshank as he lived and moved and worked, not as a mere list of plates. Numerous illustrations fill the volume. The two epochs of the title divide the artist's long career into its early and later periods.
44742-the-life-of-george-cruikshank-in-t:
The Life of George Cruikshank, volume two of two, is a life book by Blanchard Jerrold. It came out in eighteen eighty-two. This book takes up the first age of the draw mans life at its part on a jest year book. A town press man set that book on foot in eighteen thirty-five and hired the hand to draw it. It was a glad fit for the more plain side of his mood and gift, Jerrold says.

Past past ten years and nine that book ran, and it gave him a sure wage in a life of shift luck. Its near two hundred and fifty cuts hold some of his best watch work and his most keen shows of folly and cant. Great pens of the age lent their aid to its text. His wit stayed as fresh in the last book as in the first.
4478-lord-ormont-and-his-aminta-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Lord Ormont and His Aminta opens in Aminta's amber dressing-room, in a mood of languor. Mrs. Nargett Pagnell sadly notes a long month of separation, and begs her niece for an exact statement of the situation, items will do. Then she slips into prattle and holds the field, a worthy, good, intolerable woman.

The book's chapters show effects of a prattler's doses, Mrs. Lawrence Finchley, and a flash of the bruised warrior. A short passage in the game played by two follows, with the secretary taken as an antidote. Lord Ormont, old soldier, and Aminta, his young wife, play their marriage game under society's eyes.
4484-the-amazing-marriage-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Amazing Marriage opens with small causes, as a clock sounds a late morning hour of the night. Gower Woodseer stands at his hotel door, after parting from Fleetwood and his merry company, under stars low over a ridge of pines. Beneath the roof lies the household whose fortunes the novel follows.

The book's chapters follow the prisoner of his word, Henrietta's letter on the great event, and an irruption of Mistress Gossip. A pendant, the opening stage of the honeymoon, and a bride from foreign parts tasting old England follow. Down Whitechapel way and the girl Madge close the book, as marriage, gossip, and money entangle.
44875-the-cruise-of-the-midge-vol-1-of-2:
Michael Scott, the author of Tom Cringle's Log, wrote this sea tale in two volumes, printed at Edinburgh and London in 1836. The part held here is volume one. An epigraph from Pope's Essay on Man heads the title: reason the card, but passion the gale. The teller was born an Irishman of an Irish mother and schooled in Scotland, his father's land.

His father sailed his own ship in the Virginia trade, and the boy served four years in an uncle's counting-house. Chapters promise the Midge in a hornet's nest, the tale of Serjeant Quacco, the wreck of the Hermes, and the destruction of a slaver. Gambling, yarn spinning, and Cape missionaries fill the cruise.
4490-celt-and-saxon-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Celt and Saxon opens with Miss Mattock, as Mrs. Adister O'Donnell faces the task of composing epistles. She dislikes letter writing, Meredith notes, because she cannot conceive an idea disconnected from her letter's main theme, and she regards words independent of ideas as conjuring. Her native superiority despises the art.

The book's chapters follow a dinner party, Rockney, and the Mattock family, with the great Mr. Bull and Celtic and Saxon views of him. Something of Richard Rockney follows, with crossing the Rubicon, Captain Con's letter, and Mars convalescent. Meredith's unfinished novel of nations continues its witty comparison of Irish and English minds.
44977-the-complete-poems-of-sir-john-dav:
The Complete Poems of Sir John Davies, volume one of two, was edited by Alexander Grosart with a memorial introduction and notes. Chatto and Windus issued it in London in eighteen seventy-six. The edition belongs to the Early English Poets series. Grosart dedicates it to Gladstone, repeating a dedication first made when the poems appeared in the Fuller Worthies' Library.

In his letter, the editor praises Davies as many men in one: a farsighted and practical statesman, a philosophic thinker, an orator, a lawyer, and a poet. In Gladstone, he says, all Britain, Europe, and America recognize the elder man's equal. The earlier collection had met so instant a welcome, Grosart adds, that demands for copies soon outran the printing.
44978-the-complete-poems-of-sir-john-dav:
Complete Poems of Sir John Davies, volume two of two, is an edition by Alexander Grosart. Chatto and Windus of London issued the Early English Poets volume in 1876. Grosart supplies a memorial introduction and notes for the Elizabethan poet works. Contents open with the epigrammes, many printed here for the first time.

Short Latin titled squibs run on gulls, books, and named butts of wit in turn. Ad Musam heads the list, followed by pieces on Rufus, Quintus, and others. Davies, lawyer poet of the dance of life, shows his sharp court wit here. Scholars gain the minor verse of a major metaphysical age figure in full.
44994-a-lady-s-tour-in-corsica-vol-2-of-:
Gertrude Forde wrote a lady's tour in Corsica in two volumes, with volume two printed at London in 1880. En route for Bavella, with an eccentric landlord, opens the road. The forest of Bavella, Sartene, and the Lion of Roccapina follow. Bonifacio and its curiosities take two chapters. A sermon by the wayside leads toward Vico.

Evisa among the hills, giant forests, and Porto, La Piana, and Carghese fill the middle. From Carghese to Ajaccio, Bocognano bugbears, and the forest of Sorba come next. The Inzecca, the last of Antonio, and to Bastia from Corte lead to a history of Corsica at the close. Sainte Lucie di Tallano is the halting place for the forest of Bavella, she begins. Sollenzara on the east coast is dirty and unwholesome, she warns. A sharp eyed lady rides the wild island end to end.
45029-on-the-yukon-trail-radio-phone-boy:
James Craig's On the Yukon Trail was published by Reilly and Lee in 1922, second in the Radio-Phone Boys stories. Curlie Carson, a boy with the most perfect radio ears known to the service, works for the United States Bureau of Secret Service of the Air. The book opens in a tent on the Valdez Glacier, a gale bulging the walls. Joe Marion, Curlie's pal from earlier adventures, shivers in his sleeping bag on the ice. Their errand is dangerous: a man of great resources is sabotaging the radiophone in Alaska.

His aim is to imperil Munson, a great Arctic explorer, by breaking up his radiophone messages. Twenty-seven chapters carry the boys from The Whisper from Afar to Diamonds and Other Things. Joe goes missing; Curlie vanishes; a bear charges; a wild stampede breaks out.
45313-a-system-of-practical-medicine-by-:
A System of Practical Medicine, volume two, was published at Philadelphia in 1885. Lea Brothers issued the set, written by American authors. William Pepper edited the work, with Louis Starr assisting. Pepper held the chair of medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. This volume covers general diseases continued, then diseases of digestion. Rheumatism opens the book, by Howard. Gout, rickets, scurvy, and purpura follow, each by a named hand. Diabetes and hereditary syphilis close the first part.

The digestive half starts with the mouth and tongue. Cohen treats the tonsils, throat, and gullet in turn. Welch writes five pieces on the stomach: ulcer, cancer, bleeding, widening, and lesser ills. Johnston treats indigestion of the bowels and colic. The volume shows American medicine in full textbook form.
4535-sylvia-s-lovers-volume-2:
Elizabeth Gaskell's Sylvia's Lovers continues in this second volume, covering chapters fifteen through twenty-nine. Philip Hepburn, who went to bed with humble, penitent gratitude after a sudden turn from despair to hope, now faces a difficult question, an engagement, and rejected warnings. Chapters trace an eddy in love's current, an important mission, love and loss, a rejected suitor, and deepening shadows.

Retaliation, brief rejoicing, coming troubles, a dreary vigil, gloomy days, an ordeal, and wedding raiment follow in quick succession. Readers of this middle volume watch Sylvia's courtship tighten and darken, as promises made in hope meet the hard facts of war, work, and pride. It should be read after volume one, since its power depends on knowing Monkshaven, Sylvia, and the rivals already in play.
45394-the-life-of-sir-humphry-davy-bart-:
Life of Sir Humphry Davy, volume one of two, is a biography by John Ayrton Paris. Paris, a physician and fellow of the Royal Society, knew the great chemist world. The second volume stands as a companion Gutenberg ebook to this first part. Davy rose from a Penzance apothecary shop to the head of British science.

Miners safety lamp, laughing gas, and new metals made his name across Europe. Poetry and chemistry shared his youth, and Paris tells both sides of the man. Royal Institution lectures made Davy the most famous science showman of his age. Science biography of the period keeps this life as a standard portrait.
45456-history-of-julius-c-sar-vol-1-of-2:
Napoleon the Third wrote this history of Julius Caesar, of which this copy is volume one. The volume was entered at the Ministry of the Interior in March 1865, the notice states. Sanctioned editions in French, English, German and American issues are listed by their publishers at the front.

Harper in New York carried the authorized American edition, that notice records for buyers. An emperor who had risen by a coup studied the Roman who crossed the Rubicon before him. Battles, laws and the fall of the republic fill his learned volumes, written with maps and scholars at hand in the Tuileries palace library.
45532-history-of-julius-c-sar-vol-2-of-2:
History of Julius Caesar, volume two, covers the wars in Gaul in the life of Caesar written by the Emperor Napoleon the Third of France. Harper and Brothers published the English edition in New York in 1866.

A publisher's note recalls the sovereigns who studied Caesar before Napoleon. Charles the Eighth of France admired the Commentaries, and a monk's French version was made for him in 1480. Charles the Fifth filled his copy with notes in his own hand and sent a mission into France to study the campaigns on the ground. The Sultan Soliman the Second gathered copies from all over Europe and had the work turned into Turkish for his daily reading. The volume then gives Napoleon's own account of the conquest of Gaul, campaign by campaign.
45763-the-new-england-historical-genealo:
The New England Historical and Genealogical Register came out four times a year at Boston. Volume one, number two, is dated April 1847. Drake published the journal for the society behind it, and Cogswell edited the issue. Its pages mix lives, letters, lists, and family lines.

A memoir of Samuel Sewall, chief justice of Massachusetts Bay, leads the number. His own letter follows, with one from Gookin. Lists name the folk who sailed on the Golden Hind and the Speedwell, and all the ministers of Boston. Other pages treat the first settlers, capital offences, and long lives. Family lines for the Cotton, Butler, and Minot houses close the set.
45801-the-house-of-defence-v-2:
The House of Defence, Volume Two, is the last half of a tale by Benson. The host print is one of a set of the tales of Britain for the lands past the sea. That set may not be brought to Britain or her far lands. Each book of the set is sold on its own, the front says. The first words of the host text are not the tale at all.

Those words name the most late books of the set, with the date of the mid year of nineteen seven. A tale of the days of a star stone by Wells heads that list of trade words. That work is call a new study of days to come and of things as they should be, in the style of a famed hand of France.
45890-a-decade-of-italian-women-vol-1-of:
A Decade of Italian Women is a work in two volumes by T. Adolphus Trollope. The first volume came out in London in 1859 from Chapman and Hall. Trollope was also the author of a book on the girlhood of Catherine de' Medici. A picture of Vittoria Colonna, from a painting in the Colonna Gallery at Rome, stands at the front of the book.

In his preface Trollope sets out a test of a social order. The degree to which a society has found the right place of woman, and put her in it, marks how far it has come in the arts of civil life, he holds. The volume is the first half of a work that treats the lives of Italian women as its theme. The text as shown opens with that broad claim and its defence.
45891-a-decade-of-italian-women-vol-2-of:
Volume two of T Adolphus Trollope's Decade of Italian Women, published at London in 1859, by the author of The Girlhood of Catherine de' Medici. Its frontispiece is Bianca Cappello, from Allori's painting in the Uffizi.

The contents treat four lives. Tullia d'Aragona, the cardinal's daughter, is styled Aspasia rediviva. Olympia Morata's ten chapters follow her from good old times in Ferrara through flight from Schweinfurth to a last home at Heidelberg, asking what she is to us. Isabella Andreini, the great actress, gets a single long essay on her art, her writings, and her epitaph. Bianca Cappello closes the volume, balancing her accounts at the Medici court. History readers get four Renaissance women in Trollope's full-dress biographies.
4610-the-letters-of-horace-walpole-earl-:
Horace Walpole's letters continue in this second volume, covering 1749 to 1759, with letters now first collected marked in the contents. The volume opens in 1749 with letters to Sir Horace Mann on proceedings in Parliament. They cover a formidable minority headed by the Prince, Lord Egmont, innovations in the Mutiny Bill, and a new Navy Bill. Later letters report debates, a jar at Leicester House, King Theodore of Corsica, and the spread of Methodism.

May letters describe rejoicings for the peace, a jubilee masquerade, and fireworks. They add English credulity, a projected chastisement of Oxford, union between the Prince's party and Jacobites, and the disgrace of Maurepas. Walpole's eye for gossip, epigram, and bon-mot never flags. Readers get a vivid, gossipy record of mid-century politics and society, best read in sequence with volume one.
46429-romantic-ireland-volume-1-2:
Romantic Ireland, volume one of two, is a travel book by the Mansfields, illustrated by Blanche McManus Mansfield. Page printed it at Boston, copyrighted in 1904, in the Travel Lovers' Library. A frontispiece shows the Rock of Cashel, and the plates run from the Cliffs of Moher to a brooch from the Hill of Tara.

Contents begin with the land and its people, then romance and sentiment, and religious art and architecture. A chapter blends the Scotch Irish, and another surveys Irish industries, with plates of peat choppers, a cottage spinner, and a cottage loom. Dublin and about there fills a long chapter, and the road from Kilkenny to Cork Harbour closes this volume.
46439-romantic-ireland-volume-2-2:
Romantic Ireland, volume two, by the Mansfields, illustrated by Blanche McManus Mansfield, was printed by Page at Boston in 1904. It belongs to a Travel Lovers' Library of two volume tours, alongside Florence, Paris, Venice, and Japan. A frontispiece shows the cross and round tower of Monasterboice.

Twelve chapters carry the tour around the island. Queenstown, Cork, and Blarney open it, with Glengarriff and Bantry Bay next. Killarney and its lakes follow, then the coast of Limerick, the Shannon and its lakes, and Galway and its bay. Achill to Sligo, the Donegal highlands, and Londonderry with the Giant's Causeway fill the northern run. Antrim and Down, the Boyne valley, and Belfast and Armagh close the volume. The illustrations list castles, abbeys, and harbours by the dozen: Blarney Castle, Muckross Abbey, Ross Castle, the Gap of Dunloe, the Skelligs rocks, and the Claddagh at Galway among them.
46531-the-yoga-vasishtha-maharamayana-of:
Valmiki's Yoga-Vasishtha Maharamayana fills four volumes in seven parts, and this book is the third volume, bound in two parts as one. Vihari-Lala Mitra rendered the work from the original Sanskrit. The volume holds the Upasama Khanda and the Nirvana Khanda. Contents shown here cover the Nirvana-Prakarana, Book Six, on ultimate extinction.

Chapters treat the perfect calm of the mind and the unity of Brahma. Rama's perfect rest, the spread of ignorance, and the fastening of true knowledge follow. A long tale tells of Bhusunda, the crow of great age on Mount Meru, and of Vasishtha's visit and talk with him. Living liberation, its doubts, and the stilling of the mind fill the later heads.
46572-studies-in-the-history-and-method-: Studies in the History and Method of Science, volume one of two, is a scholarly essay collection. Its pages range across early science with Greek, Hebrew, and Arabic passages set in full. Old money sums appear in pounds, shillings, and pence in the period style. Dense footnotes and a full index serve readers of historical method. The text keeps author brackets, sic notes, and archaic roman numerals throughout.
46577-frederic-chopin-his-life-letters-a:
Moritz Karasowski wrote Frederic Chopin, His Life, Letters, and Works. Emily Hill turned the German text into English. William Reeves issued Volume One at London in 1879. A portrait of Chopin fronts the book. Robert Schumann praised him in the motto. The boldest poetic spirit of the age, Schumann called him.

Early manhood and a first journey open this volume. Prince Anton Radziwill stands among Chopin's friends there. A Berlin trip and letters home follow. Vienna, Prague, Teplitz, and Dresden fill a tour chapter. Two Vienna concerts mark that road. Letters to Titus Woyciechowski show the young man's mind. A farewell concert in Warsaw ends an era here. Chopin then leaves his native city for good. Early life writing like this fixed the pianist's story for English readers.
466-the-gaming-table-its-votaries-and-vi:
Andrew Steinmetz surveys gambling across ages and lands in the first of two volumes. He opens with gaming as a world-wide passion, then traces dice and cards among Hindus, Egyptians, Greeks, and Roman emperors. France, England, Brighton, German spas, and America each get their turn.

Steinmetz, a barrister, writes from fact and anecdote, naming lords, poets, and sharpers ruined at the table. Lotteries, lady gamesters, and laws against play fill later chapters. The volume reads as a vivid social history of a vice that, in his day, still cleaned out noblemen and clerks alike.
46621-sheppard-lee-written-by-himself-vo:
Sheppard Lee, Written by Himself came out in New York in 1836 from Harper & Brothers, in two volumes. Volume one is framed as Lee's own account of his birth, his temper, and his long hunt for an easy life. Its first book bears the dry heading of how to spend a fortune and how to win one back.

Lee farms badly, shuns lawyers, and leans on his servant, the honest James Jumble. He hunts office, makes a set speech in his village, and digs at the Owl-roost for Captain Kid's buried gold. A strange dream and a blow struck in the wrong place land him in the odd fix the contents call the most sad ever known to a man. Book two turns to good living, prison, and a happy sportsman, John H. Higginson.
46622-sheppard-lee-written-by-himself-vo:
Volume two of Sheppard Lee, Written by Himself, ends a tale of a soul in strange bodies. Harper and Brothers issued the book in New York in eighteen hundred thirty six. A proud verse on new shine fronts this last half. Book four walks Lee through a miser’s rich, sad house.

The miser’s children and the fate of the firstborn fill those chapters. A man may serve more dead than alive, one head quips. Lee hunts a fresh body and meets a philanthropist next. Book five turns to the good Samaritan Abel Snipe in full. Young Jonathan argues points of conscience for Yearly Meeting. Zachariah Longstraw schemes to mend his luck by Lee’s skin. Mob law, Lynchdom, and a dark last act close Lee’s road.
46649-the-chronicles-of-newgate-vol-1-2:
Arthur Griffiths wrote The Chronicles of Newgate, in two volumes, from Chapman and Hall at London in 1884. Griffiths had been an army major and was one of the crown inspectors of prisons. He had written on Millbank prison before this work. His preface tells of near five years of work and a mass of papers. He was forced to cut much, and to squeeze more, lest the book grow past all bounds.

Newgate, he says, is in itself a sum of the crime history of England. It stood for centuries on one site, hard by the Old Bailey court. Its claims on public care go past the sad tales of those it held. Griffiths traces its tale age by age, cell by cell. Readers get a grim, full tour of London crime and its most famed jail.
4720-wacousta-a-tale-of-the-pontiac-cons:
John Richardson's Wacousta, or The Prophecy, continues in this second volume of three, opening on the evening of a day fertile in melancholy incident, to which the first volume was devoted. That evening the drawbridge of Detroit is lowered for the third time since the garrison was invested. It moves not with a disregard shown by rattling chains, but with caution attesting secrecy of purpose. No array of armed men denotes a hostile expedition.

Most troops, overcome by the day's harassing duties, have retired to rest. A few guards walk their posts, apparently to check midnight drowsiness, but really to witness preparations going on by torchlight. Richardson writes the Pontiac conspiracy as frontier romance, with siege, prophecy, and divided loyalties. Readers should start with volume one, since this volume carries its plot, characters, and secrets forward without retelling them.
47222-quintus-claudius-a-romance-of-impe:
Ernst Eckstein's Quintus Claudius, a romance of imperial Rome, is kept here in volume two of Clara Bell's translation from the German. The title page marks it revised and corrected in the United States, and a publisher's list at the front prices the whole shelf of Eckstein romances.

Quintus Claudius itself went at a dollar in paper covers, or a dollar seventy-five in cloth for the set of two volumes. Hertha, done by Mrs Edward Hamilton Bell, stood at fifty cents in paper; Prusias and The Will matched the Quintus Claudius price; Nero, Aphrodite, and The Chaldean Magician fill out the list. Eleven volumes in cloth, boxed, cost eight dollars seventy-five cents.
47236-studies-of-the-greek-poets-vol-2-o:
John Addington Symonds wrote these studies of the Greek poets, and Harper issued the second volume at New York in 1880. A German motto heads it: to live, resolute, in the whole, the good, the fair. Greek tragedy fills the front of this half.

Nemesis, the balancing doom, stands as the key idea of tragedy, Symonds holds. The Attic crowd, the Persian War, and the fixed store of myths frame his account. Athens in the age of Euripides takes the long view. Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides stand in a row for weighing. Medea, Hippolytus, and Electra pass in turn. Symonds then turns to the scraps of lost plays that anthologies kept. His rich, warm prose made Greek verse a living read for his age.
47243-the-sportswoman-s-library-vol-2-of:
Volume 2 of The Sportswoman's Library is a set of pieces on sport for women, edited by Frances E. Slaughter. It came out in 1898 from Archibald Constable in Westminster and Longmans, Green in New York. Pictures by W. L. Wyllie, Cuthbert Bradley, and from photos go with the text. The book is given, with leave, to the Marchioness of Worcester, called a keen sportswoman.

The contents open with pieces on cruising and small yacht racing on the Solent, by Miss Barbara Hughes. Punt Racing, by Mrs. W. L. Wyllie, stands next. In Red Deer Land, by Mrs. Penn-Cuythen, stands third in the part of the list shown. A sketch of punts racing at the start stands at the front, drawn for this library by Wyllie. The volume gathers women's field and water sports of its day.
4726-john-lothrop-motley-a-memoir-volume:
Oliver Wendell Holmes, Sr., continues his memoir of John Lothrop Motley in this second volume, covering 1860 to 1866, when Motley was forty-six to fifty-two. It opens with residence in England, the outbreak of the Civil War, and letters to the London Times. A visit to America follows, with appointment as minister to Austria, Lady Harcourt's letter, and Miss Motley's memorandum.

The winter of 1859 to 1860 was passed chiefly at Oatlands Hotel, Walton-on-Thames. In 1860 Motley hired a house at 31 Hertford Street, May Fair, London, having just published the first two volumes of his History of the Netherlands. When civil war threatened and broke out at home, his love of country would not let him stay silent. Readers should start with volume one, since this volume carries Motley's middle years forward without retelling his youth.
47297-parzival-a-knightly-epic-vol-1-of-:
Jessie Weston Englished a grail epic in Parzival, a knightly epic by Wolfram von Eschenbach, volume 1. Stechert of New York print this copy in 1912, an anastatic reprint of the London edition of 1894. The translation is dedicated to the memory of Richard Wagner. His genius has given fresh life to the creations of mediaeval romance, the dedication says.

This volume holds books one to nine. Gamuret leads, then Herzeleide, Gurnemanz, and Kondwiramur. Anfortas, Arthur, Obilot, Antikonie, and Trevrezent fill the run. An argument heads each book. Book one tells how Gamuret of Anjou, at the death of his father King Gandein, refused to become his brother's vassal. He went forth to seek fame and love guerdon for himself. He fought before Alexandria and came to Patelamunt, where a queen stood besieged.
47298-parzival-a-knightly-epic-vol-2-of-:
Wolfram von Eschenbach wrote Parzival, a knightly epic, and Jessie Weston Englished it; this second volume is a 1912 reprint of the London edition of 1894. Contents name the books in turn: Orgeluse, Arnive, Eidegast, Klingsor, Gramoflanz, and Feirefis. Lohengrin closes the poem, with appendices and notes behind. A summary at the head of Book Ten sets out Gawain's adventures in that book.

Gawain, the summary says, fell in with a maiden and a wounded knight, helped the knight, and rode to Logrois. He met Orgeluse and wooed her, and she repaid him with scorn. A mocked squire, a stolen charger, and a fight won against Lischois Giwellius follow. Gawain comes at last to Terre de Merveil, well treated by the boatman and his daughter Bené. The verse opens as the year of truce ends.
47317-letters-and-literary-memorials-of-:
Letters and Literary Memorials of Samuel Tilden, volume two, is a set of papers edited by John Bigelow. Harper and Brothers published the volumes at New York and London in 1908. The volume opens among the letters of 1876, the year of Tilden great campaign.

A letter from David Wells at Norwich, of 6 January 1876, stands early in the shown text. Wells writes that he cannot better testify his admiration of the governor message than by asking for an early copy in pamphlet form. He wants it for more careful reading and preservation in his keeping. Tilden, the governor who broke the canal ring and lost the presidency of 1876 by one electoral vote, speaks in these volumes. Bigelow memorials fix the record of the wisest of the also rans, in his own letters and in the tributes of the men who knew his work.
47415-spanish-america-its-romance-realit:
Enock wrote this first volume on Spanish America, romance, reality, future. Unwin printed it in London, first published in 1920. Twenty five illustrations fill the book, a Colon statue up front. Enock had written on the Andes, Peru, Mexico, and Ecuador.

Contents open with a preface, then a reconnaissance and informal geography. A historical outline takes chapter two of the survey here. Central America begins the country chapters that follow in the volume. Press praise for the South American Series stands quoted in front. Martin Hume edited the series, and a Times notice calls it the most noteworthy there.
47432-babylon-volume-2:
Babylon, volume two, is a novel by Grant Allen, who wrote as Cecil Power. Chatto and Windus of London issued the three volume novel in eighteen eighty five. Twelve pictures by Macnab illustrate this second volume of the tale. Allen other works named include Philistia and Strange Stories.

Chapter fifteen, A Door Opens, finds Colin Churchill of full age in Italy. Colin has tired of working for Cicolari, moulding clay and carving copies. Busts, statuettes, and small classic pieces no longer feel like true sculpture. He gleans hints in a half amateur way from museum torsos there. His dream is Rome, a real studio, and life as a true sculptor.
47535-the-posthumous-papers-of-the-pickw:
The Posthumous Papers of the Pickwick Club, volume two, is the great comic tale by Charles Dickens, here with plates by Cecil Aldin for Dutton of New York. The heads promise rich sport: the tale of the goblins who stole a sexton, a hard slide on the ice, and Bob Sawyer's wild party in the Borough. The core of the half is the trial of Bardell against Pickwick, told in full. Sam Weller and his father shine in scene after scene of wit.

Then Pickwick goes to Bath, hears the tale of Prince Bladud, and falls into the Fleet, the jail for debt. There he meets strange bed mates and makes a stern vow. Fans of Dickens get the club at its peak: farce, law, and a warm heart in the storm.
47600-illustrations-of-exotic-entomology:
Illustrations of Exotic Entomology, volume two, presents Dru Drury's figures and descriptions of foreign insects in a new edition brought down to the present state of the science. J O Westwood edited the edition, and Henry G Bohn of London published it in 1837. Westwood added the systematic characters of each species, with synonyms, indexes, and other new matter.

The whole work contains upwards of six hundred and fifty figures of insects from abroad. Each plate pairs the insect's portrait with remarks and reflections on its nature and properties. Drury had gathered his specimens through a network of colonial contacts, and his books set the pattern for insect illustration. This second volume continues the survey through the insect orders as the science then arranged them.
47661-life-of-sir-william-wallace-of-eld:
John Carrick wrote this Life of Sir William Wallace of Elderslie, the first of two volumes. The biography appeared in Constable's Miscellany, a cheap Edinburgh series. An epigraph from Thomas Campbell praises Wallace as a knight without equal. Its subject is William Wallace of Elderslie, the Scottish knight.

The series advertisement explains the Miscellany's plan. Begun in January 1827, it reprinted valued works without cuts at low prices. It also issued new treatises by leading authors. By this volume, fifty-two numbers were already before the public. Each work could be bought on its own. Vignette title pages came with every volume, and maps or portraits appeared at times. Wallace's life thus reached readers far beyond costly editions.
47662-life-of-sir-william-wallace-of-eld:
Life of Sir William Wallace of Elderslie is the next part of a two part life, out at Edinburgh in eighteen thirty. John Carrick wrote the life for a set of mixed works of writ, lore, and art. A verse line calls its lead the most brave knight a horn ever sang to. Parts of this book take up his post as guard of the realm.

He raids the foe land, is envied by the great, and meets the foe host at a moor. The great fight past a town, from the counts of both lands, takes a part. His give up of the guard post, the fall of a great fort, and a siege of a next fort fill the mid list. His trip to France and the take of a sea rogue stand in the rows.
47690-canadian-scenery-volume-1-of-2:
The first volume of a picture book of Canadian scenery. W H Bartlett supplied the drawings. N P Willis wrote the literary department. Virtue and Company published it at London. Five prose sections frame the plates. They cover discovery, settlement, later events, and the inhabitants' condition. Travellers' impressions of Canada close the text.

The engraving list runs to dozens of views. Quebec from across the St Lawrence appears early. Niagara's whirlpool, Toronto, Montreal, and the Thousand Isles follow. Wolfe's and Montcalm's monument stands among the Quebec plates. Rafts in squalls and voyageurs' burial places add human touches. Such steel-engraved volumes sold the colonies to British drawing rooms. Bartlett toured Canada in the late 1830s sketching for them.
47691-canadian-scenery-volume-2-of-2:
Canadian Scenery holds views and text on Canada in a two book set. Drawings by W Bartlett fill the steel plates of the grand work. The hosted text is the second volume of the two. Willis, a famed hand at travel prose, wrote the text for the plates.

A front plate shows Montreal from its mount in broad soft light. Church halls, log slides, falls, and canal locks crowd the plate list. Parts treat the two great towns, the east shires, and hints for new folk. Sport in the wilds and a Niagara trip close the wide survey set. The work drew British eyes to Canada in the age of sail and steam.
47730-defense-of-the-faith-and-the-saint:
Defense of the Faith and the Saints, volume one of two, was written by B H Roberts and printed at Salt Lake City in 1907. Roberts had also written The Gospel and Outlines of Ecclesiastical History. The Saints of the title are the Mormon people, whose faith he defends.

In his foreword Roberts says he once meant to make a scrap book of tales and mixed pieces. Work and events drew him instead to themes of doctrine and past, in defense of his church. Through the years those pieces grew into a mass of stuff, from which this set was picked. More stuff stayed in hand, so he called this volume one. Readers meet a leading Mormon voice making his case in print.
47791-brief-lives-vol-2:
Brief Lives, volume two, by John Aubrey, gathers short lives of contemporaries set down between 1669 and 1696. Andrew Clark edited the volume from the author's own manuscripts. The Clarendon Press at Oxford published it in 1898, with facsimiles. This volume runs from the letter I to Y.

Aubrey mixes fact, gossip, and hearsay in brief entries. Ingelbert is credited here with the plan to bring water from Ware to London, a work Sir Hugh Middleton financed and took the fame for. John Innocent, dean of Saint Pauls, appears by way of his coat of arms and his school. Henry Isaacson, secretary to Bishop Lancelot Andrews, gets a few lines. Clark's notes and footnotes correct and extend the text.
47833-arch-ological-essays-vol-2:
Archaeological Essays, volume two, by the late Sir James Simpson, was edited by John Stuart and published at Edinburgh in 1872. Simpson, one of the Queen's physicians for Scotland and professor of medicine and midwifery at Edinburgh, wrote on the past as keenly as on chloroform. The volume gathers papers read to learned societies over twenty years.

The lead essay studies leprosy and leper hospitals in Scotland and England, first read in 1841. Later pieces treat Greek medicine vases, Roman army doctors, Roman medicine stamps found in Britain, and early notices of syphilis in Scotland. Medicine and antiquities meet on every page.
47964-the-talk-of-the-town-volume-1-of-2:
The Talk of the Town, volume one, is a novel by James Payn, author of By Proxy, published by Smith, Elder in London in 1885 in two volumes. Payn was among the most popular novelists of his day. The chapters promise a comedy of talk: an audacious criticism, a collector's gratitude, two poets, the examiners, and an evening at Vauxhall.

The narrator begins with his great-aunt Margaret. As a young man, he says, nothing surprised him more than very old people, those patriarchs who link two or three generations in one span. Aunt Margaret, who would have been a hundred a few years back, is his supreme example, and her story is the book. Payn's manner is the point: a garrulous, clubbable narrator turning family memory into town talk, with illustrations of Miss Margaret lifting her eyes from her plate in welcome.
47965-the-talk-of-the-town-volume-2-of-2:
The Talk of the Town, volume two, is the second half of a novel by James Payn. Payn also wrote the novel By Proxy. Smith, Elder and Company published this second edition in London in 1885. The volume opens at chapter nineteen of the story. Chapter titles run from Another Discovery to Farewell. A true lover, a bargain, and an unexpected ally appear early. Two actresses, a royal patron, and a play follow.

Illustrations are listed for the volume, with a dramatic frontispiece. One shows a man crying begone to two figures. The opening chapter begins with folks not in accord. Fear on one side sharpens that discord, the text says. The final chapters carry titles of disgrace, clay feet, and comfort. Readers of the first volume get the tale's second act here. The chapter list alone sketches a society novel of love and reputation.
4798-the-complete-poetical-works-of-perc:
The Complete Poetical Works of Percy Bysshe Shelley, volume two, is the Oxford edition of 1914, edited by Thomas Hutchinson. It includes materials never before printed in any edition of the poems. Its contents open with early poems of 1814 and 1815, including a stanza written at Bracknell. Stanzas of April 1814, poems to Harriet and to Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin, Yet Look on Me, and Mutability follow.

On Death, A Summer Evening Churchyard, and a poem to Wordsworth follow, with Feelings of a Republican on the Fall of Bonaparte and a note on the early poems by Mrs. Shelley. Poems of 1816 include The Sunset, Hymn to Intellectual Beauty, and Mont Blanc, with a cancelled passage, a fragment called Home, and a fragment of a ghost story. Poems of 1817 open with Marianne's Dream and poems to Constantia singing. Readers get Shelley's early verse in a scholarly Oxford text.
48149-fundamental-philosophy-vol-1-of-2:
Fundamental Philosophy, volume one, is a work by James Balmes, a Spanish priest and thinker. Henry Brownson translated it from the Spanish. Sadlier issued the two-volume set in New York in 1856. The first book of the work treats certainty. Its chapters ask what certainty is and where it rests. The contents run from the senses to the idea of the absolute.

Balmes asks if a science beyond the senses exists. He holds that sense alone cannot supply it. The philosophy of the self fails the same test. Leibniz and his monads enter the argument. Universal identity is weighed in two chapters. Brownson's preface vouches for the translation's faithfulness. Balmes was Spain's leading Catholic thinker of his age. His book brought scholastic rigour to modern questions.
48155-history-of-ancient-pottery-greek-e:
Walters built a history of old pottery on the work of Samuel Birch, and Scribner of New York published the second volume in 1905. Three hundred pictures go with it, eight of them in colour. This volume takes up the pictures painted on Greek vases.

A first chapter joins vase scenes to myth and to the old poets. Homer and the stage give the painters their themes. Then the gods come in order. Zeus, Hera, and the sea god lead, with the gods of Eleusis behind them. Apollo and Artemis, the smith god, and the goddess of love all have their due. Learning to read and sort these scenes is the book's task.
48187-memorials-of-old-london-volume-2-o:
P H Ditchfield edited Memorials of Old London, here in the second of two volumes. Bemrose and Sons published it at London and Derby in 1908. The set stands in the Memorials of the Counties of England series. The Crab Tree Inn at Hammersmith fronts the volume. The contents open with the palaces of London, by R S Mylne. Elizabethan London by T Fairman Ordish follows.

Pepys's London and the old London bridges come next. The clubs, inns, and coffee-houses of old London fill the middle. Literary shrines and Crosby Hall come late. The pageant of London, with the city churches and Christ's Hospital, closes the set. Many hands divide the capital's past between them, inn by inn and bridge by bridge.
48275-the-philosophy-of-history-vol-2-of:
The Philosophy of History, volume two, holds talks given at Vienna by Frederick von Schlegel, turned into English by James Burton Robertson and printed at London in 1835. A life of the author goes with the text. Talk ten takes the Christian view: the rise of the faith set against the fall of Rome. Talk eleven turns to the old Germans and the march of the north tribes. The rise of Mahomet and his creed fills the next, with the new realm of the Saracens.

Later talks treat the Guelfs and Ghibellines and the birth of romance verse and art. The last span runs from the Reformation to the balance of power, and ends on hope of a new birth for the world. Deep readers get a bold scheme of the past.
48390-social-england-under-the-regency-v:
Social England Under the Regency, by John Ashton, was issued at London by Ward and Downey in two volumes. The set, demy octavo and profusely illustrated, sold at thirty shillings. Ashton had already written Social Life in the Reign of Queen Anne, Old Times, and Dawn of the Nineteenth Century. This work continues his picture of English manners into the Regency years.

Volume one is held here. Ashton builds his social history from the print and paper record of the period, as his earlier volumes did for the age of Anne and the century's dawn. The publisher's list bound before the title page prices his companions among the season's illustrated books. The Regency, the years of the Prince Regent's rule before George the Fourth's reign, supplies the setting: its fashions, pleasures, scandals, and street life.
48535-spanish-america-its-romance-realit:
Spanish America, volume two, by Enock, treats the lands of that name in romance, reality, and future. Twenty six pictures and a map go with the text. A bronze statue of Bolivar at Caracas fronts the volume. The book stands in a South American series from the same house. That series covered Chile, Peru, Mexico, Argentina, and more. Reviews quoted at the front praise the set for commerce men and investors.

Enock had written on Peru, Mexico, and Ecuador before. His aim here is a broad survey rather than one country alone. The series editor, Martin Hume, lent his name to the line. Readers of the day got history, travel, and trade prospects in one cloth volume. The work shows British interest in the region at its height.
48746-encyclopedia-of-diet-a-treatise-on:
Encyclopedia of Diet, volume two, is a treatise on the food question by Eugene Christian. The set runs to five volumes in all. Its subtitle promises chemistry of food in plain language. It also promises the chemistry of the human body. The art of uniting those two in eating is its aim. Right eating is meant to establish normal digestion. It is also meant to remove the causes of digestive disorders.

The volume was published in New York in 1917 by the Corrective Eating Society. Lesson eight of the course fills this volume. It treats foods of vegetable origin at length. Grains are taken up first in that lesson. Their uses as energy, as nitrogen source, and as remedial food are set out. Nuts and peanuts follow in the contents list. The book reflects an early health food movement in America.
48752-leon-roch-a-romance-vol-1-of-2:
Pérez Galdós wrote Leon Roch, a romance in two volumes, and Clara Bell rendered this first volume from the Spanish for a New York printing of 1888. Galdós had written Gloria before it. The edition calls itself authorized and revised in the United States. A first chapter, From the Same to the Same, opens the tale in letters.

Life at a watering place follows, with talk in which Spaniards praise their own country and countrymen. Chapter heads promise more talk on the Spanish character, two men and their schemes in life, and a last illusion. Names in the heads include Pepa, Leopoldo, Gustavo, and María Egyptiaca. A husband and wife, a way of living side by side, and deserters close the shown list.
48768-the-works-of-the-emperor-julian-vo:
Works of the Emperor Julian, volume two, gives his later orations and letters. Wilmer Cave Wright rendered the Greek into English for Harvard University Press. The bilingual edition appeared at Cambridge, Massachusetts, in nineteen thirteen. Orations six, seven, and eight stand first in this second volume.

A letter to Themistius the philosopher and one to Athens follow them. A fragment of a letter to a priest is also kept in the set. The Caesars, a satire on past emperors, forms a set piece here. Misopogon, or Beard Hater, mocks Julian himself and Antioch in reply. First studies by the translator head each piece in the volume.
48780-social-england-under-the-regency-v:
Social England under the Regency, volume two of two, was written by John Ashton and published in London in eighteen ninety. Ward and Downey issued it, with ninety illustrations across the set. Ashton also wrote Social Life in the Reign of Queen Anne and Old Times. His method is the chronicle of everyday doings, year by year.

This volume opens with anti-Corn Bill riots and an attempt to steal the Crown. Chapter two brings the news of Waterloo and follows Napoleon to the Bellerophon. The years eighteen sixteen to eighteen eighteen unroll in chapter heads. They cover Spa Fields riots, resurrection men, gas lighting, and the first sovereigns. The death of the Princess Charlotte and the finding of the Scotch regalia close the run. Ashton preserves the Regency as its newspapers lived it.
48816-big-game-shooting-volume-2-of-2:
Big Game Shooting, volume two, belongs to the Badminton Library of sports and pastimes. The Duke of Beaufort edited that library, assisted by Alfred Watson. Longmans published this volume at London in 1894 with many hands at work. Clive Phillipps-Wolley leads the list of sportsmen who wrote its chapters.

Arctic hunting by Arnold Pike opens the contents of the second volume. The Caucasus and its mountain game, both by Phillipps-Wolley, follow in the list. Caucasian aurochs and the argali of Mongolia come from Littledale in the contents. The chamois gets a chapter from Baillie-Grohman among the alpine sports. Stag hunting closes the heads shown in this roll of the volume. Trophies from ice to alp fill the gentleman hunter handbook.
48893-mademoiselle-de-maupin-volume-1-of:
Mademoiselle de Maupin, volume one, was written by Theophile Gautier. Barrie printed this Philadelphia edition in 1897. It stands in a series called The Realists. Burnham made the complete translation. Le Sueur etched the plates and Toudouze drew more. A bibliographical notice opens the volume. The novel's start was modest, it says, for all its later fame. The title first appeared in Renduel's catalogue in 1833, beside a life of Hoffman. Gautier was twenty two and little known. A two volume work was a daring venture then.

For two years the author abandoned and resumed the book. Family tradition says his father locked him in his room to force pages from him. The frolicsome young man escaped by the window. By the end of 1834 only the first volume stood finished, and the publisher complained.
49071-james-s-account-of-s-h-long-s-expe:
James's Account of S H Long's Expedition, part two, is a reprint of an eighteen nineteen to twenty expedition record. It forms volume fifteen of the Early Western Travels series, edited by Reuben Gold Thwaites. That series reprinted rare accounts of the aborigines and of social life in the middle and far West. The part was issued at Cleveland in nineteen hundred five.

Major Long's party explored the Platte, Arkansas, and Red River country for the United States. Edwin James, its scientist, wrote the account of plants, animals, peoples, and hardships met. Thwaites adds notes, an introduction, and an index for modern readers. Part two carries the return and the southern rivers of the march.
49175-memoirs-of-the-empress-josephine-v:
Madame de Rémusat, lady-in-waiting to the Empress, wrote these memoirs of the Empress Josephine, and this first volume is a New York printing under an 1879 copyright. A picture of Josephine's coronation fronts the book. A preface by Paul de Rémusat and portraits and anecdotes by the author come before the memoirs proper. Book One opens in 1802 with family affairs at Saint Cloud.

Her first evening there, General Moreau, and her husband's making as prefect fill the first chapter. The habits of the First Consul and of Madame Bonaparte stand in the same head. Later chapters follow the return of old court customs and a journey to Belgium. The arrest of Georges Cadoudal and the death of the Duc d'Enghien darken the close of the shown contents.
49176-memoirs-of-the-empress-josephine-v:
Madame de Remusat, lady-in-waiting to the empress, continues her Memoirs of the Empress Josephine in volume two, issued by P F Collier and Son of New York. The chapters here cover 1805 to 1807 and open with the state of Paris during the war. The marriage of Eugene de Beauharnais and Napoleon's bulletins and proclamations set the scene.

Later chapters take up the death of Pitt, the emperor's civil list and household expenses, and fetes at court and Malmaison. Jena, Eylau, Friedland, and the Treaty of Tilsit carry the war story, while Josephine's jealousy threads the private one. A court insider writes.
49244-fundamental-philosophy-vol-2-of-2:
Fundamental Philosophy, volume two, is a work by the Reverend James Balmes, turned from the Spanish by Henry Brownson. The set came out at New York, Boston, and Montreal in 1856. This volume holds the fourth book, On Ideas, which asks how the mind knows what it knows.

The chapters take up sensism, Condillac's statue, and the gap between ideas drawn from shape and those known by thought alone. Balmes weighs Kant against the school of Aristotle and asks if pure thought can see truth on its own. He closes on the soul's reach for more than sense can give. The book brought Spanish Catholic thought to English readers in plain debate form.
49255-spanish-america-vol-1-of-2:
R H Bonnycastle, a captain in the Royal Engineers, wrote a descriptive, historical, and geographical account of Spain's dominions in the western hemisphere. Volume one was issued in London with maps of Spanish North America and South America. An engraving compares the heights of mountains in those regions. A quote from Paradise Lost on Columbus opens the title matter.

The work covers Spain's lands, continental and insular, in two volumes. Bonnycastle writes as a serving engineer with an eye for ground and distance. His account suits British readers of 1818 who wanted a clear survey of a vast empire. Maps and the altitude plate support the text throughout.
49272-leon-roch-a-romance-vol-2-of-2:
Leon Roch, volume two of two, is the closing half of a Spanish romance by Perez Galdos. Clara Bell turned the novel into English for an authorized edition of 1888. Contents of this volume open with a chapter on the Castilian nobility and moral laws. A picture that might be a Zurbaran but is only by Goya follows in jest.

The revolution, suing or defiant, and the ice gives way mark the rising crisis. Return to consciousness, will she die, and a visit by Leon Roch follow. A parting and later turns bring the marriage and faith conflict to its end. Galdos probes Spanish honour and church power through one household storm.
49343-old-court-life-in-spain-vol-1-2:
Frances Elliot's Old Court Life in Spain, from Putnam of New York and London, retells the legends and chronicles of early Spain in two volumes. She dedicates the work to Humphry Ward, on whose researches she says she leans heavily.

This first volume runs from Don Roderich and the gathering of the Gothic chiefs through the landing of the Moors and the battle of Guadalete. Tales follow of Córdoba, of Pelayo proclaimed king by the Goths, of Bernardo del Carpio, and of the death of Roland. The longest thread is the Cid: his killing of the Conde de Gormez, his marriage, his banishment, and his death and burial. Elliot draws on Prescott, Irving, and Lockhart's Spanish Ballads, and photogravure plates show the Alhambra and the great mosque at Córdoba.
49412-the-women-of-the-american-revoluti:
The Women of the American Revolution, volume two of two, by Elizabeth F Ellet, was printed in a 1900 edition with a new opening by Anne Hollingsworth Wharton. Ellet gathers lives of women who stood by the men of the Revolution. The volume opens with Martha Washington.

Ellet says all who care for Washington past will want to know the woman who shared his thoughts and plans. She praises Martha calm dignity in shade and in splendor alike, at her husband side in gloom and on the heights. She grants that a home bound life gives a life writer scant stuff to work with. Other lives in the volume treat wives, mothers, and helpers of the cause. Readers get the war seen through its women.
4965-waverley-or-tis-sixty-years-since-v:
Walter Scott's Waverley, subtitled Tis Sixty Years Since, continues in this second volume with Mr. Gilfillan marching his prisoner toward Stirling on a delightful autumn afternoon. Dinner hour in Scotland sixty years since was two o'clock, so by four Gilfillan leads his followers stoutly along, eyeing his hero and longing for controversy.

The march becomes a debate, as the Presbyterian minister cannot resist arguing with his captive. Scott sets the Jacobite rising of 1745 against such small human encounters. Readers following Edward Waverley's adventures get the novel's middle movement, where romance meets the hard politics of rebellion.
4972-frederick-chopin-as-a-man-and-music:
Frederick Niecks's second volume on Chopin turns to the composer's loves and his life with George Sand. Various accounts tell of their first meeting. Chopin's first impression of her is weighed. The two characters are compared. Portraits of both follow, with an account of her power of pleasing.

The volume also covers Chopin's publications in 1837 and 1838 and his playing at court and at concerts in Paris. Niecks weighs gossip against evidence throughout, asking why an artist's choice of partner so often puzzles outsiders. Readers get a careful biography of Chopin's middle years, grounded in letters and contemporary report.
49843-the-history-of-java-v-1-2:
Sir Thomas Stamford Raffles, formerly lieutenant-governor of Java, wrote this history of the island, in a second edition of 1830 dedicated to the Prince Regent. Raffles tells the Regent the Javanese hold British valour and justice in high respect.

His preface is careful to limit his severe remarks on the Dutch administration in Java to its colonial officers, not the Dutch nation. The orders from Holland, he says, breathed liberality; the tyranny was local. Raffles governed the island for nearly five years under the East India Company. Readers get the founding English account of Java's people, land, and antiquities from the man who ruled it.
49845-william-cobbett-a-biography-in-two:
Edward Smith writes a fighter's life in William Cobbett, a biography, volume 2, printed in London in 1878. Sampson Low and partners made the book, in two volumes. The chapter heads of this volume are Cobbett's own words, set as boasts and defiance. They march year by year through the life.

Chapter fourteen, for 1805 and 1806, heads itself: I never sat myself down anywhere, without making the fruits and flowers to grow. The next cries: I did destroy their power to rob us any longer without the robbery being seen. They naturally hate me, heads another. Compared with defeating me, defeating Buonaparte is a mere trifle, heads 1809 and 1810. The folly, common to all tyrants, is that they push things too far, heads 1810. To put a man in prison for a year or two does not kill him, heads the prison years.
49941-old-court-life-in-spain-vol-2-2:
Frances Elliot wrote Old Court Life in Spain, here in volume two. Putnam put it out at New York and London, with pictures. Elliot had written Old Court Life in France before this book. A plate shows the Darro river and the tower of Comares. Contents open with the fiesta of the Corpus Domini at Granada.

Don Pedro, Maria de Padilla, and Albuquerque fill the next chapters. Blanche de Bourbon, a wronged queen, takes her tragic place. A declaration of love, a marriage at Valladolid, and a cloister follow. The murder of Don Fadrique darkens the middle of the volume. A new king, Enrique de Trastamare, rises against his brother Pedro. The Black Prince defeats Enrique and reinstates Pedro on the throne. Enrique then murders Pedro, and the wheel turns again. Elliot gives Spain's cruel court age in warm, full narrative.
4999-the-notebooks-of-leonardo-da-vinci-:
Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks, in this second volume, gather the master's notes on sculpture and related arts. The editor notes with surprise that the horse statue of Francesco Sforza appears only in passing. Leonardo worked on it for years. Yet thirteen notes in his hand throw light on that famous work's strange history.

Earlier writers knew only a few of the passages, numbered 712, 719, and others. The volume arranges the new material to show Leonardo thinking through sculpture. No editor is named in the record. Readers get Leonardo at work in fragments: practical, curious, and endlessly observant about making things stand and move.
50054-the-female-quixote-or-the-adventur:
Charlotte Lennox wrote a novel about a young woman named Arabella who reads too many romances. The second form, checked and fixed, dates to 1752 in the copy used here. Lennox gave the book to the Earl of Middlesex with a shy, frank address. Her note grants fear of blame and hope of aid as her true motives.

Arabella's father, a marquis, fell from court favor and left the great world behind. His girl grows up fed on grand tales of love and honor. She then takes real life for a stage set by those tales. Readers get fun and sharp sense in a tale plainly kin to Don Quixote.
50184-english-caricature-and-satire-on-n:
English Caricature and Satire on Napoleon the First, volume one, by John Ashton, was published by Chatto and Windus of London in 1884. One hundred fifteen pictures, drawn by Ashton himself, go with the text. Ashton also wrote a history of the chap books of the eighteenth century. The frontispiece shows the exile at Longwood in April 1820.

Ashton says plainly that the book is not a history of Napoleon. It reprints the bulk of the prints and squibs England poured on its great enemy, with just enough history to make them clear. Most are humorous, some silly or spiteful, a few too coarse to reprint. Gillray and Rowlandson mostly signed their work; unsigned pieces are assigned on the word of a British Museum keeper.
50185-english-caricature-and-satire-on-n:
John Ashton gathered English caricature and satire on Napoleon in volume two. Chatto and Windus printed it in London in 1884. Ashton drew one hundred fifteen illustrations for the two volumes. Contents run by chapter from the high thirties onward here.

Chapter thirty eight treats invasion squibs and the Cadoudal plot. The Duc d Enghien execution and Captain Wright case follow closely. Napoleon proclaimed emperor and his coronation fill the next chapters. Ulm surrender, Trafalgar battle, and peace proposals come in chapter forty two. Peace talks, Fox death, and a blockade of England fill the next chapter in line.
50218-old-court-life-in-france-vol-1-2:
Frances Elliot wrote Old Court Life in France, Volume One. G P Putnam's Sons issued it at New York and London. Elliot had written a Diary of an Idle Woman in Italy. Picture of Old Rome bears her name too. The book goes to her niece, the Countess of Minto. Francis the First opens the contents.

Charles de Bourbon and a brother-sister tale follow. The Quality of Mercy heads chapter four. All Lost Save Honour names the fifth. La Duchesse d'Etampes takes the seventh. Catherine de Medici enters at chapter nine. A Fatal Joust and the widowed queen follow her. Mary Stuart and her husband stand at twelve. Saint Bartholomew's horror fills chapter twenty. Don Juan and Charmante Gabrielle come late. Court life in anecdote marches from Francis to Louis the Thirteenth in a lady's lively telling of love and knives.
50219-a-journal-of-the-disasters-in-affg:
Lady Sale kept a journal of the British disaster in Afghanistan in the years 1841 and 1842. John Murray issued it in London in 1843, and the copy shown had reached its sixth thousand. Lady Sale was far from England while the book went through the press. A brief note warns that some spellings of eastern words may err.

The table of contents traces revolt at Cabul, loss of forts, and lack of food. It then follows the retreat, the loss of guns, and the final fight at Gundamuk. Hostage taking and captivity close the grim tale. Readers gain a near, day by day view of a famed military collapse.
50225-danger-at-mormon-crossing-sandy-st:
Danger at Mormon Crossing, by Roger Barlow, was published by Simon and Schuster of New York in nineteen fifty-nine. The story is the second of the Sandy Steele Adventures. The series list also names Black Treasure, Stormy Voyage, and Fire at Red Lake. Sandy Steele is a boy of sixteen with a taste for wild country.

The first chapter, The Big Cats, opens at the Cook family's table. Arthur Cook, a tanned giant, urges Sandy to settle the trip by telephone that night. His son Michael arrives with milk and an enormous slice of layer cake. The contents promise white water, Dog Leg Falls, a hidden cave, and capture. The story of Mormon Crossing itself waits for the penultimate chapter. Barlow wrote outdoor adventure for boys in the Hardy Boys' decade.
50514-chronicles-of-newgate-vol-2:
Major Arthur Griffiths wrote Chronicles of Newgate, volume two of the set. The Grolier Society issued it in London in a capped, numbered run. Griffiths had served as an inspector of prisons in Great Britain. The set forms part of a History and Romance of Crime.

The Gaol Fever leads his grim contents with a tale of pestilence. That typhus bred in the packed, foul air of Newgate’s wards. In seventeen hundred fifty it spread to the Old Bailey with death. The Black Assize of old shows its reach to bench and bar alike. No house doctor served the gaol in those dark years, he notes. Men took the king’s shilling to flee its stench and moral rot. The gaol’s rebuilding, famed crimes, and kind reform fill the span. A sketch of the Tower of London closes the second volume.
50607-katherine-lauderdale-vol-1-of-2:
Marion Crawford wrote a novel of Katharine Lauderdale in two books. Volume one came out in New York and London in 1894. Alfred Brennan drew its plates for the tale's scenes. Crawford wrote Saracinesca and Pietro Ghisleri in past works. Fifteen parts fill this first book of the Lauderdale tale.

A place like none in the world stands in a plate at page ten. She rose at once and feigned work by the lone light, one key says. What have you chose, she asks in a plate at page 203. Kitty, do not do what I have done, a late key pleads in earnest. New York wealth and old names give the tale its bright ground. Heart plots rule it.
50624-lorenzo-de-medici-the-magnificent-:
Alfred von Reumont wrote the life of Lorenzo de' Medici, called the Magnificent. Robert Harrison turned the German text into English. Volume one of two came out in London in 1876.

The translator owns that the task was no easy one. Reumont had searched each scrap of paper on the Medici and their times. His preface turns to Italy in the late 1400s, as the Renaissance took shape. The life aims to give a vivid sense of that Medicean age. Readers meet Florence, its art and its power through one man's story. Harrison gave English readers the full life in their own tongue.
50625-lorenzo-de-medici-the-magnificent-:
Lorenzo de' Medici the Magnificent, volume two of two, was written by Alfred von Reumont and translated from the German by Robert Harrison. Smith, Elder, and Company published it in London in eighteen seventy-six. This volume continues the fourth book, on the time of Lorenzo himself.

Chapter six treats Lorenzo as a poet, from his love poems for Lucrezia Donati to the carnival songs. Chapter seven turns to Marsilio Ficino and Cristoforo Landino, the philosophers of his court. Ficino's translations of Plato and Plotinus anchor the discussion. Landino's Dante commentary follows, with Leon Battista Alberti at Camaldoli. Chapter eight covers Luigi Pulci, author of the Morgante Maggiore, and Angelo Poliziano. Reumont writes cultural history as court biography, with learning worn lightly.
50727-spain-v-2-of-2:
Spain, volume two, is a travel account by Edmondo de Amicis of Italy. Stanley Rhoads Yarnall rendered the Italian text into English for this edition. Merrill and Baker of New York and London issued the pictured two volume set. This deluxe printing was limited to one thousand numbered copies in all.

Volume two tours Aranjuez and Toledo first, then Cordova and Seville. Cadiz, Malaga, Granada, and Valencia close the southern circuit of Spain. Plates show the Alcazar at Seville, the Gate of the Sun at Toledo. Moorish arches, the Court of Oranges, and the Alhambra courts are pictured. De Amicis writes as a charmed foreign guest in old Spanish cities.
50747-the-expositor-s-bible-the-book-of-:
George Adam Smith wrote The Book of the Twelve Prophets, volume two, in the Expositor Bible series edited by W Robertson Nicoll. A C Armstrong and Son issued the book in New York in eighteen ninety eight. The volume treats Zephaniah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Obadiah, Haggai, and Zechariah chapters one to eight. It then takes up Malachi, Joel, Zechariah chapters nine to fourteen, and Jonah. Some fifteen hundred sixty footnotes gather at the chapter ends.

Smith was a doctor of divinity and doctor of laws. The text prints Greek and Hebrew words in their own letters, Μαλαχιας and מלאכיה among them. A note explains that an expression like A raised to B marks a superscript letter. Some Hebrew letters missing from one section have been restored in square brackets, the transcriber notes. Bible students get a full Victorian commentary on the later minor prophets.
50850-old-court-life-in-france-vol-2-2:
The hosted text is the second volume of Old Court Life in France by Frances Elliot. It was published by Putnam's Sons in 1893. A plate at the front shows the meeting of Henry the Third and the Duke of Guise.

The chapters run through the French court of the sixteen hundreds. A keeper of the royal conscience and a death on the scaffold come early. The end of the cardinal follows, then the queen regent and the dashing Duc de Beaufort. Charles Stuart of England crosses the tale. The ladies' war and the fall of Mazarin fill the middle. Louise de la Vallière, the convent of Chaillot, and Fouquet the finance minister close the list given here. Elliot tells court life as a string of scenes and persons, in a bright, gossipy style.
50886-katherine-lauderdale-vol-2-of-2:
Crawford ends a society tale in Katharine Lauderdale, volume 2 of 2, printed in New York and London in 1894. Macmillan made the book, with copyright the year before. Brennan draws the plates. Crawford had writ Saracinesca and Pietro Ghisleri. A frontispiece shows the heroine: she was very white as she turned her face to him.

Chapters sixteen to thirty fill this volume. The plate list tells the beats in captions: I am glad to see you, my dear child, he said warmly. She knew that life could never be the same again, if she could not believe her son. Chapter sixteen opens on a late walk: Katharine let Ralston accompany her within a block of Robert Lauderdale's house, and then sent him away. It is getting late, she said; it must be nearly ten o'clock.
50994-the-cambridge-book-of-poetry-for-c:
The Cambridge Book of Poetry for Children was edited by Kenneth Grahame and published at the Cambridge University Press in nineteen sixteen. Grahame had written The Golden Age, Dream Days, and The Wind in the Willows. This entry holds parts one and two of his anthology for young readers.

Part one begins for the very smallest ones, with rhymes and jingles. Merry are the Bells, Curly Locks, and Pussy-Cat Mew open the book. Familiar objects follow: the moon, the star, and a kitty considered three ways. Sections for those a little older bring in the seasons and the country. Three poets offer daffodils in a row: Shakespeare, Herrick, and Wordsworth. Grahame's choices shaped the nursery canon for the century: old rhymes first, then real poetry graded gently upward.
510-the-purcell-papers-volume-2:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu gathers Irish tales in this second volume of the Purcell Papers, framed as a priest's legacy. A countess's secret history opens the set, followed by the bridal of Carrigvarah, a strange event in the life of Schalken the painter, and scraps of Irish ballads. Names are changed where the living might be hurt.

Le Fanu writes in rich, eerie prose, mixing family pride, ghostly dread, and country talk. The painter's tale, of a devilish visitor, ranks among his most famed. The volume preserves his early mastery of Irish gothic, where old houses keep old sins.
51099-amadis-of-gaul-vol-2:
Amadis of Gaul, volume two, is part of the great romance of chivalry. Longman of London issued this edition in 1803. The authorship is given to Vasco Lobeira. Four volumes hold the whole tale. This volume opens in the heat of book one. Chapter thirty-six finds Amadis near London. Ardian the Dwarf gallops up with ill news. Oriana has been carried away, he reports.

Amadis spurs toward the city at once. The queen throws the king's best sword to his squire. That blade never had its equal, she says. Amadis misses a bridge and falls in a brook. The sword reaches him through Gandalin's hands. Such rescues were the seed of all later romance. Don Quixote's madness fed on this very book.
51300-spanish-america-vol-2-of-2:
Spanish America, volume two of two, was written by R H Bonnycastle, a captain in the Corps of Royal Engineers. Longman and partners published it in London in eighteen eighteen. The full title promises a descriptive, historical, and geographical account of Spain's dominions in the western hemisphere.

The volume carries maps of Spanish North and South America. An engraving compares the altitudes of the mountains in those regions. This second volume covers the captaincy general of Caracas and the provinces of Venezuela. It then treats the viceroyalty of Peru, intendancy by intendancy, from Truxillo to Arequipa. The viceroyalty of Buenos Ayres, or La Plata, follows. Bonnycastle wrote for British readers suddenly interested in Spain's crumbling American empire.
5144-my-life-volume-2:
Richard Wagner's autobiography, in its English translation of 1911, continues his life story in its second volume. Part Three covers the years 1850 to 1861, opening with his wife Minna finding quarters near Zurich, in the parish of Enge, while Wagner lived in exile after the Dresden rising.

The volume follows the composer's work, friendships, and restless moves through those years, as he planned the great operas that would define his career. Readers interested in Wagner will find here his own account, candid and self-justifying, of the middle period in which his art and his legend took shape.
51629-delaware-or-the-ruined-family-vol-:
Delaware, or The Ruined Family, volume two of a tale in three volumes, was printed at Edinburgh for Robert Cadell in 1833. The title family stands at Emberton Park. Sir Sidney Delaware has signed a bill for twenty five thousand pounds in favour of Lord Ashborough. The days till the bill falls due slip away unnoticed, so sure is he that the money will be ready.

The volume opens by musing that the sand in the hour glass of happiness is finer than that of common cares. Sir Sidney rests on the word of Mr Tims and thanks Burrel in general terms for his advice. A miser uncle, governed by his nephew through the two strings of avarice and fear, holds back his hand for a time. The young stranger at Emberton waits at the centre of the web.
51702-a-guide-to-the-study-of-fishes-vol:
David Starr Jordan, president of Leland Stanford Junior University, wrote this guide to the study of fishes. Henry Holt and Company published it at New York in 1905, with colored frontispieces and 507 illustrations in two volumes. The second volume opens with a plate of the Oniokose, or demon stinger, of Japan, shown changing its surface colors to match lava rocks, red algae, or deep water.

Volume two begins with the ganoids, their classification and fossil kin, and then takes up the bony fishes order by order, from herring kin through the salmon family. Long chapters treat the whitefish, lake herring, Quinnat salmon, and the parent-stream theory, then the trout, charr, grayling, and smelt. Lantern fishes, lizard fishes, and the eel-like fishes follow, with living and fossil forms treated together for the student working through the whole class.
51704-fern-vale-or-the-queensland-squatt:
Fern Vale, or the Queensland Squatter, volume two of three, is a novel by Colin Munro. Newby published the set in London in 1862 from Welbeck Street, Cavendish Square. The volume holds thirteen chapters in its contents, paged to chapter thirteen at page 325. Its first chapter carries a motto from Macbeth on withered, wild figures on the heath.

What are these, so withered and so wild in their attire, the motto asks of its scene. Tom, in the first lines, is certain that some fellows have been up to mischief on the station. Queensland in the early 1860s was new pastoral country, and the squatter novel was its first fiction. Munro middle volume works the station, its hands, and its dangers through thirteen chapters of incident, in the form the London circulating libraries demanded for colonial tales of that day.
51756-the-history-of-chemistry-volume-2-:
The History of Chemistry, volume two of two, is a history of science by Thomas Thomson, regius professor of chemistry in the University of Glasgow. Henry Colburn and Richard Bentley published it in London in 1831. The second volume's seven chapters begin with the foundation and progress of scientific chemistry in Great Britain. Sweden and France follow, then analytical chemistry.

Electro-chemistry, the atomic theory, and the present state of chemistry close the volume. The first chapter pairs two contrasting workers. While Cavendish extended the bounds of pneumatic chemistry with the caution and precision of a Newton, Priestley proceeded with a rapidity quite unexampled. His happy talents and inventive faculties, Thomson writes, did more than any other British chemist to make the science popular. A passage preserved in the copy traces Priestley's start.
51937-daireen-volume-2-of-2:
Daireen, volume two of two, is a novel by Frank Frankfort Moore. The hosted text resumes the story in its later chapters. Lottie walks with Colonel Gerald and begs him to tell her all she wants to know. The colonel, smiling down at her bronzed face to face, answers that she knows as much as he does.

Lottie presses him on the mystery about Mr Markham. Talk in the book tells of a man floating about on a wreck, restored only after great difficulty. Folk say he is very rich, yet no one can see where the money he lives on comes from, since he can have had little with him when he was picked up. The volume carries the tale of this castaway and his secret toward its close. Moore's novel mixes shipwreck, wealth, and courtship in the manner of late Victorian fiction.
51968-the-life-and-adventures-of-peter-w:
Robert Paltock's Life and Adventures of Peter Wilkins appears here in the second of two volumes, from Reeves and Turner at London in 1884, with a preface by Bullen. The title page retells the whole: a Cornish man shipwrecked near the South Pole passes through a subterranean cavern into a new world. There he saves and marries a Gawry, a flying woman, and is carried to the country of the Glums and Gawrys, men and women that fly. Cuts show the structure and mechanism of their wings.

Volume two's chapters bring Youwarkee's father Pendlehamby on a state visit: the guests marvel at poultry, a cart, and fishing, and are terrified by the firing of a gun. Peter dresses his wife in English habit, unrecognized, and feasts the flying court. The tale claims Wilkins's own telling aboard the Hector; he died landing at Plymouth in 1739.
52002-mitchelhurst-place-a-novel-vol-2-o:
Mitchelhurst Place is a tale in two parts by Margaret Veley, of which this is the next part. It came out at London in eighteen eighty-four. Veley was known past a past tale. Heads of this part bear names of a lost note, a last rest day, moon shine, a mans rue, and loves post man. A last head bears a month name of the year past two.

The part opens as the post man of the place climbs to the great house on his round. A young man hangs past the gate in wait for him. Dew greys the road grass and pearls hang on the fine webs past bush and blade. The old man has borne his bag past thirty years and knows the late chief of the house. He fumbles the notes in his hand, shy of which name to seek.
52003-memoirs-of-the-marchioness-of-pomp:
Memoirs of the Marchioness of Pompadour, volume 1 of 2, claims to be writ by herself and turned from the French. The London print bears the year 1766. The title page promises the motives of wars, treaties, and embassies in the courts of Europe.

An editor's first word lifts the book past mere court gossip. These pages, he says, give the history of a reign of wars, plots, and leagues. They show the cabals of courtiers and the rise and fall of generals and ministers. The frame is the court of France in the last twenty years of Lewis the Fifteenth. The lady was born Poisson and wed le Normand.
52215-memoirs-of-the-marchioness-of-pomp:
These memoirs of the Marchioness of Pompadour, said to be written by herself, came into English from the French and were printed at London in 1766. P Vaillant in the Strand and W Johnston in Ludgate Street sold the two volumes. The part held here is volume two. The title promises the motives of wars, treaties, embassies, and talks across the courts of Europe.

Cabals of courtiers and the rise and fall of generals and ministers fill the bill. The scene is the court of France in the last twenty years of the reign of Lewis the Fifteenth. The voice grants that the king visited her habitually yet kept a taste for passing loves, whose remorse, she says, always brought him back to her.
52251-constantinople-v-2-of-2:
Volume two of Edmondo de Amicis's Constantinople, in Maria Hornor Lansdale's translation from the fifteenth Italian edition, was published by Coates of Philadelphia in 1896. Photogravures by Gilbo illustrate it, a girl of the harem at the front. The contents run from Turkish Women through the Walls, the Old Seraglio, and the Last Days, to the Turks and the Bosphorus.

The opening chapter corrects a traveller's expectation.
