After all one hears of the thraldom of Turkish women, the first sight is of them everywhere, at all hours, coming and going as freely as the women of any European city. The veiled figures in white and coloured mantles seem, at first, like nuns, or masqueraders. None is ever seen with a man, and they appear to belong to no one, which the chapter sets out to explain.
5226-life-and-letters-of-thomas-henry-hu:
Leonard Huxley's Life and Letters of Thomas Henry Huxley continues in this second volume, covering the years 1870 through the mid-1880s. Its chapters follow Huxley year by year, through his work in science, education, and public debate, with letters that show his friendships, controversies, and family life.

The volume presents Huxley, Darwin's great defender, in his most active middle period, lecturing, writing, and shaping British science. Readers get a portrait built from Huxley's own words, and a detailed record of Victorian science at the moment it became a public force.
52343-the-white-prophet-volume-2-of-2:
The hosted text is the second volume of The White Prophet, a novel by Hall Caine set in Egypt and the Sudan. It was published in London by William Heinemann in 1909, with pictures by Caton Woodville. The frontispiece cries, it was he; it was Gordon.

The volume takes up the third book of the tale, called The Light of the World. Helena wakes to a house in stir. The great Bedouin chief is at Omdurman. Her master sends the people down to the river to bring him up in state. The stranger, an Englishman and a Christian, is to be received in the mosque itself. Talk of a plot against the prophet and against England fills the plates and the pages. Helena waits in dread as the shouts of the crowd come nearer.
5235-the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-:
Charles James Lever's Harry Lorrequer continues in this second volume, covering chapters eleven through seventeen. Harry tries his hand at making love for a friend at Cheltenham, and revisits Dublin and Tom O'Flaherty. He samples boarding-house society and joins a chase. He recalls the Peninsula, with a repeated chapter number in the print copy noted by the editors.

The volume holds only this middle stretch of Harry's confessions, and its comedy moves between England and Ireland. Readers following the novel in order will find matrimonial adventures, theatricals, and regimental anecdotes that complete the set, told with Lever's usual high spirits.
52567-arminell-a-social-romance-vol-2:
Arminell, a social romance in three volumes, came from the pen that wrote Mehalah and John Herring. Methuen of London issued volume two in 1890. Chapter nineteen, Little John Nobody, opens the part held here. Giles Inglett Saltren has broken a promise to his mother and told Arminell that he is not the nobody folk take him for.

Giles, called Jingles, has lived lonely in a great house. His schooling lifts him above his mother's class, while pride and doubt bar him from the class above. He and Arminell share interests and a like solitude, and he longs to meet her without the wall between them. Guilt pricks him by evening, then fades. The volume turns on class, secrets, and two young lives kept apart.
52575-the-cuckoo-in-the-nest-v-1-2:
Oliphant wrote a novel dated 1892, in two volumes, that opens at the Seven Thorns, a country inn on a quiet road. The inn once served coach travel, with stables for half the horses in the county. Now most rooms stand shut, and only the kitchen and a small parlor see much use.

The Hewitt family, who keep the inn, were once strong yeomen who farmed their own land. Their fall in means is felt as keenly as that of any proud house in the county. Village callers, rare tourists, and farmers on market day make up the slow trade as the tale begins.
52621-society-in-america-volume-1-of-2:
Harriet Martineau wrote Society in America, in two volumes, of which this file holds the first, issued at New York and London in 1837. Martineau had made her name with Illustrations of Political Economy. Her introduction opens with a warning on the reading of nations. To seize the character of even one man in its secret workings takes a philosopher, and to draw it with truth takes a poet.

From that start she doubts the quick verdicts of travelers who paint a national portrait from a carriage window. Each observer, she argues, brings an image with him and finds what it lets him see. The book that follows is her own attempt at the harder task, drawn from her American travels and set down for readers on both sides of the Atlantic.
52685-society-in-america-volume-2-of-2: Volume two of Society in America completes a two-part study of how life is lived in the United States. The front pages carry a London publisher's list dated June 1837, with new plays and novels of that season. That list dates the volume and shows the trade world it came from. Readers who work through the first volume turn here for the rest of the account.
52749-the-history-of-korea-vol-2-of-2:
The History of Korea, volume two, by Homer Hulbert, continues a history of the country. The Methodist Publishing House issued it at Seoul in 1905. Hulbert edited The Korea Review, and the volume is illustrated.

The first chapter's head reads like a war bulletin in short lines. China's reply to Japan, the Chinese march on P'yŭng-yang, and treachery fill its start. Victories at Hăng-ju, the Japanese suing for peace, and the evacuation of Seoul follow. The great battle of Chin-ju and a loyal dancing-girl stand in the list. The text opens on the final struggle in the north. General Sim was long returning from Nanking, past the fifty days agreed. At last he entered P'yŭng-yang on the sixth day of the twelfth moon. The Japanese retreat from the north was to begin there.
52756-the-cuckoo-in-the-nest-v-2-2:
Volume two of The Cuckoo in the Nest, a novel by Mrs Oliphant, came out in the English Library series at Leipzig. The series was issued by Heinemann and Balestier for readers on the continent. Its volumes could not be brought into Britain or the colonies, by the terms on the title page. The novel was complete in two volumes.

Oliphant was the author of Kirsteen and Diana, among many other tales. Her name on a series list promised sound, observant fiction of manners. The English Library sold British novels to travellers and residents abroad. Each volume was cheap, handy, and printed for that market alone. This second volume carries the story of the cuckoo in the nest to its close. The title hints at a stranger lodged within a family, the classic Oliphant theme.
52819-defense-of-the-faith-and-the-saint:
B H Roberts defends his church in Defense of the Faith and the Saints, volume two, issued at Salt Lake City in 1912. The volume fulfills a promise made when the first appeared, and its chief part is a debate. Theodore Schroeder argues the origin of the Book of Mormon; Roberts answers him section by section.

Schroeder's case rests on Solomon Spaulding's lost manuscript and on Sidney Rigdon's alleged part in passing it to Joseph Smith. Roberts replies with the facts of the Spaulding manuscript, the Conneaut witnesses, and attacks on E D Howe's credit. A full paper duel is preserved.
52850-barbers-manual-part-1-text-book-on:
The Barbers' Manual and Text Book on Taxidermy joins two trades in one small volume. McConnaughay wrote it from his own shop experience. He published it at Chicago in 1898. The price was a dollar and a quarter. A portrait of the author faces the text.

A preface explains the dual character frankly. Part one instructs barbers, especially the young and less experienced. Its recipes were tested over thirty-one years of shop work. Part two teaches taxidermy. The author practised that art for twenty-three years. He preserved and sold hundreds of specimens. Tanning hides for mats and rugs makes a third trade. The book promises to save money and make money for its buyer.
531-the-gaming-table-its-votaries-and-vi:
Andrew Steinmetz closes his history of gambling in this second volume, turning from nations to sharpers and clubs. Polite cheats, professional gamesters, duels, suicides, and gaming houses fill the chapters. Dice, cards, piquet, faro, hazard, cockfights, and the turf each get a turn, with odds explained.

Steinmetz, a barrister, mixes anecdote with moral warning, showing how fraud, passion, and chance ruin men of all ranks. Fortune-telling by cards and card tricks close the book on a lighter note. The volume serves as a vivid record of Victorian gaming life at its sharpest.
53125-the-war-of-women-volume-2:
Alexandre Dumas closes his Fronde tale in The War of Women, volume two, issued by Little, Brown in Boston in 1903. The volume opens under the head The Vicomtesse de Cambes, two days from Bordeaux. The dukes and their army lie ten leagues off, and the princess must choose a quiet entry or a forced one.

Her council of war is a council of women: Madame la Princesse, Madame de Tourville, Claire, and her maids of honor, with Lenet heard but not heeded. The plan is boats, a rush down the river, and shouts of Vive Condé and Down with Mazarin. Grand intrigue follows.
53527-the-existence-and-attributes-of-go:
Stephen Charnock wrote The Existence and Attributes of God, here in a reprint issued at Grand Rapids in 1996. William Symington's life and character of the author goes with the text. The work first appeared as discourses under the same name, in an edition of 1853. Two volumes stand in one. The contents of the first volume open with the life of the author, then a preface.

Discourse one treats the existence of God. Its text is the first verse of the fourteenth Psalm: the fool has said in his heart, there is no God. The reprint keeps the old spellings of Charnock's time, as its notes explain. Page numbers of the original book stand in braces through the text. Footnotes are gathered in a single section at the end. The edition is the third printing of the reprint, dated January 2000.
53629-the-life-and-letters-of-ogier-ghis:
Charles Thornton Forster and F H Blackburne Daniell set down the life and letters of Busbecq. C Kegan Paul and Company issued Volume One in London in 1881. Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq served as imperial ambassador in the sixteenth century. Four Turkish letters fill most of this first volume.

Busbecq shows the Turk when Turkey dictated to Europe, the editors write. Catherine de Medici, Guise, and Marguerite walk his French scenes as well. Gibbon, Ranke, and Motley all drew on his letters for their histories. Readers gain a genial guide three centuries deep into courts and camps.
53630-the-life-and-letters-of-ogier-ghis:
The Life and Letters of Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, volume two, by Charles Thornton Forster and F H Blackburne Daniell, came out in London in 1881. Busbecq was a knight and envoy of the Empire. A cross of his house town, of the thirteenth century, ornaments the book. A Greek line on the title page praises a man who saw the towns and minds of many folk.

This volume holds his letters from France, first to Maximilian, then to Rodolph. Near a hundred letters fill the book, with an appendix and index. A first note sorts the French men whose works light up his age. De Thou the historian was his close friend. Brantome left tales of court life. History fans get a sharp envoy's mail from a grand court.
53669-portable-flame-thrower-m2-2:
Portable Flame Thrower M2-2 is War Department Technical Manual TM 3-376A, issued at Washington on May sixteenth, nineteen forty four. The manual is marked Restricted. A note states the rules for sharing restricted matter with folk in United States service. The order is signed for the Secretary of War by G C Marshall, Chief of Staff. J A Ulio, the Adjutant General, attests the order. Lists of units to receive the manual head the book.

Inside, troops get the facts and care of the portable flame thrower M2-2 for field use. Such manuals treat parts, fuel, firing, cleaning, and safety in strict order. The distribution list names engineer combat battalions, regiments, and headquarters units among the users. Historians of war gear will value a primary manual from the heart of the Second World War. The dry, exact prose shows how the Army taught deadly tools.
53674-the-tuzuk-i-jahangiri-or-memoirs-o:
Jahangir, the Mughal emperor, wrote these memoirs, translated by Rogers and edited by Beveridge. Volume one of two covers the first years of his reign in India. Rogers worked from an edition printed at Ghazipur in 1863 and Aligarh in 1864, the preface explains.

That text was made from a single defective manuscript, Beveridge warns at the front. He collated it with manuscripts in the India Office and the British Museum for corrections. Proper names especially gained, and many notes were added, as an emperor's own record of hunts, drunk cups, rebellions and justice reaches English.
53686-melmoth-the-wanderer-vol-2:
Melmoth the Wanderer is a tale in four volumes, printed at Edinburgh in 1820. The title page names no author, only the author of Bertram. Volume 2 opens in chapter 6, deep in a long tale told by a Spaniard to Melmoth.

The Spaniard has just read a letter from his brother and shakes with joy and tears. Hope of freedom wakes in him after long shut in life. Yet he must hide his joy, act calm with his house mates, and burn the dear letters. His fear and hope drive this dark, tense stretch of the tale.
53716-the-tuzuk-i-jahangiri-or-memoirs-o:
Emperor Jahangir's own memoirs fill the second volume of the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri in English dress. Alexander Rogers made the translation, and Henry Beveridge edited the text for print. The volume runs from the thirteenth New Year's feast of the reign to the nineteenth.

Inside, Jahangir records court gifts, ranks, posts, and hunts in close detail, year by year. The opening entry marks March 10, 1618, when his fifty-first year began with a weighing feast and fresh appointments. He notes fine horses, rings of ruby and emerald, letters from Shah Abbas of Persia, and lamps set round a tank at night. Readers get a ruler's daybook of Mughal court life, frank about favor, rank, and pleasure.
54374-red-spider-volume-1-of-2:
Red Spider is a novel in two volumes by Sabine Baring-Gould, published in London by Chatto and Windus in 1887. Baring-Gould had earlier written John Herring and Mehalah. This hosted file holds the first volume.

The preface tells how the tale began. As a child in the parish where the story is set, the author had a trusty nurse with a romantic past. Carrying him over a brook, she fell when a plank broke, held him above her head, and saved him unhurt. A German story read years later recalled her career to him. Baring-Gould wove her thread into pictures of village life in a forgotten corner of Devon. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
54375-red-spider-volume-2-of-2:
Volume two of Red Spider, a Devon novel by Sabine Baring-Gould, author of Mehalah, published by Chatto and Windus in 1887. The contents run from chapter nineteen, A Dead Dog, to a settlement and a bowl of broth.

The volume opens on a lamb-killing scare. Oliver Luxmore keeps watch badly, sleeping over cider posset while another lamb is worried. Hillary offers to watch for a guinea, and spends the nights with grave Honor, whose company, to his surprise, pleases him more than Kate's lively talk. Chapter titles promise a hand of glory, a hare hunt, bitter medicine, and a china dog. Baring-Gould, parson and folklorist, mixes Dartmoor superstition with a love story.
54431-isabel-clarendon-vol-1-of-2:
George Gissing wrote Isabel Clarendon, in two volumes, of which this is the first. Chapman and Hall published it at London in 1886. A French line heads the title: it was more than a view, alas, it was a world that had been effaced. The first chapter opens on the roads between Salcot East and Winstoke. Two roads join the parishes, the old and the new. The new road, made about mid-century, runs rather less than five miles.

The old road fetches a compass of well-nigh ten. The White Hart Inn at Salcot marks where the roads part, and Winstoke Rectory where they rejoin. Gissing notes the ancestral leisureliness of that corner of the county. The new road was built just when it was least needed. A silk manufactory at Salcot had decayed, and no market waited at Winstoke.
54432-isabel-clarendon-vol-2-of-2:
George Gissing wrote a novel in two volumes, with volume two printed in London in 1886. A French line fronts it, that more than a life, alas, a whole world had been effaced. Vincent Lacour rises at eleven on dark mornings and breakfasts by half past twelve. An elastic interval of leisure to begin the day seems to him a primary condition of tolerable existence.

From his windows he sees laden omnibuses hastening citywards. He thinks with contemptuous pity of the poor wretches who must present at bank, office, or shop by a fixed hour. Under no circumstances would he support life that way, he tells himself. The backwoods would be preferable. Gissing's cool eye on money, leisure, and class drives the tale of Isabel Clarendon.
54612-the-principles-of-biology-volume-1:
Herbert Spencer laid out his system of life science in this first volume, and Appleton issued it at New York in this print of 1910. The Principles of Biology aims to do for living things what his philosophy did for all things: find the laws beneath.

Organic matter opens the data of biology. The acts of forces on it, and its back-acts on them, follow. A close grasp of life itself comes next: life as a fit between the thing and its world. The degree of life, Spencer holds, tracks the degree of that fit. Growth, structure, and function fill the book's proofs. Waste and repair, heredity, and variation stand in the list, years before such sums were common in one book.
5462-the-sisters-volume-2:
Georg Ebers continues his ancient Egyptian romance The Sisters in this second volume at Memphis. The chapter opens inside the city's white walls, where the old palace of the kings stands amid bastions and ramparts. Built of plastered brick, it holds courts, corridors, chambers, and halls without number, with painted wooden outbuildings and a pillared banqueting hall in the Greek style.

The palace setting prepares the volume's court scenes, where Greek and Egyptian worlds meet in one royal household. Ebers describes the buildings with an archaeologist's care, making place part of the story. Readers get a richly detailed stretch of historical romance, set in a Memphis of stone, color, and ceremony.
5468-joshua-volume-2:
A chamberlain ushers Hosea into the audience chamber in the second volume of Georg Ebers's Joshua. Subjects summoned before the king usually waited for hours, but the Hebrew's patience is not tried long. The palace, normally full of a gay and noisy crowd, lies hushed in the deepest mourning, with slaves and warders silent.

The audience takes place against that mourning, giving the volume a solemn, courtly tone. Hosea, the figure later known as Joshua, stands before Egyptian power at a moment of grief and decision. Readers get a biblical-era romance told through palace ceremony, restraint, and waiting.
54751-the-war-in-syria-volume-2-of-2:
Sir Charles Napier, a commodore of the Royal Navy, wrote this account of his own war on the Syrian coast. Parker printed the second volume at London in 1842. Napier tells the tale in the first person, as the man who bore the brunt at sea.

A gale on the Egyptian and Syrian coasts opens the volume. Napier comes back to Marmorice Bay and trades stiff letters with the admiral, the general, and the envoy. The row turns on the Convention, the pact that settled the war's end. His answers fill page after page. Sea officers and state men alike clashed in this paper war, and Napier prints his side in full for the world to judge.
54923-in-wildest-africa-vol-2:
In Wildest Africa, volume two, was written by Schillings. Hutchinson published it in London in 1907. Frederic Whyte made the translation. Over 300 photographic studies, from the author's own negatives, fill the work. They were taken by day and by night. This volume runs from chapter eight to chapter sixteen, in the book's own numbering. A primeval forest opens it. Schillings hunts elephants with Wandorobo guides. Rhinoceros-hunting and the capturing of a lion follow. A dying race of giants and a vanishing feature of the velt take the middle.

Camping out on the velt and night photography close the volume. The picture list is long: Kilimanjaro, hippopotami, crested cranes, and a wounded buffalo. Masai spearmen and Wandorobo hunters stand among the portraits. Schillings was a pioneer of the camera in big-game country, and the book rests on his plates.
55178-poetical-works-of-robert-bridges-v:
Poetical Works of Robert Bridges, volume two, gathers the verse of the poet in one place. Smith, Elder printed the volume in London in 1898, at Oxford's university press. Its contents are Shorter Poems, New Poems, notes, and an index of first lines.

The Shorter Poems had a life before this gathering: four books came out at the Clarendon Press in 1890. Private and cheap issues followed through the decade. The New Poems, by contrast, are collected here for the first time. Book one of the Shorter Poems is given to a friend named only by initials. It opens with an elegy to a clear and gentle stream. The poet sits again where he sat as a boy, under the boughs. Swans sail past, fish lie cool in their pool, and the minster bell hums before evening.
55239-italian-yesterdays-vol-2:
Italian Yesterdays book two is a past and faith set by Mrs Hugh Fraser. A Dodd Mead house of New York brought it out in nineteen thirteen. Fraser wrote of a state wife life in Japan in past books of hers. Part one treats saints of the church in Rome in old days. Aglae and Boniface, two ways of love, open that saint scheme.

Pain, death by faith, and a church of Saint Boniface close their tale. Alexis the pilgrim ends as a rag beggar in that same church. Benedict the Blessed and his twin Scholastica fill the next part whole. Cave life, snares, and the start of monk life mark his path. Gregory the Great, pope in plague time, fills part three of the book.
55241-the-chautauquan-vol-05-november-18:
The Chautauquan, volume five, number two, came out in November eighteen hundred eighty four. The monthly served the Chautauqua Literary and Scientific Circle as its organ. Lewis Miller of Akron led the circle that year. J H Vincent ran its course of home study.

Set reading for November leads the issue. Richard Grant White writes on the bonds of speech. Home chemistry takes up the traits of water. Greek life and Greek myth fill two study parts. Drink and its causes get a stern science lesson. Kitchen work treats wheat, rye, and corn in turn. Star maps for November and notes for local circles close the plan. Self-taught adults round the country used such guides.
55458-the-curse-of-kehama-volume-1-of-2:
Robert Southey wrote The Curse of Kehama, a long poem in two volumes, here in its third edition from Longman of London, 1812. Southey inscribes the poem to Walter Savage Landor, the author of Gebir. A proverb heads the title page: curses are like young chickens, they always come home to roost.

The preface lays the poem's foundation in Hindu belief. Prayers, penances, and sacrifices, Southey writes, possess an inherent value, owing nothing to the motive of the man who performs them. They are drafts upon heaven which the gods cannot refuse to pay. By this road the worst men have gained power formidable to the deities themselves. Kehama is such a man, a rajah whose penances buy him godlike force, and whose curse drives the tale. Poetry readers of 1812 got India as a stage for a war of spells.
55829-history-of-spanish-and-portuguese-:
Bouterwek wrote a past of Spain's and Portugal's letters in two books. Ross turned it from the German into English for this press. Volume one, on Spain's letters, came out in London in 1823. No like work had yet come out in English, its front holds. Yet the theme had shown rich gains where men had dug, it says.

Snips of lore from those lands had pleased all who found them. But snips lack the whole shape that a true past gives in full. Bouterwek spans bards, plays, prose, and court verse in his plan. Names and works are set in time's own road for the eye. His front words beg a fair read for a much felt gap. Letters fans get a first map.
55886-on-molecular-and-microscopic-scien:
Mary Somerville wrote On Molecular and Microscopic Science, and John Murray issued the first of two volumes in London in eighteen hundred sixty nine. Somerville had won fame for books on the heavens and on physical geography. Friends such as John Herschel and John Tyndall helped check sheets for the press.

Part one treats atoms and the stuff of matter. It takes up force, the study of mixed stuff, and waste put to use in coal tar colors. Sun light split by a prism gets a long section. Part two turns to plant life seen through lenses. Sea weeds, fungi, lichens, and mosses each get a full account. Tiny sea forms face the title page.
55987-letters-of-asa-gray-vol-2:
Jane Loring Gray edited the letters of her husband Asa Gray, the botanist, in two volumes copyrighted in 1893. Volume two opens with a second journey in Europe. Gray sailed for England with Mrs Gray in a sailing packet on June 11, 1850. Steamers ran regularly, but the longer voyage was chosen for her health.

In England Gray renewed old friendships and met younger men of science at Mr Ward's house. A letter to John Torrey from Ghent, dated July 16, 1850, regrets the delay in writing. Later sections hold letters to Darwin and others. Travel in Europe and America and final journeys close the volume, which runs to 1888.
56033-old-virginia-and-her-neighbours-vo:
The second volume of Old Virginia and Her Neighbours by John Fiske. Houghton Mifflin first published the work in 1897. This volume opens with the coming of the Cavaliers. Fiske depicts the colony in rich detail. Farms, game, and songbirds fill his pages. Virginia also stood near the hoped-for Northwest Passage. He contrasts her plenty with a barer New England.

Fiske then corrects popular errors about the Cavalier migration. The Cavalier and Roundhead split, he argues, was political, not social. Family histories carry much of the evidence. The Lees and the Washingtons receive long treatment. George Washington's ancestry gets its own discussion. His detailed contents list argues a thesis throughout. Genealogy and county names preserve real history.
56396-history-of-spanish-and-portuguese-:
The second volume of Frederick Bouterwek's history of Spanish and Portuguese literature is given wholly to Portugal. Thomasina Ross translated the work from the German, and Boosey and Sons published it at London in 1823. Bouterwek begins with the rise of Portuguese poetry at the end of the thirteenth century. King Diniz was himself a poet, and the royal family produced more. The great songbooks of the age are called the Cancioneiros Geraes.

The second book runs from the start of the sixteenth century toward the end of the seventeenth, the age when Portuguese power and poetry rose together. Bernardim Ribeyro and his romance Menina e Moça get close attention, and Camoens stands behind the whole account as the one Portuguese name English readers knew. Bouterwek drew on a learned Portuguese friend for much of his matter.
56535-spain-in-1830-vol-2:
Henry Inglis, author of Solitary Walks through Many Lands, wrote this account of Spain in 1830, and Whittaker, Treacher and Company published the second volume at London in 1831. The volume opens with the journey from Madrid through La Mancha, across the Sierra Morena, and by Cordova to Seville.

The contents promise the gardens of Aranjuez, a reformed robber as traveling companion, the husbandry of La Mancha, and the wine of Val de Penas, with Don Quixote never far away. In Seville, Inglis studies Moorish customs, the cathedral, the Alcazar, Murillo's pictures, and the orange trade. A chapter on Xeres gives ten years of sherry export tables and the making of pale and brown sherry. Wretched Cordova, its great mosque, and the descent of the Guadalquivir to Cadiz fill out the Andalusian journey.
57126-the-greek-philosophers-vol-1-of-2:
Alfred William Benn wrote this history of Greek philosophy, volume one of two, published at London in 1882. Much of it first appeared in the Westminster Review, and the preface defends treating the subject as a connected whole.

A critic who singles out one thinker, Benn argues, exaggerates his hero and credits him with ideas borrowed from predecessors. A new idea becomes intelligible only by tracing the tendencies it continues, combines, or contradicts. He acknowledges deep debts to Zeller's great German history, above all where knowledge of a philosopher rests on fragments or second-hand reports. Later chapters of the second volume treat the sceptics, the religious revival, and Plotinus. Students get Greek thought as one system, in English prose.
57326-the-history-of-duelling-vol-1-of-2:
J G Millingen wrote The History of Duelling, with tales of famed encounters. Richard Bentley issued volume one in London in eighteen hundred forty one. Its bounds run from the first ages to the author’s own day. Single fights throw light on each age’s manners, Millingen holds.

True duelling was unknown to the ancients, his second part argues. Their wars gave set combats: the Battle of the Thirty stands famed. Kings sent challenges in that bold age: Francis and Charles the Fifth. Ordeals gave the duel its root in the wild north faiths, he holds. Gundebald, king of the Burgundians, set the code of the judicial fight. Hot iron, hot and cold water, cross, and poison tried the accused. Paid champions fought for those who could not wield a blade. Court ladies watched those grim shows from their high seats.
57365-thames-valley-villages-volume-1-of:
Thames Valley Villages, volume one of two, is a topographical book by Charles G Harper. The title page matter lists Harper's many works on English roads and places. His road books cover the Portsmouth Road, the Dover Road, the Bath Road, and the Great North Road to Scotland.

He also wrote literary landmarks of the Ingoldsby country and of Hardy's Wessex, books on the Dorset and South Devon coasts, and tales of haunted houses. This volume turns his eye from the great highways to the villages of the Thames valley. It is the first of a pair, the second being a companion volume. Harper wrote and drew his way across England for readers who loved its roads, inns, and villages. His books mix history, anecdote, and description of place. The Thames volume belongs to the same shelf of journeys on foot and by coach.
57366-thames-valley-villages-volume-2-of:
Charles Harper wrote Thames Valley Villages, of which this file holds the second volume. Harper made his name with books on England's great roads: the Portsmouth, Dover, Bath, and Exeter roads among them, and volumes on the Hardy country and the old inns of England. Here he turns from the highway to the villages along the Thames, visiting them in turn with his pen and pencil.

Books of this kind mixed history, anecdote, and drawing. A coaching road or a river valley gave Harper his thread, and each village along it a chapter of church, inn, and famous residents. Harper's two volumes preserve that world village by village, written for readers who liked their topography served with stories.
57450-cassell-s-book-of-birds-vol-2:
Thomas Rymer Jones reworked Cassell's Book of Birds, Volume Two. Cassell, Petter, and Galpin issued it at London. Doctor Brehm's text stands behind the work. Four volumes hold the whole set. Four hundred engravings aid the text in all. Colored plates join the black cuts there.

A purple crested corythaix fronts this volume's view. It stands at natural size in that plate. Catchers continued open the contents here. Hawks of many kinds lead that part. The Laughing Hawk and Double-toothed Hawk stand named. Sparrow Hawk and Gos Hawk follow in the list. Singing hawks take their own group next. Raptorial birds fill the early pages in force. The eagles open their clan after them. A household bird book from Brehm's great German work put hawks and eagles on Victorian parlor tables in fine cuts.
5751-st-george-and-st-michael-volume-2:
Volume two of St George and St Michael picks up the romance at chapter seventeen, with a fire engine, moonlight and apple blossoms, and an enchanted chair. Molly and a white horse follow, with a damsel who falls sick. A cataract comes next, with Amanda, Dorothy, and Lord Herbert. A great mogul, Richard Heywood, a witch's cottage, and the moat of the keep carry the tale toward Raglan stables and an apparition.

The second volume deepens the Civil War romance, as lovers, marquises, and household folk navigate siege, loyalty, and rumor. Readers who finished the first volume will find the same blend of history, mystery, and domestic feeling, now with higher stakes. The story rewards reading in order, since its charms and dangers grow from choices made in earlier chapters.
57566-on-molecular-and-microscopic-scien:
On Molecular and Microscopic Science, volume two, is a science work by Mary Somerville. Spottiswoode printed it in London for the two volume set. Somerville also wrote The Mechanism of the Heavens and Physical Geography. Her Connection of the Physical Sciences stands in that author list too. A Latin tag hails God as great in great things and greatest in least.

The frontispiece shows Galeolaria lutea, a small sea creature in fine detail. Volume two presses into the minute world that lenses reveal to man. Crystals, cells, and tiny life forms fill its plates and its chapters. Somerville wrote for general readers who sought sound science in plain form. Few women of her age won such rank in science publishing.
57570-famous-composers-and-their-works-v:
John Knowles Paine, Theodore Thomas, and Karl Klauser edit lives of the great composers in volume two of a set issued by J B Millet Company at Boston. Copyright dates to 1891; this printing is 1906. Music files ride with the text.

Franz Joseph Haydn opens the volume. He was born in the night of March 31, 1732, at Rohrau on the river Leitha. The village is so small that common maps omit it. His father Mathias was a master wheelwright, from a line of humble hand-toilers. His mother Maria Koller cooked in Count Harrach's household. Three of the family's twelve children grew into musicians. Johann Michael became a church composer. Johann Evangelist sang without special excellence. Steel engravings and printed music season the lives. The set served parlour readers who played what they read about.
57628-the-principles-of-psychology-volum:
The Principles of Psychology, volume one of two, is the great treatise of William James, professor of psychology in Harvard University. Henry Holt of New York published this edition in 1918. James dedicates it to his dear friend François Pillon, in acknowledgment of what he owes to the Critique Philosophique. His preface admits the book's scale frankly.

The treatise grew up, he writes, in connection with his classroom instruction, though some chapters are more metaphysical than suits beginners. The work has grown to a length no one can regret more than the writer himself. A man must be sanguine, he jokes, to hope for many readers of fourteen hundred continuous pages. Yet by skipping judiciously, many sorts of readers will find it of use. A note preserved in the copy gives his reading advice.
57634-the-principles-of-psychology-volum:
Principles of Psychology, volume two of two, is the second half of the great work by William James. James held the psychology chair at Harvard when he wrote the landmark text. Henry Holt of New York issued this printing of the second volume in 1918. Contents here begin at chapter seventeen, on sensation and its split from perception.

Imagination follows, with James on vague images and the visile, audile, and motile types. Galton researches on mental imagery feed that chapter of the classic work. Sensation, contrast, and the projection of feeling outward ground the volume opening. Students gain the mature James on mind in the form that taught generations.
57639-pumps-and-hydraulics-part-2-of-2:
Pumps and Hydraulics, part two of two, is a trade manual by William Rogers on pumps of every kind. Audel published it in New York and London, with rights dated nineteen o five. Part one holds the general ground; this part takes the special machines in turn. Its long title page lists hand pumps, power pumps, and steam pumps among the subjects.

Air pumps, vacuum pumps, and compressors open the contents of this second part. The air lift pump and the steam fire engine follow in their own sections. Mining, marine, and sugar house pumps get grouped treatment in the middle. Valve setting, management, and working rules come with tables for the engineer. A glossary of pump terms and a history of the art are added. The elements of water and air science close the manual's scheme.
57701-the-history-of-duelling-vol-2-of-2:
John Gideon Millingen wrote The History of Duelling, printed in London by Richard Bentley in 1841. This file holds the second of the two volumes. Millingen, a doctor and fellow of the Royal Society, traces personal combat from the earliest times down to his own day.

The second volume deals chiefly with Great Britain and Ireland. It explains how trial by battle came to England with the followers of William the Conqueror, and how the practice slowly died out. Famous cases follow, along with the views of leading judges on the law against duels. Later chapters cover duels under James the First, including Lord Bacon's speech in the Star-Chamber. The book serves readers who want the facts and the law behind a deadly custom.
57756-exploration-of-the-valley-of-the-a:
Exploration of the Valley of the Amazon, part one of two, is a United States Navy report by Herndon and Gibbon. The Navy Department sent the two lieutenants to survey the river and its lands. A first plate shows the cathedral of Lima, drawn by Gibbon, at the front. Project Gutenberg holds the second part beside this first part of the work.

Herndon part descends from the Andes to the Amazon and down the great river to the sea. Gibbon part, in the second volume, treats the Bolivian tributaries of the system in its survey. The expedition of 1851 to 1852 was the first full American survey of the Amazon valley in print. Its reports of soil, timber, trade, and navigation fed both science and ambition in the United States. The work remains a baseline record of the valley before rubber, railways, and settlement remade its banks.
57771-exploration-of-the-valley-of-the-a:
Lardner Gibbon wrote part two of the Exploration of the Valley of the Amazon, an official report printed at Washington in 1854. The Navy Department directed the survey. Gibbon and William Lewis Herndon, both lieutenants in the United States Navy, split the great river between them. Herndon's part one appeared separately. Congress ordered ten thousand extra copies of the reports for the House of Representatives.

Gibbon's half follows his route through Bolivia and down the tributaries toward the main stream. A lithograph at the front shows llamas traversing the Andes laden with silver. The President transmitted the report to Congress in January 1854. The two parts together gave American merchants and officials their first full survey of the Amazon valley: its rivers, peoples, products, and prospects for trade. The report remains a primary record of the region before steam navigation changed it.
57777-james-russell-lowell-a-biography-v:
Horace Elisha Scudder wrote this biography of James Russell Lowell, and Houghton, Mifflin and Company published its second volume at Boston and New York in November 1901. The frontispiece shows Lowell in 1882, from a painting, and other plates give his study and the hall at Elmwood, his Cambridge home.

Volume two opens with Lowell and the war for the Union, from 1858 to 1865, when he superintended the Atlantic Monthly, a magazine of literature, art, and politics. Chapters on his poetry and prose, a third journey in Europe, and politics follow. The Spanish mission and the English mission take up his years as an American minister abroad. Scudder closes with the return to private life and the last years. Appendices follow on the Lowell ancestry, a list of Lowell's writings in order of publication, and the Lowell memorial in Westminster Abbey.
5796-journeys-through-bookland-vol-2:
Volume two of Journeys Through Bookland, edited by Sylvester for children, opens with a little chimney sweep from the days of open fireplaces. A footnote explains that houses once held a network of huge chimneys through which a small boy could work his way, brushing soot as he went. From that working child's story, the volume leads young readers through further tales, poems, and lessons.

The collection is built for family reading, mixing classic stories with guidance for parents and teachers. Children meet adventure, fancy, and moral tales in short, manageable pieces, while adults get a structured path through children's literature. The volume suits homeschooling, bedtime reading, and anyone building a young reader's library one journey at a time.
58046-the-red-court-farm-a-novel-vol-1-o:
The Red Court Farm, volume one, is Mrs Henry Wood's novel in the Tauchnitz copyright edition, volume 965 of the Collection of British Authors. Bernhard Tauchnitz of Leipzig published it in 1868, in two volumes, for continental circulation. Mrs Wood's name sold the book: East Lynne heads her long list.

The story's ground is a bleak plateau on the English coast near France, with old whispers of smuggling. Below the cliffs lies the Half-moon, a small beach closed in by rocks, reached from the sea at high water and by a narrow path at low. Robert Hunter and his wife open the tale; Clara Lake's dream follows, then an accident. Red or green, Justice Thornycroft's visit, going fishing, and catching a chill build the middle. Colour blindness, Mary Jupp's explosion, and the dream worked out lead to the new mistress of the Red Court.
58047-the-red-court-farm-a-novel-vol-2-o:
Volume two of The Red Court Farm is a novel by Mrs. Henry Wood, issued at Leipzig in 1868. Tauchnitz published it in his collection of British authors for continental readers. Wood had written East Lynne and Trevlyn Hold. This volume opens its third part at a school in London. Two years have passed, and it is June again. Miss Jupp keeps a small select boarding school at Kensington.

Eighteen chapters carry the volume's action. Captain Copp and Isaac Thornycroft's stratagem come early. Wilful disobedience and a last interview raise the tension. A crowd in the early morning and a shooting from the heights turn the tale dark. A coroner's inquest and a funeral follow. Curious rumours and a ghost at the churchyard porch deepen the mystery. The truth is disclosed to Justice Thornycroft at the close.
5809-following-the-equator-a-journey-aro:
Part two of Mark Twain's Following the Equator covers chapters nine through nineteen, on the way to Australia and beyond. Chapter nine opens with a Pudd'nhead Wilson maxim that human environment makes climate, then notes a September night close to Australia, with Sydney fifty miles distant. Passengers are called to the bow to see a fine sight in the dark, where the sea's surface escapes the eye.

We travel with Twain through ports, lectures, and colonial encounters, hearing his jokes about climate, custom, and empire. The part balances shipboard life with shore excursions, as Twain tests guidebook claims against what he sees. It suits readers following Twain around the world in order, and it stands alone as vivid travel writing from the age of steam.
58093-round-the-sofa-vol-2:
Round the Sofa is a set of tales by the author of Mary Barton and the Life of Charlotte Bronte. The hosted text is volume two of two, issued at London in eighteen fifty nine. Contents name five pieces. They are The Accursed Race, The Doom of the Griffiths, Half a Lifetime Ago, The Poor Clare, and The Half Brothers.

The frame of the book places a company round a sofa, telling tales in turn. Mr Dawson had often come in and out while his sister told of Lady Ludlow, the text begins. The Monday after that tale ended, the company felt at a loss for talk. They had grown used to listening, the narrator says. Her brother offers a paper he drew up for a society. It was compiled from a French book, he warns, and is rather dry in itself.
5819-the-gilded-age-part-2:
Part two of The Gilded Age, by Twain and Charles Dudley Warner, covers chapters ten through eighteen, and it opens days after a funeral. Something happens that will change the drift of Laura's life and shape her character in greater or lesser degree. Major Lackland, once a man of note in his state, a man of extraordinary natural ability and learning, enters the story as Laura's fortunes turn.

Readers follow the novel's satire of speculation, politics, and social climbing through Laura's widening world. The part balances Washington schemes with personal choices, showing how money and reputation tempt even strong characters. It suits readers following the Gilded Age in order, since Laura's decisions here set much of the later novel in motion.
58345-within-the-maze-a-novel-vol-1-of-2:
Mrs Henry Wood wrote Within the Maze, issued in the Tauchnitz line of British authors at Leipzig in eighteen hundred seventy two. Wood had won vast fame with East Lynne. Volume one holds twenty two chapters. The right to English the tale stayed held by the press.

Widow Andinnian lives in an ugly old house by a market town. Fine gardens hide it from the noise of the road. Her late husband left six hundred pounds a year in thirds. Adam, her loved first son, shares her home and hearth. Karl, the young son, serves as an army officer. He has two hundred a year and his pay alone. A will that slighted Adam stirs her wrath. Lucy Cleeve and a dark secret drive the plot.
58346-within-the-maze-a-novel-vol-2-of-2:
Mrs Henry Wood, author of East Lynne, wrote this novel, whose second volume Bernhard Tauchnitz printed at Leipzig in 1872 in his Collection of British Authors, a copyright edition in two volumes. The contents of this volume promise Scotland Yard, a lawyer's office, afternoon service, and watching a house, among its twenty-three chapters and conclusion.

The volume opens the morning after a thunderstorm, with Lucy coming down to breakfast with sad eyes and a pale face. Her night has been one of mental pain. She wears a mask of cheerfulness for Karl's sake, and the Lloyds are expected from Basham to see the hot-house plants at Foxwood. Threads named in the chapter list, from Nurse Chaffen on duty to news for Tatton and Cleeve at fault, carry the household's hidden trouble toward its end.
5837-sketches-new-and-old-part-2:
Part two of Mark Twain's Sketches New and Old opens with Answers to Correspondents, written about 1865. Addressing a moral statistician, Twain declares he wants none of the man's statistics, having lit his pipe with the whole batch. He hates such people, he says, always ciphering how much a man's health is injured and his intellect impaired by this or that habit.

Twain offers his epistolary comedy at its sharpest, as fake letters invite real jokes about reformers, numbers, and human folly. The part gathers further sketches in the same vein, each answering a correspondent with wit rather than patience. It suits readers who enjoy Twain's early newspaper humor, and anyone who has ever wanted to answer a scold with a laugh.
5855-personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-vo:
Volume one, part two of Sheridan's Personal Memoirs covers chapters nine through fifteen, opening with an expedition to Booneville. Headings treat destroying supplies, Confederate stragglers, success of the expedition, a reconnaissance, and the importance of bodily sustenance, before the Battle of Booneville and a recommendation for appointment as brigadier general. The expedition, Sheridan notes, was composed of the Second Michigan and other troops.

Readers get Sheridan as a rising cavalry commander, learning raiding, supply, and battle in the western theater. The memoir favors brisk operational detail, with hunger and horses mattering as much as heroics. It suits Civil War readers following Sheridan's early career, and it bridges his cadet years and his later fame as an army commander.
5861-personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-:
Part two of Grant's Personal Memoirs covers chapters fourteen through twenty-five, from the Mexican War's lessons to the Pacific Coast. Chapter fourteen opens with return of the army, marriage, orders to the Pacific Coast, crossing the Isthmus, and arrival at San Francisco. Grant notes that his Mexican War experience advantaged him afterward, teaching practical lessons and bringing regular officers into personal acquaintance.

We follow a young officer between wars, as peacetime service, travel, and separation shape the future general. The memoir's plain narrative favors marching, posts, and duties over romance, letting routine reveal character. It suits Civil War readers tracing Grant's formation, and it bridges his Mexican service and his later return to command.
58633-an-irish-cousin-vol-1-2:
Geilles Herring and Martin Ross wrote An Irish Cousin, a novel in two volumes, of which this file holds the first, issued at London by Richard Bentley and Son in 1889. Part one is named An Experiment. The narrator comes to Ireland on the Alaska and meets Aunt Jane, cousin Willy, and the Master of Durrus in the early chapters, each headed by a scrap of verse.

Impressions of the new country, an Irish Sunday, and a servant named Moll fill the middle. Schooling, the turf, the chase, and the road share a chapter, and the Moycullen hounds carry the hunt. The book is a comedy of Anglo Irish life seen by a newcomer, written by two hands that would make the manner famous.
58634-an-irish-cousin-vol-2-2:
An Irish Cousin, volume two, continues a novel by Geilles Herring and Martin Ross, published in London by Richard Bentley and Son in 1889. The volume holds the second part of the story, called The Cost of It. Martin Ross would later write, with her cousin Somerville, the Irish Resident Magistrate tales.

Chapter headings carry verse mottoes. Supper Extras opens this volume's action, and a study scene, a churchyard at Myross, and the entrance of Willy follow. A hand at the gate and a hidden tide appear in later titles. The first-person narrator watches a cousin whose visits stir the household. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
58704-the-sunny-south-oo-logist-vol-1-no:
The Sunny South Oölogist, volume 1, number 2, is a journal for egg collectors, published at Gainesville, Texas, in April 1886 at fifty cents a year. Its opening notes come from Southern California, where heavy rains in the lowlands and snow in the mountains have reshuffled the birds.

Driven down from their haunts, Cedarbirds, Robins, and Catbirds have taken refuge in the orange groves and vineyards, feeding by the roadsides and probing dead leaves for bugs. They do not breed there. When warm weather sets in they retire to the Sierra Madre, safe from the schoolboy egg destroyer. Water birds abound too: a hunter's bag of twenty or thirty ducks may hold twelve to fifteen species. The writer lists sets of eggs he has taken himself: Cinnamon Teal, Baldpate, Mallard, Ruddy Duck, and others. He praises the tule lands of Gospel Swamp, sixty miles from Los Angeles.
58708-the-british-journal-of-photography:
One weekly number of The British Journal of Photography, number 613 of volume nineteen, is dated February 2, 1872. It leads with an editorial on the character of certain preservative films used in dry-plate work. The piece answers a German writer who announced, as a discovery, that tannined films take moisture evenly and lose it gradually, like clean glass.

The editors reply that the fact was long known to dry-plate workers, and they turn to a live dispute. Carey Lea held that nearly complete drying made a dry plate more sensitive, while many operators swore by preservatives that kept the film semi-moist. The journal sides with Lea. Its case in point is an iodide of silver film, washed and coated with ferrocyanide of potassium. Such a film stays sensitive while moist but slows when fully dried, unless honey or glycerine is added.
58768-on-horseback-through-asia-minor-vo:
On Horseback Through Asia Minor is a travel book in two volumes by Captain Fred Burnaby. The hosted text holds volume one, with portrait and maps for the ride. Burnaby had won fame before this with his book A Ride to Khiva. The journey crosses Asia Minor on horseback in the saddle with the author.

Such rides mixed hard travel with sharp notes on land, troops, and peoples met. A soldier traveller writes for readers who want both route facts and living scenes. Proofreading notes record that old spelling is kept and clear print errors are fixed. Errata from the end of the volume have been folded into the text.
58829-teutonic-mythology-gods-and-goddes:
Viktor Rydberg wrote a study of Teutonic mythology, here in Volume Two of three. Rasmus B Anderson turned the Swedish work into English for the Norroena Society. The Viking form was issued in 1906, in just six hundred and fifty sets. The copy shown is Number 99 of that small run.

A plate shows Valkyries bearing a slain warrior to Valhalla, home of Odin. Heimdal, warder at the rainbow bridge, gets a full caption of lore. Chapters treat Mimer's Grove, the word Hel, and the kingdom of death. Scholars gain deep, dated study of northern gods and the world below.
58841-the-holyhead-road-the-mail-coach-r:
Volume two of Charles Harper's Holyhead Road, the mail-coach road to Dublin, published at London in 1902 and illustrated by the author and from old prints. This volume runs from Birmingham to Holyhead.

Harper wrote the same treatment for the Brighton, Portsmouth, Dover, Bath, Exeter, Great North, and Norwich roads. The plates show early days on the London and Birmingham Railway, Turner's Dudley, Wolverhampton across sixty years, and the Vale of Llangollen. Text illustrations take in Shrewsbury's market place, Offa's Dyke, the Ladies of Llangollen at Plas Newydd, the Waterloo Bridge, Penrhyn Castle, and the Menai Bridge. Travelers get the great Irish road town by town, in its coaching prime and railway aftermath.
58897-the-master-of-st-benedict-s-vol-1-:
Volume one of The Master of St Benedict’s, by Alan St Aubyn, is a Cambridge college tale. Chatto and Windus issued the book in London in eighteen hundred ninety three. St Aubyn had written A Fellow of Trinity before this. The Master, full of days and honour, opens the tale.

Past eighty, the Master had won wealth, fame, and late love. His road began on a bleak Yorkshire moor at the plough. A kind vicar saw the boy’s love of books and freed him. School in the next town, then a small Cambridge award, followed. Broad north speech and plain coats made him a freshman’s butt. Witty men mocked the poor youth who beat them at exams. He stayed up while his mockers went down in time. Dick’s small daughter and Pamela Gwatkin fill this first half.
58945-the-master-of-st-benedict-s-vol-2-:
Volume two of The Master of St Benedict's, by Alan St Aubyn, came out in London in 1893. St Aubyn had written A Fellow of Trinity and The Junior Dean. This half holds chapters fifteen to twenty-eight of a college tale. Its world is a Cambridge college and the town lane by Newnham.

Rain and wind open chapter fifteen, in the lane. Lucy waits late for a tryst, her umbrella blown inside out. The man she waits for is not there. His bed maker found him at dawn under his table, his drink case empty. Eric, up early at his books, was sent in his place. Word comes that the Master has passed a better night. More heads name a cousin Mary and the October term. College fans get love and drink in a fond tale of youth.
58984-audubon-the-naturalist-a-history-o:
Francis Hobart Herrick tells the bird artist's life in volume two of a two-volume biography. D Appleton and Company issued it at New York and London in 1917. Herrick taught biology at Western Reserve University.

A Healy portrait of Audubon from 1838 fronts the volume. The summary of contents shows the later career. An obituary of Audubon ran in London on the day he reached New York. John Bachman becomes his friend, and a winter in Charleston follows. His great folios go out as gifts. He travels to Florida with two assistants. St Augustine and the mud of East Florida bring misadventures. Herrick built the life from letters and papers. His book stayed the standard full account of Audubon for decades.
5899-the-physiology-of-marriage-part-2:
Balzac continues The Physiology of Marriage in its second part, on means of defence, interior and exterior. A Hamlet epigraph asks to be or not to be, and Meditation Ten opens a treatise on marital policy, supposing a man has reached the position described in the first part. From there, Balzac weighs how husbands may guard a marriage, and what such guarding costs.

Readers get Balzac's witty, provocative analysis at full stretch, mixing maxims, cases, and social observation. The second part favors strategy and irony, treating marriage as a field of maneuver as much as a bond of love. It suits readers who finished the first part, and anyone curious about Balzac's famously unsentimental view of Parisian married life.
59312-cancer-its-cause-and-treatment-vol:
Cancer, Its Cause and Treatment is a medical work in two volumes, and the hosted text is volume two. The copy shown is dated nineteen seventeen in its heading matter. A list of the author's other books stands at the front. They treat diet and hygiene in diseases of the skin, eczema, and acne. One volume analyses thirty thousand cases of skin disease, the list says.

A dedication in the copy thanks a skin and cancer hospital for its help. Its kind appreciation encouraged the author in his clinical work there, it says. A formulary for treatment went with his compendium of skin diseases, the list notes. The present volume carries his cancer work forward from a first part priced in the same list. His quarter century of skin practice stands behind the set, the list implies.
59550-cancer-its-cause-and-treatment-vol:
Cancer, Its Cause and Treatment, volume one, is a set of medical lectures. Duncan Bulkley, a New York doctor, gave them at the Skin and Cancer Hospital. Paul Hoeber of New York issued the lectures in February nineteen fifteen. Bulkley gives the book to the governors of that hospital for their aid.

Six lectures treat the nature of cancer and its spread across the globe. Frequency and place distribution fill the second lecture in the set here. The metabolism of cancer and the relation of diet to cancer follow next. Medical treatment of cancer, short of the knife, fills lecture five in full. Clinical considerations and conclusions close the course, with a bibliography after.
59578-dissertations-on-inflammation-vol-:
John Burns, surgeon in Glasgow, wrote dissertations on inflammation, with volume two printed at Glasgow in 1800. The volume holds the cure of simple inflammation and its consequences, carried on from the first. The phagedenic and some other species of inflammation follow. The spongoid inflammation, the scrophulous inflammation, and the cancerous inflammation take a dissertation each.

Archaic spelling stands as printed in this copy, the notes say, though a few plain errors have been fixed. Burns sorts inflammations by their course and their look. Each kind, he holds, sets up its own actions in the part and requires its own peculiar treatment. The method of cure is therefore arranged under the heads of the different endings of inflammation. Surgeons of 1800 get a careful system here, from a Glasgow teacher writing before germs were known.
59584-ultima-thule-or-a-summer-in-icelan:
Richard F Burton wrote Ultima Thule, or A Summer in Iceland, in two volumes, of which this is the first. William P Nimmo published it at London and Edinburgh in 1875. Maps and illustrations accompany a historical introduction. The frontispiece shows Reykjavik, the capital of Iceland. Burton dedicated the book from Trieste in March 1875 to Robert Mackay Smith of Edinburgh. Smith was himself a traveller in Iceland and a friend to the Icelander.

Burton thanks Smith for information, hospitality, and kindness at Edinburgh and elsewhere. He warns that Smith is not answerable for his freedom of speech or unpopular opinions. A motto from Tasso heads the dedication: our supreme good lies on the toilsome steep, not among founts and flowers. The Iceland summer gave his readers a far northern land then little visited.
59585-ultima-thule-or-a-summer-in-icelan:
Richard Burton wrote this account of a summer in Iceland, published by Nimmo in London and Edinburgh in 1875. Volume two of two opens with a photo of a Danish fishing station at Berufjörð. Chapter six treats a press visit to the Latin school, with libraries and collections in its summary.

Maps by Gunnlaugsson and notes on natural history and anthropology fill that chapter's tail. Tourists and tours, guides and horses, horse gear, traps and tents fill chapter seven. Excursions about Reykjavik, its islands, hot baths and salmon river follow, in Burton's sharp-eyed survey of a poor, proud island waking to visitors.
59593-history-of-denmark-sweden-and-norw:
Volume one of Dunham's History of Denmark, Sweden, and Norway was printed in London in 1839, for Longman and Taylor, as part of the Cabinet Cyclopaedia. That long series was conducted by Dionysius Lardner, with the help of eminent literary and scientific men. Dunham is billed as author of the History of Spain and Portugal in the same shelf of histories.

The preface opens on the difficulty of the ground. Scandinavia before the tenth century is the region of romance, of the wildest legends. Such legends may enter the severe domain of history only so far as they illustrate its truths, and the history proceeds on that rule. The two volumes carry the northern kingdoms from those misty beginnings toward modern times. This first volume sets out the early centuries of Denmark, Sweden, and Norway together, as their affairs were then tangled together.
59657-history-of-denmark-sweden-and-norw:
Volume two of the History of Denmark, Sweden, and Norway is by Dunham. A Longman house of London brought it out in eighteen thirty nine. It stands in the Cabinet set led by Dionysius Lardner in that age. Dunham wrote the past of Spain and Portugal in a past set book. A front cut shows Copenhagen in an engraved plate in this print.

Heads in its scheme treat the Orkney isles and their line of jarls. Rognevald, Sigurd, Hallad, and Einar stand in that jarl rank there. Find and plant of Iceland and Greenland fill next heads in scheme. A claimed find of North America gets a facts piece in that run. Ruric found of the Russian realm by north men closes those heads.
5967-what-s-mine-s-mine-volume-2:
George MacDonald opens the second volume with a story told by Ian, about a widow left poor after a well-to-do husband's death. Work is hard to find, hard to do, and hardly paid, yet the woman trusts in God and holds that whatever he pleases must be right. Only hearts of grace, Ian says, grasp such struggles.

The volume's chapters continue with Rob of the Angels, a new house, the brothers, the princess, the stag's head, Annie of the shop, and an encounter. Love allodial, a tomb, and Mercy calling on Grannie follow.
59710-thirty-letters-on-various-subjects:
Thirty letters on set subjects were printed at London in 1783 for Cadell and Evans. A note at the front plays with the old game of found papers. Cervantes and Sterne, it says, were not above such shifts, but the trick has served too often.

The first letter treats the force of custom. The writer's retirement from the world, he warns, will give his views an odd air. Truth, he says, may need the help of custom before we feel its force, yet custom alone has worked greater wonders. It has blessed nonsense in all the arts, the sciences, and even in faith itself. Later letters take up riches, cards, and duelling, then tongues, painting, and music. Shakespeare and the kinship of the arts find their place in the first volume.
59711-thirty-letters-on-various-subjects:
Thirty Letters on Various Subjects, volume two of two, is an essay set printed in London in 1783. Cadell and Evans in the Strand printed the set, with Thorn and Son in Exeter. Contents of this volume run from letter nineteen to letter twenty nine and beyond. Criticism on Quarles, the old poet, opens the shown list of the letters.

On Warm Colouring and a false principle in painting exposed follow in the contents in order. On Self Production, some phrases explained, and obstructions in the way of fame come after in turn. On Alliteration and Literation, on common superstitions, and wrong representations of the solar system close the shown heads. The familiar letter was the essay form of the eighteenth century, and these range from painting to astronomy. Their author handles each subject as a letter to a friend, learned, curious, and at ease among the arts.
59912-the-rock-ahead-a-novel-vol-2:
The Rock Ahead, volume two, was written by Edmund Yates. Tauchnitz issued the copyright edition at Leipzig in 1868. Contents finish the second book and give a third. Pursuit, Rebuffed, and Gertrude Speaks open the part shown. Book three brings recognition, a mine laid, and an explosion. The Last Chance and Twelve Months After close the tale. Chapter four of book two opens on Clement's Inn. Clearance for the new law courts has swept much of it away since, the narrator notes. In the story's days it housed a shady crowd.

Insolvent clerks, third rate attorneys, and discount men fill its chambers. Agents, cheap newspaper writers, and needy men about town lodge there too. Yates paints the Inn as a pleasant Slough of Despond. His London of small debts is drawn from close knowledge.
59997-the-poetical-works-of-john-skelton:
The Poetical Works of John Skelton, volume one, presents the Tudor poet in a scholarly edition. Alexander Dyce edited the two volumes. Thomas Rodd published them in London in 1843. Notes and an account of the author accompany the poems. Dyce sought to replace a faulty old edition.

His preface tells the edition's story plainly. The volume of 1736 was incomplete and inaccurate. Chalmers merely reprinted it with all its errors. A Quarterly reviewer called for a competent new edition. Dyce took up the task, perhaps with too much confidence. Corruptions still defy his power to mend them. He struck out many of his own conjectures before printing. The collector Heber lent him a full set of Skelton's works.
59998-the-poetical-works-of-john-skelton:
The Poetical Works of John Skelton is a set in two parts, with notes and a tale of the man and his works by Dyce. The host text is the second part of the set. It was put out at London in eighteen forty three. The first piece of this part is the famed bird tale of the bard. Its full name calls it the book made by Master Skelton, bard of the crown.

A Latin word of the hand to his readers heads that piece. It bids the work grow vast while he lives. It calls his fame a gold fame in the years to come. Then the bird speaks in his own voice. My name is Parrot, a bird of the fair land, he says. By birth I was made of a strange kind.
60072-the-forlorn-hope-a-novel-vol-1-of-:
The Forlorn Hope, volume one of two, is a novel by Edmund Yates, printed at Leipzig in eighteen sixty seven. It appeared in Tauchnitz's Collection of British Authors for continental readers. Yates dedicates the volume to the actor Charles Fechter on its opening page. Seventeen chapters make up this first half of the tale.

Sir Duncan Forbes arrives at Kilsyth by hired carriage on a foggy autumn evening. Gillies swarm out to strip the carriage of its luggage in minutes. His man Dixon has a bath, warm linen, and a bright fire ready upstairs. Forbes, twenty eight and of the Household Brigade, is used to luxury and roughing alike. That night he feels life is not all beer and skittles, as the saying goes. Chapters ahead name a resolve, a leaden seal, and a cross examination.
6022-stories-by-foreign-authors-german-v:
Four German tales fill this volume, each in translation arranged with copyright owners or made fresh for the series. Berthold Auerbach gives Christian Gellert's Last Christmas, Leopold Kompert a Ghetto Violet, Wilhelm Hauff The Severed Hand, and Adelbert von Chamisso the famous Peter Schlemihl.

Auerbach opens on 22 December 1768, as three o'clock strikes from St. Nicholas tower in Leipzig and a gentle man in a loose overcoat leaves the university, followed by a troop of students. The collection samples German storytelling from sentiment to the uncanny, with a scholar, a ghetto flower, a severed hand, and a man who sells his shadow.
6042-the-diary-and-letters-of-madame-d-a:
Frances Burney, Madame d'Arblay, covers the years 1787 to 1792 in this second volume of diary and letters, with notes by W. C. Ward and Lord Macaulay's essay prefixed. The pages open on court duties at St. James's and Windsor, with the Queen's birthday drawing room and a serious dilemma.

Counsels of a court official, Mr. Turbulent's anxiety to introduce Mr. Wellbred, eccentric Mr. Bryant, bantering a princess, and the Duchess de Polignac at Windsor fill the early entries. Burney writes as an insider watching royalty at close range, noting manners, mishaps, and the small theater of court life.
60915-discourses-on-various-subjects-vol:
Discourses on Various Subjects, volume one of two, by Jacob Duché, rector of Christ Church and Saint Peter's in Philadelphia and formerly of Clare Hall, Cambridge, is the second edition. It was printed in London in 1780 and dedicated to Lady Juliana Penn.

The preface gives the preacher's ground. The discourses were preached in his two Philadelphia churches, where he became assistant minister in 1759 and rector in 1775. The reader will find no display of genius or of learning in them, he warns. His divinity is that of the Bible, and he appeals to no other standard of truth. From his own heart he has written to the hearts of others. Universal benevolence he counts the sublime of religion. Its true taste, he holds, comes only from the fountain of infinite love, by inward and spiritual means.
6096-amelia-volume-2:
Henry Fielding's Amelia, volume two, opens its fifth book with an old acquaintance, a brace of doctors, and much physical matter. Booth pays a visit to a noble lord, affairs of Sergeant Atkinson unfold, and matters requiring no preface give way to heroic matter and the heroic behavior of Colonel Bath.

The sixth book adds panegyrics on beauty, a history looking a little backwards, and an extraordinary turn. Fielding keeps Booth and Amelia amid doctors, lords, and soldiers, testing marriage under debt and temptation. The middle instalment alone holds the focus of this account, and neither its predecessor nor its successor enters the discussion.
6147-narrative-and-miscellaneous-papers-:
Thomas De Quincey opens his second volume with the heavens as revealed by Lord Rosse's telescopes. Modern superstition, Coleridge and opium-eating, the temperance movement, on war, and the last days of Immanuel Kant follow. A footnote credits J. P. Nichol's thoughts on the system of the world.

De Quincey recalls publishing, some years earlier, a paper from the German of Kant on the age of the earth. Kant wished not to count the earth's years, since a million more or less mattered little to him, but to settle a deeper question.
61470-life-of-edwin-forrest-the-american:
William Rounseville Alger wrote this life of Edwin Forrest, the American tragedian, and Lippincott published the second volume at Philadelphia in 1877 under a motto from As You Like It. The volume opens at chapter fourteen, on newspaper estimates of Forrest and the true standard of dramatic criticism.

Alger argues that the press, a necessity and a protection against other tyrannies, alloyed its benefits with abuse that Forrest suffered in the latter half of his life. A Philadelphia paper branded him a drunkard, though he was never intoxicated in his life, and withdrew the words under threat of a libel suit. A New York paper blamed him for the driving of Macready from the Astor Place Opera House, calling him the instigator of the outrage. Through his friend Theodore Sedgwick, Forrest demanded retraction, and the editor confessed he had written with no knowledge of facts to justify him.
6170-memorials-and-other-papers-volume-2:
De Quincey's second volume of Memorials opens with Klosterheim, The Sphinx's Riddle, and The Templars' Dialogues. Klosterheim begins in the winter of 1633, set in with unusual severity across Suabia and Bavaria, though scarcely past the first week of November.

The tale opens on 8 November, or 18 November by modern reckoning, when winter campaigns had become policy in the war sweeping Germany. Blooming Edens of peace and prosperity threatened to turn to howling wilderness, and vast tracts already had. Only the second collection is treated in this entry, with the first collection set aside for its own entry. War turns Eden-like lands into a howling waste.
6175-pierre-and-his-people-tales-of-the-:
A Prairie Vagabond opens Parker's second volume, with Little Hammer, a disappointment to missionaries, Hudson's Bay officials, Mounted Police, Crees, Blackfeet, and half-breeds alike. Oblivious to depreciation, he loves the Company's post at Yellow Quill and ranges Red Deer River hospitality.

Little Hammer salutes Sergeant Gellatly with a familiar How, borrows tobacco of half-breed women, and strangely pays it back with other tobacco. She of the Triple Chevron and Three Outlaws complete the volume. This account follows the second set of tales alone, leaving the other sets to be covered elsewhere. The volume keeps its humor dry and its north cold.
6187-northern-lights-volume-2:
To-Morrow opens Parker's second Northern Lights volume. A woman ironing a white petticoat lifts her head and says nothing is the matter with the world today, it is so good it almost hurts. Snow-tipped mountains, fir and cedar foothills, and maple and ash woods in autumn tints merge to one soft red tone.

A stream roars down a ravine, air braces nerves, and the passion of life answers the passion of living in her. She lays her iron on a hot stove and takes another, touching it with care. Qu'Appelle and The Stake and the Plumb-Line complete the volume.
61915-effie-ogilvie-the-story-of-a-young:
Mrs Oliphant continues the story of a young Scottish life in the second volume of Effie Ogilvie, issued in 1886. The volume opens at chapter thirteen, with Effie coming down a country road at twilight. She carries a dainty to a sick neighbor and holds the last rose from her uncle's south wall.

Fred meets her at the corner of the byeway, and the talk turns on the sweetness of old cottage roses over forced garden blooms. Effie takes his praise as praise of her home ground, not of herself, in a scene that shows her simple, pure cast of mind. Readers get a quiet, tender tale of a young woman, her home, and the claims of love, told in Oliphant's warm domestic manner.
6193-mrs-falchion-volume-2:
Mrs. Falchion, book two, opens on the slope of the Pacific, among hills of God, as a servant brings letters on the last evening of the college year. Examinations are over, and the narrator wonders where to spend holidays, choosing between Muskoka lakes and Yosemite Valley.

Because it is his first year in Canada, he prefers not to go beyond the Dominion. The first two letters, tradesmen's bills, do not interest him, but the third brings a thumping pleasure, though not from Miss Treherne. A weekly letter from her already came that morning.
62023-the-life-of-the-rev-george-whitefi:
Life of the Reverend George Whitefield, volume two of two, completes a life of the great preacher. Whitefield crossed the Atlantic again and again to preach to vast open air crowds. Transcriber notes record punctuation standardized and small capitals replaced for the reader. Spellings of the period have been left unchanged unless a note says otherwise.

Index references have not been checked for accuracy in this digital text, readers are warned. The second volume carries the revivalist through his later missions, fame, and death. Friend of Wesley and Franklin, Whitefield shaped religion on two continents in his century. Church historians gain a period life of the Grand Itinerant in full.
6207-the-trail-of-the-sword-volume-2:
Friends in Council opens the second epoch of The Trail of the Sword. Montreal and Quebec stand as cheerful in still iron winter as any city under a more cordial sky. Men loved, hated, made and broke bargains, lied to women, kept foolish honour with each other, and did deeds of valour for a song.

Through nature's stern soul ran men with hearts of summer. On a notable day in Iberville's life, a window in a low stone house on Notre Dame Street, Montreal, might show a priest joyously playing violin. Parker sets New France winter alight with talk, honour, and music.
6212-the-translation-of-a-savage-volume-:
The Passing of the Years opens Parker's second volume of The Translation of a Savage, with Lali's slow recovery and a change upon her. The strange ride has taken the last strong flicker of desire for savage life from her, and she now knows her position toward her husband.

He never loved her, she sees, and she served only as an instrument for unworthy retaliation. As soon as she can speak after her accident, she forbids writing to him of it and asks only that he hear she is well. Her new friends, caring for her herself, cannot refuse.
6216-the-pomp-of-the-lavilettes-volume-2:
Ferrol's recovery opens Parker's second volume of The Pomp of the Lavilettes, swifter than expected, with Christine as constant attendant and self-made nurse. No one seriously interferes, though the Cure protests, not vaguely, to Madame Lavilette, who now defies or evades him as convenient.

Linkage by marriage with nobility would justify Madame Lavilette's long-baffled hopes, while the parish gossips, little heard at Manor Casimbault. By and by the Cure stops visiting, but the regimental surgeon comes often and stays late, perhaps best placed to advise and warn. The second volume alone is the subject of this entry, and the first volume is not revisited here.
6220-the-trespasser-volume-2:
Strange Encounters opens Parker's second volume of The Trespasser, as Gaston sits on horseback in a quiet corner of grounds while his uncle sketches him. When Saracen will remain quiet no longer, the uncle holds up a sketch Gaston can scarcely believe possible in the time, full of force and imagination.

Gaston leaves his uncle with a nod, rides quietly through park into village and on to moor, and turns at the top to look down. The landscape's perfectness strikes him, as if the picture had grown there, with no suburban villa or modern cottage in sight.
6225-the-seats-of-the-mighty-volume-2:
Moray writes as though one Sunday afternoon had settled his whole story, then admits the making took many weeks of solitude. In that time he saw no face but Gabord's, the jailer who brought bread and water twice a day and answered no questions about Juste Duvarney or Voban.
