The chapters here bring the Chevalier de la Darante, an officer of marines, and the coming of Doltaire, with a boast and a poisoned point to follow.

This second volume deepens the intrigue around a prisoner who must think his way out of a cell. Gabord's watchful silence, the talk of wine and crumbs, and the slow passage of days build a mood of close confinement. Parker lets Moray's voice carry the suspense, as plans form in the dark and enemies gather just out of sight.
6231-the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-:
Philip d'Avranche, first lieutenant of the Narcissus, comes ashore at the Ecrehos under the pilotage of Jean Touzel, after Admiralty orders send the ship to take soundings there. The vessel twists through rock teeth into a cove, boats put off to explore, and Philip walks the shingle to a ruined chapel in no good humour with himself or the world. Ranulph, watching from the island, has guessed the ship aright.

This volume turns on meetings at the edge of the sea, where naval duty and island life collide. Carterette keeps her small counter with hot soup, coffee, and Jersey wonders fried on a charcoal fire, a homely counterpoint to ships and orders. Parker keeps the coast itself in view, a place of reefs, tides, and narrow coves that shapes every choice his people make.
62365-the-history-of-lynn-vol-1-of-2:
The History of Lynn, volume one, is a town history by William Richards. It was printed at Lynn by Whittingham in 1812. The full title promises a history civil, church, political, and commercial. It also covers lives of note, town government, and military matters. The account runs from the earliest records to the present time. Remarks on national events are interspersed through it. Those remarks aim to show the real state of the town. Manners and conditions of the inhabitants at each period are also shown.

A long introductory account is prefixed to the history. It treats the town's situation, harbour, rivers, and inland trade. It also covers Marshland, Wisbeach, and the Fens round about. A preface says materials were gathered as long ago as Charles the Second's reign. Guybon Goddard, then recorder of the town, collected them. The work fills two volumes in all.
62378-heart-of-oak-a-three-stranded-yarn:
W Clark Russell spins a sea yarn in the second volume of Heart of Oak, issued in London in 1895. The tale is told in three strands, with shipmates taking up the story in turn. This volume opens with the crew leaving and a sail sighted from a stranded hull.

Inside, hope and doubt fight as the lookout's sail may prove to be ice, not a ship at all. The crew stacks tar barrels and brush to make a smoke signal thick enough to catch a stranger's eye. Later chapters run to southern ice, the aurora, hard fighting, and captivity, before Mr Moore takes up the tale. Readers get Russell's famed sea writing, full of cold, canvas, and the slow hope of rescue.
6238-the-lane-that-had-no-turning-volume:
Five brothers live with their sister Louison three miles from Pontiac, and Medallion first meets them by selling them a slice of farm at auction. Taken into their house during a severe illness, he finds Louison guarded by a constant, reverent courtesy, her maiden dignity shielded by every brother. The volume holds four tales: Louison's absurd romance, a little bell of honour, a son of the wilderness, and a worker in stone.

Parker's Pontiac stories turn on French Canadian village life, where custom, pride, and affection rule daily conduct. Medallion, the auctioneer turned guest, watches a household built on respect and quiet feeling. These are short, warm tales of neighbours and kin, told with humour and a fond eye for the small ceremonies that hold a parish together.
62465-the-prodigals-and-their-inheritanc:
The Prodigals and Their Inheritance, in its second part, is a novel by Oliphant, author of the famed town tales of Carlingford. It came out at London in the mid eighteen nineties, printed at a Scots press. Its parts here run on from the first book.

Its first page here is a soft dawn meet. A man comes out to meet a young wife and takes her hand. He draws it through his arm and leads her in with fond care. No trace shows of the cold hold that has ruled their life of late. She is much thrown by the change. She draws her hand back, half cross and half in awe, and asks why this is.
6251-michel-and-angele-a-ladder-of-sword:
Lempriere of Rozel, butler to the Queen, sees a sight he tells to his dying day while Elizabeth is at chapel at Greenwich Palace. Gentlemen of the rod kneel to lay a cloth as if at an altar. Salt, plate, and bread are placed with ceremony, and a duke's daughter bears a tasting knife beautiful as a rose. Lempriere, given an office where others do the work, watches court ritual with a Jerseyman's plain astonishment.

This second volume moves between palace ceremony and the choice set before Michel de la Foret, sword or book, until Trinity Day. The Queen's word gives him that choice, while Leicester sees only the sword at his side and the gold-bound book under his arm, and storms off under the trees. Parker writes Elizabeth's court as theatre and trap, where a refugee's faith must pass inspection in public.
6257-donovan-pasha-and-some-people-of-eg:
Fielding's orderly is straight enough from behind, legs like pipe stems and body like a board. But his face gives little pleasure, with a nose like rubber and eyes of dull, sullen mongrel look. Those eyes turn brownish red when he is excited, a sign all know. Selamlik Pasha calls it hashish, Fielding calls it a cross of Sudanese and fellah blood, and little Dicky Donovan has his own view of Ibrahim the orderly.

This second volume holds five tales, from Fielding's orderly and the eye of a needle to a treaty of peace, mercy at Tiberius, and a world gone mad. A woman called a blasphemer faces sheikh and ulema, while one man's plea tries to save her by calling her favoured of God. Parker writes Egypt through soldiers, officials, and villagers, with humour and a sharp eye for how rumour turns into judgment.
62585-jilted-or-my-uncle-s-scheme-volume:
Volume two of Jilted, or My Uncle's Scheme is the mid part of a novel in three volumes, published in London in 1875. Nine chapters fill this volume alone. The tale is told in the first person by a young man of business. Its spring is the scheme of his uncle Dick, a retired talker of great powers. A motto at the head of chapter one sets the love plot: in love a young man should climb, not stoop. Marriage should be a ladder, not a pit.

Uncle Dick's talk is the book's feast. He had supped with Lamb and Elliston and stood in Haydon's studio when Scott called. He advised Southey on stocks and dined with Rogers among wits. The young narrator owns he would rather hear of a boat race than of the best tale of Talleyrand. The clash of the ages drives the comedy.
62634-the-little-review-april-1914-vol-1:
The Little Review, volume 1, number 2, for April 1914, was edited in Chicago by Margaret Anderson and sold for 25 cents. Its opening piece, The Germ, looks back to 1850, when the young Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood in England started a magazine of that name for thoughts toward nature in poetry, literature, and art.

The contents show a young review finding its range: an essay on rebellion, a piece on Shaw's Man and Superman, verses for two futurists, and a sonnet by Sara Teasdale. Correspondence argues over Wells and links Rupert Brooke with Whitman. Other pieces take up women and the life struggle, equal suffrage at its first real test, and the poetry of Alice Meynell. A letter from Yeats to American poets closes the number. Readers get the second issue of a little magazine that would soon grow famous, still in its Chicago spring.
6269-embers-volume-2:
King Rufus hunts the deer in springtime, calling to Dolly with a hey ho, in the first poem of this second volume of Parker's verse. Dolly stays coy, the greenwood fills with play, and a king learns that love is not won by a day's hunting. The volume runs on through life's sweet wages, a valley, a lily flower, love lying in a cold grave, and Granada called twice over.

Epitaphs follow for beggar, maid, fool, fighter, sea reapers, and watcher, with poems on waking, forgetting, waste places, and the twilight of love. A new Aphrodite, an ancient pledge, and a tribute of King Hath widen the range, and a little child closes the run. Parker writes short lyrics of loss and praise, where a name or a place can carry a whole life.
6273-a-lover-s-diary-volume-2:
Dreams open this second volume, and a bride, a wraith, and surrender follow, with a citadel, malfeasance, and an annunciation close behind. Vanished dreams give way to a divided life, yet life is sweet, and lost footsteps lead to a closed door and a chalice. A treasure, a decree, and a morning sacrifice carry the lover onward, through the sea, a chart, and a darkened way to reunion.

Parker's later lyrics turn from courtship to endurance, as the lover learns to live on after parting and to find the message in memory. Song was gone from him, the fight was good, and absolution comes at last, with a ghost told not to vex the living. These poems are graver than the first volume's, but they keep its music, and they end with a passing that still affirms life.
6276-the-money-master-volume-2:
Thirteen years after, the clerk of the court tells a story, and the parish must judge which man matters more, the New Cure or Jean Jacques Barbille. When the Old Cure died at eighty-five, after baptising, confirming, and comforting a whole people, his young successor could command obedience but not yet love. For a time Jean Jacques took the Old Cure's human place in the district, though in a vastly different way.

This second epoch follows Jean Jacques through a great day and waking from sleep. A gate in the wall, a claim to be a philosopher, and a shrug with a who knows for an answer follow. The clerk keeps a promise, and a master carpenter faces a problem. Parker writes parish life as a contest of influence, where mills, money, and kindness all buy a hearing, but none buys a heart outright.
6282-the-world-for-sale-volume-2:
Ingolby's square head jerks forward in stern inquiry as he warns Jowett the horse dealer to take care, for a proved charge could mean a penitentiary term. Jowett, shrewd, vain, and humorous, is a favourite in both towns, has money in the bank and corner lots, and keeps low company without apology. His constant companion is Fabian Osterhaut, common property of both towns, who does a little of everything from bill posting to insurance work.

This second book turns on a sultan, matter and mind and two men, and luck. The sentence of a patrin, light, a chain of the past, and a woman from Wind River follow. A mayor fills an office, a monseigneur meets a nomad, and beacons burn. Parker writes town rivalry as a contest of talk, law, and nerve, where a British town refuses to settle affairs by knife or gun.
6290-wild-youth-volume-2:
Out on the prairie under stars, Orlando has fought the first great battle of his life and emerged victorious, though no drawn battles exist in struggles of the soul. He is tortured by the thought that none will believe the truth tomorrow, and that penalty may follow where no crime was done. Louise, who could have returned defiant hand in hand with him, wakes at daybreak glad of the victory, yet shadowed by trouble to come.

This second volume runs from a moon not alone through Louise, man unnatural, and Orlando's warning, to Filion and Fiona, outward bound, cross trails, and a superior man. At Tralee, Louise must face Joel Mazarine, who distrusts every man and woman and will distrust her with sternness. Parker writes a night's victory and a morning's reckoning, where innocence without proof must still stand its trial.
6293-no-defense-volume-2:
Michael Clones stands before a prison asking if it is near the time. His friend sits on a stone in faded coverings, pinched with cold on a November day. Seven minutes, and Dyck Calhoun will be out, God bless him. He was condemned to eight years but freed after four, grey at the temples and broken in joy. His father's estate was swallowed by creditors, and he was perhaps freed for what he told the government about the French navy.

This second book sends Dyck into the world again, toward mutiny's hour, the West Indies, and the nick of time, with an admiral's say. Between prison exit and the ship Ariadne, months roughen but do not coarsen him, and among seamen he sets himself to become their leader. Parker writes a freed man's second start, where naval service must prove whether tragedy or success will fill his three years.
6297-carnac-s-folly-volume-2:
What has happened since I have been gone, mother, Carnac asks on his return, eight months after vanishing from Montreal. Late April sun melts snow on the hills, birds sing, and his mother answers sorrowfully that Junia has been away since last fall, nursing a sick aunt in the west. Carnac shakes his head: everything is all wrong, he blundered, and he is paying the price.

This second book holds Carnac's return, the house of the three trees, Carnac and Junta, a journey by John Grier, and the reading of a will. He found Luzanne Larue, but divorce proved impossible, for their names stood signed as man and wife in a hotel book. Parker writes a spring homecoming shadowed by a past bargain that will not release him.
6331-the-pillars-of-the-house-or-under-w:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Pillars of the House, subtitled Under Wode, Under Rode, opens its first volume in London in 1875 with a birthday gift. Four boys burst through a street door with book straps over their shoulders, shouting for Felix, while five voices within answer Jolly, and a pyramid of children crowds a narrow stair. Two handsome girls, a smaller girl and boy, and a creature rolling on the stair complete the household chorus.

The first volume follows a large family through picnic, birthday, and daily life, with Felix and Geraldine at its centre and a feeble, lame boy soothed by a mother's gentle talk. Yonge writes domestic life with close attention to children, manners, and faith, as a house holds together under strain. This is volume one of two, and its story stops where the second volume takes up the tale.
63487-wee-willie-winkie-and-other-storie:
Rudyard Kipling wrote the tales in this book, the second of two in a set made for men in the ranks. It came out at London in 1914. The list of parts gives five tales. The Man Who Would Be King stands at its head, at page 3. Wee Willie Winkie comes next, then Baa Baa, Black Sheep, His Majesty the King, and The Drums of the Fore and Aft.

The first tale opens with a word from the Law as the book quotes it. A man should be brother to a prince and fellow to a beggar, if he be found fit for it. The man who tells the tale has been fellow to a beggar time and time past. He has yet to be brother to a prince, though he once came near kin with what might have been a true King.
63624-the-life-of-david-belasco-vol-2:
William Winter wrote this life of David Belasco, the second volume of which Moffat, Yard and Company published at New York in 1918, with a portrait by Arnold Genthe. A quotation under Belasco's picture calls him the natural successor of Lester Wallack, Edwin Booth, and Augustin Daly as the leading theatrical manager of America.

The contents follow Belasco's mature career: Blanche Bates rising in Under Two Flags, his first meeting with David Warfield, and their success in The Auctioneer. Winter then takes up the fight with the Theatrical Syndicate, including sworn testimony in Belasco against Erlanger. Later chapters cover Du Barry, the first Belasco Theatre and its opening night, The Darling of the Gods, Warfield in The Music Master, and letters and incidents of 1905.
637-the-letters-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Sidney Colvin continues Stevenson's letters in this second volume, from Bournemouth through America to Samoa. Life at Bournemouth, a winter in the Adirondacks, Pacific voyages, and long Samoan years fill the sections. Letters to Mrs. de Mattos, friends, and family track work, illness, and island life.

Stevenson writes with the same wit and warmth as in volume one, now from a farther shore. His Samoan letters show a writer at home in a new world, yet still tied to old friends. The volume closes the set as a rich, moving record of a life lived largely by pen.
64208-hans-holbein-the-younger-volume-1-:
Arthur Chamberlain wrote this first volume life of Hans Holbein the Younger. Dodd, Mead printed it in New York in 1913, two volumes. Two hundred fifty two illustrations fill the set, twenty four coloured. A self portrait drawing in ink and chalks fronts volume one.

Contents open Hans Holbein the Elder and his family at Augsburg. Youthful days, first Swiss years, and Lucerne work follow in turn. Citizen of Basel and the town hall wall paintings come next. The Dance of Death woodcuts and the Meyer Madonna fill later chapters. Portraits of Erasmus and his circle and designs for painted glass fill the middle chapters.
64670-philip-rollo-or-the-scottish-muske:
James Grant wrote a tale of Scottish musketeers in two volumes, with volume two printed at London in 1854. Grant had written Romance of War and Jane Seton. Tis a tale of campaigning, of love, and invading, of marches, bivouacs, and enfilading, the motto sings. Book the eighth opens with a discovery.

The arms of expectation, the rose leaves, and winter quarters with the secret of Gabrielle follow. The capture of Burg, Saint Mark's day, and the fireship fill the book. Book the ninth brings the sisters, the forest of Eckernford, and Ulrick, Count of Merode. The white powder, the nuns of Saint Knud, and the bombardment of Kiel lead to Wallenstein himself. Scots swords serve in the German wars.
65049-the-evolution-theory-vol-2-of-2:
The Evolution Theory, volume two, collects lectures by August Weismann, professor of zoology at Freiburg. Arthur Thomson and Margaret Thomson translated them with the author's cooperation, and Edward Arnold printed the set in London in 1904. The lectures in this volume run from number twenty to number thirty six.

Regeneration opens the volume, with figures of starfish arms and a planarian cut into nine pieces. The share of the parents in building up the offspring follows. Then comes a long test of whether gained traits can be passed on, and objections to the claim that they cannot. Germinal selection takes two lectures, and the biogenetic law one. Later lectures treat amphimixis, in breeding, how place and isolation shape new species, and how species arise and die out, closing with spontaneous generation and evolution.
65144-derval-hampton-a-story-of-the-sea-:
Derval Hampton is a sea novel by James Grant, author of The Romance of War. This text is volume two of two, published in London in 1881. Its chapters promise a wet sheet and a flowing sea, Turtle Island, and a warship called the Holyrood. The volume opens with Derval facing another long spell at sea.

Captain Talbot is on shore as the ship readies, and a cab sets Derval down by the gangway. Old shipmates Joe Grummet and Harry Bowline welcome him warmly. He learns that Girtline has left in bad health and asks after his successor. Grant fills the tale with voyages and stirring adventures in the sailing navy manner.
65214-hans-of-iceland-vol-1-of-2:
Hans of Iceland, in its first volume of two, is an early romance by Victor Hugo, given here in the Centenary Edition from Boston. The run was limited to one thousand copies. A portrait of Hugo stands at the front. The introduction owns the book's birth in plain terms. It is the work of a very young man, writ at eighteen in a fit of fever. One thing in it is real, the piece says: the young man's love. The rest is invention, for youth has no store of fact to draw on.

The plates name the chief folk of the tale. Schumacker blesses a young couple, and sits in a prison garden with his daughter. Ordener bids Ethel farewell. Hans of Iceland finds the body of his son, Gill Stadt. The tale is set in the north, among mines, prisons, and old wrongs.
65226-john-a-love-story-vol-1-of-2:
John, by Mrs Oliphant, was published in 1870. Blackwood issued the love story at Edinburgh and London. It had first run in Blackwood's Magazine. Chapter one opens with a confession from the narrator. She cannot describe the story's first scene, she owns. A runaway horse is a thing many writers could paint to the life. She was never run away with, and does not know how it feels. So she begins where the excitement ends. Kate Crediton opens her eyes on a sofa. A thousand bells ring in her ears. Cool wetness lies about her head, and she cannot move.

Her father bends over her in tears, begging her not to stir. A man holds her pulse; fragrant water is sprinkled on her brow. John, all the same, begins with her fall.
65227-john-a-love-story-vol-2-of-2:
John, volume two of two, is a love story by Mrs. Oliphant, printed at Edinburgh and London in 1870. Blackwood issued it, after it first ran in Blackwood's Magazine. The volume opens at chapter fifteen, in the middle of John Mitford's courtship.

Oliphant reflects on how hard it is to fit life's great moments back into common days. Youth finds it doubly hard to come down from the heights of passion. John is no matter-of-fact man, and his love has broken up his whole life. He knows the rapture and despair of his brief courtship cannot last. Yet he feels life's theory must henceforward stand on a higher level. The volume carries a young lover's education.
65755-jill-vol-1-of-2:
Jill, volume 1 of 2, is a novel by E A Dillwyn. Macmillan published it in London in 1884. Jill narrates her own story, and the first chapter is Jill introducing herself. She begins with a thesis about adventure. Men, she has heard, are more adventurous than women. From that opinion she differs.

Timidity and sensitiveness, she argues, blight the spirit of enterprise. Those qualities are assigned to the weaker sex. So female adventurers look rarer than male ones, though nature sows the seed impartially. Given health, courage, and fair play, the craving for change asserts itself. The contents promise the proof in Jill's own life. Foreign travel and a widow's manoeuvres come early. A photograph matters twice in the volume. A few London prices and a street incident fill middle chapters. Ajaccio and a driving expedition through Corsica close the volume's list.
65758-jill-vol-2-of-2:
Jill, volume two of two, is a novel by Dillwyn. Macmillan published the work at London in 1884. The contents of this closing volume run to fourteen chapters. Titles promise a mortuary chapel, a new use for a bier, and a departure from Corsica.

The first chapter opens with captives being readied for a forced march. Coarse cloth is tied across their faces to stifle any cry for help. Their feet are freed so they can walk, under threat of instant stabbing. Each captor carries a Corsican vendetta knife in an inside pocket, ready to hand. Later chapters bring Captain Norroy, a notice to quit, and a discovery. A hospital stay, a catastrophe, and a change of fortune close the tale. The volume ends the two part story of Jill.
65872-chronicles-of-pharmacy-vol-1-of-2:
Chronicles of Pharmacy, volume one, is a history of pharmacy by Wootton. Macmillan published it in London in 1910. A publisher's note records that the author died while the book was in the printer's hands. His friend MacEwan, editor of The Chemist and Druggist, revised the proofs. The contents list fourteen chapters for this first volume. Myths of Pharmacy opens the story. Pharmacy in the time of the Pharaohs follows.

Later chapters treat pharmacy in the Bible and in Hippocrates. The line runs from Hippocrates to Galen, then to Arab pharmacy. A chapter brings the art from the Arabs to the Europeans. Pharmacy in Great Britain gets a chapter of its own. Magic and medicine, dogmas and delusions, and masters in pharmacy follow. Royal pharmacists and medicines from the metals close the list. Illustrations show gods and healers of the ancient world.
65934-for-love-and-life-vol-1-of-2:
For Love and Life, volume one, by Mrs Oliphant, came out at Leipzig in 1874. Bernhard Tauchnitz issued it in his line of British authors. The tale runs to two volumes. A motto from Ivanhoe, on the disinherited, heads the book. Chapter one is called On the Shores of Loch Arroch. Three people walk slowly by the water there. An old invalid leans on a young man's arm.

A girl of about twenty walks with them, golden haired and grave. The narrator stresses that the women are farmer folk, proud and open hearted. They have lived for ages on that farm by the loch. The young man's air sets him apart from them. Class, love, and family duty form the ground of Oliphant's tale.
65935-for-love-and-life-vol-2-of-2:
For Love and Life, volume two, completes a novel by Mrs Oliphant. Tauchnitz issued it at Leipzig in 1874. The edition belongs to a collection of British authors. Translation rights were reserved. Oliphant's many earlier novels are listed in front. The Chronicles of Carlingford stand among them.

The volume opens with a chapter called Intoxication. Its first page reflects on a crisis in a man's life. That crisis comes when another's happiness first hangs on his own. Edgar has received this idea with intoxicating force. Three years earlier he nearly proposed to Gussy Thornleigh. Then he was rich and petted by the world. Now effort and sacrifice are required of him. Dancing attendance on a lord no longer tempts him. Love has remade his pride.
66040-english-poems-volume-02-of-2:
Fernando Pessoa wrote these English poems, and this copy holds the third set, an epithalamium, printed at Lisbon in 1921. Olisipo, the publisher named on the title page, was Pessoa's own imprint for the poems. The wedding poem opens with a call to set all shutters open for the day.

Let the day come in like a sea or a din, the speaker cries at dawn. No nook of useless shade should tell the mind that some things are sad, for this day all are glad. The bride awakes as the full sun rises, caught between joy and fear on the morning of her marriage.
66054-the-little-review-april-1915-vol-2:
The Little Review for April 1915, volume two number two, came from Margaret C Anderson's press in Chicago's Fine Arts Building. Anderson edited the monthly, which covered literature, drama, music, and art at fifteen cents a copy. Her own piece, Mr Comstock and the Resourceful Police, leads the editorial matter.

The table lists verse by William Saphier, Skipwith Cannell, and David O'Neil, Richard Aldington on the poetry of Paul Fort, and John Gould Fletcher on vers libre and advertisements. John Cowper Powys discusses Henry James in the book pages. A young modernist monthly shows its range.
66375-the-charterhouse-of-parma-volume-2:
The Charterhouse of Parma, Volume Two, is the last half of a great tale by Stendhal. Scott Moncrieff made its English form. It was put out at New York in nineteen twenty five. A list of that hand's works stands past the title leaf. This half starts at the tale's part of years past ten. An add on of two scraps stands at its back.

The list of parts runs from that part to the last part of the tale. The two scraps bear the names of a tale told by a man of the tale and of a count and the press of a prince. The first part of this half starts with the young hero in chase of love. He is in a small town near the great town of the tale.
66492-the-ancient-volcanoes-of-great-bri:
The Ancient Volcanoes of Great Britain, volume one of two, is a geology work by Sir Archibald Geikie. Geikie was director general of the Geological Survey of Great Britain and Ireland, as his long title page states. Honours from universities and academies across Europe and America fill half that page. Seven maps accompany the work, its opening notes.

Britain has no live volcanoes, but its old hills hold the roots of ancient ones. Geikie reads lava flows, ash beds, and worn cones in Scotland, Wales, and Ireland as the record of those fires. Survey maps and field work of a lifetime stand behind the prose. The book made deep time visible in familiar British scenery.
6660-theological-essays-and-other-papers:
Thomas De Quincey, author of Confessions of an English Opium-Eater, gathers theological essays and other papers in this second volume. Its contents run from secession from the Church of Scotland and a toilette of the Hebrew lady to Milton, Charlemagne, modern Greece, and Lord Carlisle on Pope. The opening essay, dated 1844, warns of a great revolution in Scotland.

De Quincey writes with his usual force and fancy, turning church politics into high drama. Lord Aberdeen's Act, he says, may calm the strife, but danger has not yet passed. Volume two shows De Quincey at his most learned and combative, on faith, letters, and nations.
66860-my-diary-north-and-south-vol-1-of-:
My Diary North and South is the first of two volumes of an eyewitness journal of the American Civil War. Its author is William Howard Russell. Bradbury and Evans published it in London in 1863. Russell was the most famous war correspondent of his century. His diary records what he saw travelling through both sides of the conflict.

The introduction refuses all apology for the book that follows. Russell explains instead why the diary exists and what it tries to show. The volume is dedicated to Richard Quain, a physician, in regard and gratitude. A working reporter rather than a general, Russell wrote from camps, battlefields, and drawing rooms. His Northern and Southern observations shaped British opinion of the war. They did so while the war was still being fought.
67222-harvard-psychological-studies-volu:
Harvard Psychological Studies, volume two, is a research collection edited by Hugo Munsterberg, issued in 1906. Its opening section treats Emerson Hall, the new home of the Harvard laboratory. Chapters cover the growth of experimental psychology at Harvard and the need for the hall. Emerson as a philosopher and the place of the science also get chapters.

The studies that follow group by theme. Optical studies treat binocular vision, eye movements during dizziness, and visual irradiation. A section on feeling takes up how feeling is expressed. The contents show a young science setting out its rooms, its tools, and its first questions in print. Each paper is by a named worker in the laboratory, listed in the table.
67282-the-principles-of-biology-volume-2:
Herbert Spencer sets out how living forms are built in volume two of his Principles of Biology. D Appleton and Company issued the revised and enlarged edition at New York in 1900. The first copyright dates to 1867.

Part four treats morphology, the science of form. Chapters weigh the make-up of plants, then of animals. Differentiation and the shapes of branches, leaves, and flowers follow. Vertebrate skeletons and animal cells get their own studies. Part five turns to physiological development. It traces how outer and inner tissues divide their labour. Spencer argues that the split between form and function holds only at the surface. Push inquiry deeper, he says, and the line grows nominal. His system tried to ground all life in one law of evolution.
67460-the-sin-of-monsieur-antoine-volume:
The Sin of Monsieur Antoine is a tale by George Sand, in English dress by Burnham Ives. This is the first part of a set that pairs it with a next tale of the same hand. Twelve plates past the works of a paint hand grace the book. Parts run past a manor, a mill lord, a carve man, a jail take, and a first love.

The tale opens in a town named as one of the least fair spots in France, on the edge of two shires. Past one hundred poor houses line its few streets past two or three rich ones. The town is famed past leagues for the suit love of its folk and for the hard road to it. Yet guests brave its wilds and its dire stone ways. Plate words show a young man meet a maids fresh voice at a thicket of wild rose.
67776-fairy-tales-volume-1-of-2:
Marion Florence Lansing compiled and edited a first volume of fairy tales for the Open Road Library of Juvenile Literature. Charles Copeland drew the pictures. Rumpelstiltskin opens the book, with a miller's daughter ordered to spin straw into gold or die. A tiny man helps her, three turns of the wheel at a time.

Other tales include Doll in the Grass, The Frog Prince, Cinderella, and Hans in Luck. Diamonds and Toads, Puss in Boots, Rapunzel, and Beauty and the Beast follow. The Steadfast Tin Soldier and Hop o' my Thumb close the main set. Notes at the back add background for young readers and teachers.
67845-ireland-the-people-s-history-of-ir:
Ireland: The People's History of Ireland, volume one, is John Finerty's history of the island. The Co-operative Publication Society issued it in New York and London, from a 1904 copyright. Finerty led the United Irish League of America, and Daniel O'Connell fronts the book.

Book one runs from the earliest times to the Reformation. The land itself comes first: its divisions, features, soil, climate, and scenery. The first inhabitants and the faith of ancient Ireland follow. Saint Patrick's coming takes a chapter: captive and swineherd for years, he escapes. He returns, the head says, as the regenerator of the nation. Ancient laws, the Danish invasion, and the battle of Clontarf in 1014 follow. Civil wars, the Norman landing at Wexford, and the coming of Henry the Second close the part.
67925-the-prose-works-of-percy-bysshe-sh:
Richard Herne Shepherd edited the prose works of Percy Bysshe Shelley from first forms. Chatto and Windus issued Volume One in London in 1897. Two youthful romances, Zastrozzi and St Irvyne, lead the contents. The Dublin and Marlow pamphlets stand with them in the volume.

A lost work, A Refutation of Deism, was found again and printed here. Letters to Leigh Hunt and a letter to Lord Ellenborough add sharp, brave prose. A review of Hogg's romance, dug up by Professor Dowden, joins the finds. Shelley students gain proof that a great poet writes strong prose too.
67926-the-prose-works-of-percy-bysshe-sh:
Volume two of Shelley's prose, in the complete works edited by Richard Herne Shepherd, gathers the essays and translations. Chatto and Windus issued the set at London. The prose fills two volumes within five.

A Defence of Poetry leads this volume, starting at page one. An essay on the literature, arts, and manners of the Athenians follows. Shelley then turns to Plato. He renders the Symposium, called here The Banquet, and the Ion. The Menexenus and pieces of the Republic come next. A note on a passage in Crito follows. The Assassins, a prose tale fragment, stands among the essays. On the Punishment of Death begins near the close. The set adds a bibliography of Shelley and a full index.
68039-the-tower-of-london-vol-2-of-2:
The Tower of London, in its second part, is a past tale of the great fort by the Thames. Its hand was a lord of a famed Scots house. He kept a seat on the board of the state portrait room. A wealth of prints fills the book. It came out at London in the first years of the last age.

A front print shows the fort in the days of the first king of its new line. That cut is by a famed hand of that age. Its parts here take the kings house by house. The cut king and the rule of the sword come early. The gay king and the last of the line come next. Crown pairs, a lone queen, and three kings of one name close the run.
68126-my-diary-north-and-south-vol-2-of-:
Volume two of William Howard Russell's diary of America during the Civil War, published in London in 1863. Russell was the famous Times correspondent, and his contents run down the Mississippi to Vicksburg and Jackson, then back north.

Entries note slaves for sale at Memphis, cannon practice at Camp Randolph, and forced return from the South. Later chapters weigh the North's apathy against the South's earnestness and consider the position of Great Britain toward the belligerents. The road home passes Chicago, Niagara, and West Point, then Washington, where irritation against Britain runs high. Readers get the war's first years through the sharpest journalistic eyes of the age.
68175-the-cornhill-magazine-february-186:
The Cornhill Magazine, volume one, number two, for February eighteen sixty, was issued in London by Smith, Elder and Company. The contents list opens with Nil Nisi Bonum and a piece on invasion panics. Thomas Hood verse From Horace, To Goldenhair, stands at page one hundred forty nine. Serial fiction fills much of the number. Art, science, and essays share the pages in Victorian mix.

Framley Parsonage runs in chapters four, five, and six in this number. Alfred Tennyson poem Tithonus stands at page one hundred seventy five. A long Hogarth essay treats the painter boyhood, and Studies in Animal Life treats ponds and rock pools. That piece marvels at gnat larvae, at races that scarce need males, and at a new red hydra. Lovel the Widower runs in chapter two. Readers get a rich taste of a great new monthly at its start.
68176-angola-and-the-river-congo-vol-2:
Joachim John Monteiro wrote Angola and the River Congo, here volume two of two, issued in London by Macmillan and Company in eighteen seventy five. Monteiro was an associate of the Royal School of Mines and a corresponding member of the Zoological Society. A map and illustrations aid the text. Chapter one treats the country from Ambriz to Loanda. Mossulo, Libongo, bitumen, and the rivers Dande and Bengo fill it.

Chapter two treats the city of Loanda, its natives, slavery, convicts, theatre, and morals. Chapter three treats the division of Angola, wretched pay of officials, and abuses by authorities. The silver mines of Cambambe and a journey there follow. Chapter four treats the province of Cazengo, gold, wild coffee, and iron smelting. The river Quanza and the falls of Cambambe fill chapter five. Travel readers get a mining engineer Angola, plain and sharp.
68470-fossil-plants-vol-2:
Seward, professor of botany at Cambridge, wrote this textbook on the plants of the rocks. Fossil Plants, volume two, came from the University Press in 1910, with 265 plates. Its students sat between two sciences, as the title owns: botany and geology.

A cut stem of a Permian fern, Thamnopteris, heads the book in fine detail. The sphenophylls, a lost order kin to the horsetails, open the volume. Kidston and Gwynne-Vaughan's work on the old fern stems stands behind the plates. Seward wrote the standard English sum of his field: coal plants, fern stems, and seed ferns set in order, with each kind drawn and weighed.
6931-sunny-memories-of-foreign-lands-vol:
Harriet Beecher Stowe continues her sunny memories of foreign lands in this second volume, told in letters home. Letter nineteen opens with breakfast, Macaulay, Hallam, and Milman, then lunch at a Surrey parsonage and dinner at Sir Edward Buxton's. Later letters record dinner at Lord Shaftesbury's, an antislavery meeting at Exeter Hall, and visits to Windsor, Eton, and the poet Gray.

Further letters bring Kossuth, Pembroke Lodge, dinner at Lord John Russell's, and Lambeth Palace, with Clarkson, Joseph Sturge, Gladstone, and the Archbishop of Canterbury's sermon. Stowe writes as a famous American guest in England, warm, observant, and ever mindful of slavery's cause. The volume is a travel letter book of high society and reform.
69332-les-beaux-messieurs-de-bois-dore-v:
George Sand wrote a French novel, here in its second volume, rendered by G Burnham Ives for a subscribers' set of her masterpieces. Sand was Amandine Lucille Aurore Dupin, Baroness Dudevant. The volume runs from chapter forty to chapter seventy four. Twelve photogravures after paintings by H Atalaya illustrate the book.

Pictures show Bois-Doré conferring with a rector, Mercedes wounded before the château, and Guillaume d'Ars proposing marriage. The marquis uses Eastern cosmetic secrets taught by a Moorish woman to keep his beard and brows dark. His young companion Mario asks no awkward questions. Sand mixes romance, disguise, and old French manners.
69392-eminent-doctors-their-lives-and-th:
The hosted text is the second volume of Eminent Doctors, a set of lives of leading medical men by Bettany, a lecturer on botany at Guy's Hospital medical school. It was published in London by John Hogg. The author takes his motto from praise of men whose aim was to ease pain and save life.

The chapters pair names with the work that made them known. Addison and Bright stand with the diseases that bear their names. Simpson stands with the use of anaesthetics. Lister stands with antiseptic surgery, and Jenner with the fight against typhoid fever. Other chapters treat the newer surgery, court physicians, and care of the insane. The volume closes with men known for skin, throat, and parasite work.
6940-old-mortality-volume-2:
Walter Scott's Old Mortality continues in this second volume with a council of war in a shepherd's hut. A quarter of a mile from the field of battle, leaders of the Presbyterian army meet in a miserable cottage, the only enclosed spot near at hand. Burley guides Morton toward the hut, where a wild confusion of sounds greets them instead of the calm gravity fit for such a council.

Discord and loud uproar strike their new ally as an evil omen for measures to come. The volume follows Morton among the Covenanters after battle, as factions argue and the rising's fate hangs in the balance. Only this volume's own course is told here, from the hut council onward through the quarrels that shape the war.
69406-eminent-doctors-their-lives-and-th:
Eminent Doctors: Their Lives and Their Work is a two-volume set of medical biographies by G T Bettany, lecturer on botany in Guy's Hospital Medical School. John Hogg of London published the first volume, printed at the Ballantyne Press in Edinburgh and London. A line from G A Sala stands at the head: the lives of good, brave, learned men who work to ease pain and save life hold an inexpressible charm.

Bettany's preface complains that medical biography had not taken its due place in the nation's thought. Anecdotes of big fees and brilliant operations had crowded out real lives, he argues. Aikin's memoirs, Macmichael's Lives of British Physicians, and Pettigrew's Medical Portrait Gallery were the chief records before him, and the last was too costly for most readers. His volumes set out to fill that gap.
6943-the-heart-of-mid-lothian-volume-2:
The second volume of Scott's Heart of Mid-Lothian opens in a darkened room of grief. Mrs Saddletree enters to find her guests sunk in misery, the old man laid in bed after a long swoon, curtains drawn, and Jeanie sitting motionless at his side. Kind but blunt, Mrs Saddletree opens the window, draws the curtain, and urges her kinsman to sit up and bear his sorrow like a good man and a Christian.

His hand falls lifeless as she lets it go, and the scene sets the volume's somber key. Only this volume's course is followed here, as the household bears its blow and Jeanie faces what must be done. Scott keeps the focus close on family feeling, even as the law's shadow hangs over the house.
69591-the-conquest-of-the-great-northwes:
The Conquest of the Great Northwest, volume one of two, by Agnes C Laut, was printed at Toronto by the Musson Book Company under a 1908 copyright. Laut had written Lords of the North and Pathfinders of the West. A plate shows Collier famous picture of Hudson last hours.

The book tells the story of the Adventurers of England known as the Hudson Bay Company. It opens new pages in the history of the Canadian Northwest and the western states. Part one treats Henry Hudson four voyages, then the adventures of the Danes on Hudson Bay under Jens Munck. Part two brings Radisson, the pathfinder, who found Hudson Bay overland. The charter, the first shareholders, and the coming of the French fill later chapters. North fans get fur trade empire building in a brisk, story led history.
69629-the-princess-casamassima-volume-2-:
Henry James wrote The Princess Casamassima, first published in 1886, and Macmillan issued this two-volume edition in London in 1921. This hosted copy is the second volume. It opens in the middle of the tale, at the start of Book Third, chapter 22.

Hyacinth, the young bookbinder at the heart of the novel, wakes early after a night with scarce a wink of sleep. From his window he sees an old garden with parterres in curious figures and lawns that strike his London eye as fantastically green. A mossy brick parapet looks down on a canal or moat, and the great house behind him rises grey under ivy, with gables and chimneys on odd lines. The scene holds him between the world he came from and the world he has entered. Readers get the second half of James's study of a radical young craftsman in high society.
69805-the-little-review-april-1916-vol-3:
The Little Review for April 1916 is one monthly issue of a Chicago magazine of literature, drama, music, and art. Margaret Anderson is named as editor and publisher on the cover. The issue is volume three, number two, priced at fifteen cents. Four poems by Carl Sandburg open the number, with a portrait of the poet.

The contents list a piece by Dreiser addressed to another writer, and a letter from London by Ezra Pound. A sorrowful demon story, poems by other hands, and a study of German poetry follow. Regular parts include a New York letter, a theatre page, book discussion, and the reader critic column. A contest for free verse is announced in the issue. The number shows the magazine's mix of new poetry and sharp talk.
69839-the-piccinino-volume-1-of-2:
George Sand wrote The Piccinino, here volume one of two, in the Masterpieces of George Sand series printed only for subscribers by George Barrie and Son at Philadelphia. G Burnham Ives translated it. Six photogravures after Oreste Cortazzo illustrate the book. Thirty five chapters fill this first volume. Chapter one is The Traveller.

The Traveller Story, Monsignore, and Mysteries follow. The Casino, The Staircase, and A Glance come next. Mila, Problem, and The Grotto of the Naiad stand early. Magnani, Agatha, and Barbagallo fill the middle chapters. Il Piccinino himself appears at chapter twenty four. The Destatore Cross, Diplomacy, and Jealousy follow. Apparitions, The False Monk, and Witchcraft raise the close. The Escalade, The Ring, and At the Fountain end the volume. Novel readers get a Sicilian bandit romance.
69939-essays-in-medical-sociology-volume:
Essays in Medical Sociology, in its first part, gathers the past works of Blackwell, the first woman doctor of physick of her land. It came out at London in the first years of the last age. Her word at the front tells why the set exists.

At the ask of friends, she says, she has let her works of past years be set in one even form. Truth never grows old, she holds, though it may need new dress for new phases of life. She will rejoice if her words help the young workers of the day. Its essays take the human side of sex, the duty of doctors in laws on foul disease, rescue work amid vice and sickness, and the buy and sale of women.
69998-essays-in-medical-sociology-volume:
Essays in Medical Sociology, volume two, by Elizabeth Blackwell, was printed in London in 1902. The first essay, on women in medicine, was an address given in October 1889. Blackwell spoke at the London School of Medicine for Women. She notes that Paris schools and hospitals stood open to women without bar. She counts few women doctors in Britain next to thousands in the United States.

Other essays treat faults in medical training and why hygiene congresses fail. Later pieces take up method in biology and Christian socialism. One essay attacks the decay of town government. An address at the opening of the Women's Medical College in New York is also here. A closing piece is called The Religion of Health.
70032-zanzibar-city-island-and-coast-vol:
Richard Burton, the great traveller and tongue man, wrote this second volume on Zanzibar and the East African coast. Tinsley Brothers printed it in London in 1872. A plate of a Nyika man heads the book, in the dress of the mainland folk.

From Zanzibar to Mombasah opens the road. Mombasah, or Mvita, takes the next long part. A visit to the Kisulodi-ni mission house follows, then the people of the coast. Burton knew this shore from his years of travel in Arabia and Africa. His sharp eye caught trade, faith, custom, and tongue in one sweep. The two volumes form his full report on a spice isle and its wild coast.
70078-the-heathery-or-a-monograph-of-the:
Andrews figured and described the whole tribe of heaths in a work of six volumes. Bohn of London issued volume two in a second edition, corrected and enlarged, in 1845. Each kind is shown in a colored plate. Latin and English accounts stand side by side, with the parts of the flower cut open and named.

A long essay at the front treats the growing of these tender plants. The Cape, Andrews says, is the sole market of the genus, and fresh kinds pour in too fast for the pencil. He names the kinds most hard to keep, and warns that damp and fog are their great foes in this island. They must stand alone in a house of their own, with air free to come and go. The entries then march in order, each with its marks of stem, leaf, and bloom set out in full.
70122-the-conquest-of-the-great-northwes:
Agnes Laut wrote this second volume of The Conquest of the Great Northwest, printed in New York in 1908. The subtitle calls it the story of the Adventurers of England known as the Hudson's Bay Company. A plate shows Lord Strathcona, formerly Donald Smith, a governor of the company. Contents continue Part Three, the coming of the pedlars.

One chapter gives the voyage up to Fort William and the life of grandeur there. Another gives Henry's adventures at Pembina and the first white woman in the West. Thirty years of probing follow, with the advance up the Saskatchewan and the building of Edmonton. Mackenzie and McTavish quarrel in the next, as the Nor'westers press into Hudson Bay waters and defy the charter. David Thompson dashing for the Columbia, and Fraser finding his way to the sea, close the heads shown.
70561-the-writings-of-origen-vol-1-of-2:
Frederick Crombie put into English The Writings of Origen, in a first book of two from Edinburgh in 1869. Crombie taught the close study of the Bible at Saint Andrews. A short note at the front sets out the life and worth of Origen. A first word by Rufinus leads into the main work.

The chief work is On First Things, in four books of its own. It deals with God, with Christ, and with the Holy Spirit. It asks how souls fall, what the end will be, and what form the angels take. A letter to Africanus and the first book of the work Against Celsus fill the rest. The note says the first two works are given whole. Church thought of the third age comes through in full voice here.
70628-a-popular-history-of-the-united-st:
Mary Howitt wrote this popular history of the United States for general readers, and the first of its two volumes runs from the discovery of America to the settling of the colonies. It begins with the Vikings, Columbus, and the Cabots, follows De Soto to the Mississippi, and tells of Raleigh's Virginia ventures, the founding of Quebec in 1608, and Hudson's last voyage. Harper and Brothers published the volume at New York in 1860, with many engravings.

The later chapters settle into the colonies themselves: Jamestown and Captain John Smith, Pocahontas, the famine years, and the planting of Maryland under Lord Baltimore. Howitt tells the story in a clear narrative style, with the explorers' sufferings and the colonists' quarrels kept in view. A second volume carries the account on to her own time.
70629-a-popular-history-of-the-united-st:
A Popular History of the United States of America, volume two of two, is a history by Mary Howitt, printed at New York in 1860 with many engravings. A frontispiece shows Washington resigning his commission as commander-in-chief. The second volume opens with the commencement of the great wars. Its first chapter treats the war of the Austrian succession and the siege of Louisburg.

The contents run through Franklin's scheme for general union, Braddock's discomfiture and death, and the outrage on the Acadians. The campaign of 1759 brings the scheme for the conquest of Canada, Amherst at Ticonderoga, and Wolfe's siege of Quebec. Howitt wrote the history of the continent from its discovery to the present time for general readers. Her narrative joins the French wars to the birth of the republic. The volume is a popular Victorian telling of America's making, in two fat illustrated parts.
70644-caroline-the-illustrious-vol-1-of-:
W H Wilkins portrays a queen in Caroline the Illustrious, volume one of two, from Longmans, Green in 1901. His subject is Caroline of Ansbach, queen-consort of George the Second and four times queen-regent. The preface claims she was by far the greatest of Britain's queens-consort, wielding more sway than any queen-regnant save Elizabeth and Victoria.

For ten years, Wilkins argues, Caroline governed England with Walpole, and the reign should bear her name. He draws on unpublished papers from the Hanoverian Archives, above all on her betrothal and marriage, and warns that Lord Hervey wrote with bias.
70693-the-writings-of-origen-vol-2-of-2:
The Writings of Origen, volume two, holds his great work Against Celsus, books two to eight. Clark published it at Edinburgh in 1872 in the Ante-Nicene Christian Library. Frederick Crombie translated most of the volume for that series. The late Cairns turned books seven and eight into English for it.

Roberts and Donaldson edited the library of the fathers down to the year 325. Origen answers the pagan Celsus point by point in this defence of the faith. Miracles, prophecy, and the life of Jesus fill the ground of their old quarrel. A pagan attack lost in its own book survives inside the Christian reply here. Victorian churchmen put the fathers into English dress in this long series.
70717-spenser-s-faerie-queene-vol-1-of-2:
Spenser's Faerie Queene, volume one, prints books one to three of Spenser's great poem in a scholar's text. Smith edited it for the Clarendon Press at Oxford, first published in nineteen o nine. The volume forms part two of a three volume set of Spenser's poetical works. Reprints of nineteen sixty one and nineteen sixty four kept the first sheets in use.

The introduction tells how the text was built from the old printings afresh. The quartos of fifteen ninety and fifteen ninety six and the folio of sixteen o nine were weighed. The broken seventh book came first in the folio of sixteen o nine alone. Readings of fifteen ninety six not taken are all kept in the notes below. Changes of spelling that touch sound or grammar are noted for students of the tongue. Punctuation follows the old copy save where it would mislead a modern reader.
70726-the-traveller-s-oracle-or-maxims-f:
The Traveller's Oracle, or Maxims for Locomotion, part two, is the Horse and Carriage Keeper's Oracle. John Jervis, an old coachman, wrote it, and Kitchiner revised it; Colburn printed a second edition in London in 1827. Its title promises rules for purchasing, keeping, or jobbing horses and carriages, with accurate estimates of every expense.

The contents price the whole establishment. They cost out a groom and one horse in your own stable, and one horse at livery. They cost out a coachman, a carriage, and two horses in your own coach house too. Chapters describe a handsome town chariot and the travelling chariot of Bonaparte, list the duties on servants, carriages, and horses, and teach the art of managing coachmen. Fifteen things a good coachman will not do are enumerated, and an easy plan closes the book for finding every hackney coach fare.
7086-life-of-her-most-gracious-majesty-t:
Sarah Tytler's life of Queen Victoria continues in this second volume, edited with an introduction by Lord Ronald Gower. The contents open with royal progresses to Burghley, Stowe, and Strathfieldsaye, then the Queen's powder ball and her first visit to Germany. Railway speculation, failure of the potato crop, Peel's resolutions, the birth of Princess Helena, and a visit from Ibrahim Pasha follow.

Autumn yachting, Spanish marriages, and winter visits lead to Prince Albert's installation as chancellor of Cambridge and the Queen's visit to Scotland's western isles and Ardverikie. French fugitives, the People's Charter, a first stay at Balmoral, and fresh attacks on the Queen fill later chapters. Only this second volume's matter is described here.
70864-history-of-zionism-1600-1918-vol-1:
The History of Zionism covers the years 1600 to 1918 in two volumes; this file holds volume one. The work traces the idea of a Jewish return to Palestine across three centuries, long before the modern movement took political shape. Its span runs from early modern stirrings to the end of the Great War. The index of the whole work was printed with the second volume.

Volume one follows the forerunners. Religious hopes, messianic movements, and early schemes of settlement appear in turn. The narrative builds toward the nineteenth century, when national feeling and persecution in eastern Europe gave the old hope new forms. By 1918 the Balfour Declaration had made Zionism a question of world politics. A history written at that moment carries the excitement of a movement arriving. The book remains useful for its gathering of early texts and episodes.
70865-history-of-zionism-1600-1918-vol-2:
History of Zionism, 1600 to 1918, volume two, is the second half of a long history of the Zionist movement and the thought behind it. The dates in the title mark the span: three centuries, from the early stirrings of the idea to the close of the First World War. The work closes with a full index.

The edition's own notes show the care taken with the text. Spelling in the listings has been put in order, though the older spellings of the period are left as they stand in the body of the book. Quotations inside quotations have been given distinct marks for clarity. The notes warn that index references have not been checked for accuracy, an honest limit. What the reader gets is a big, documented survey of how the return to Zion was argued, organised, and pursued across three hundred years.
71048-memoirs-of-the-princesse-de-ligne-:
Memoirs of the Princesse de Ligne tells the life of a Polish dame. Lucien Perey shaped the book, and Laura Ensor put it in English. This first of two books came out in London in 1887. It starts with her kin, a prince who was a church chief in Poland.

Civil wars in that land drive the chief out to Paris in his age. His niece, the young Helene, comes with him to that gay town. She is put to school in a great nunnery school of the town. The dorm, the rules, and the small wars of the girls fill the tale. Two camps of girls, the blues and the reds, fight their mock wars. Ill health, a kind nun, and stern pains mark her first years there. Balls at the school and great dames of the court crowd the later parts.
71051-memoirs-of-the-princesse-de-ligne-:
Memoirs of the Princesse de Ligne, volume two of two, follows an Austrian house. Lucien Perey edited the memoirs; Laura Ensor translated them into English here. Scribner and Welford issued the New York printing in 1887 in full. Chapter four brings the Prince Bishop to Paris and a family marriage.

Letters from kin and court fill the record of Bel Œil festivities. Prince Charles journeys to Berlin and Saint Petersburg in chapter six. Portraits of Frederick the Great and the Empress Catherine stand out there. War with the Turks makes the Prince a Russian general in chapter nine. Warsaw diets, divorce suits, and the storming of Ismail close it.
71064-the-yoga-vasishtha-maharamayana-of:
The Yoga Vasishtha Maharamayana of Valmiki stands here in part. Volume two of four, part two of two, is this portion. Its scanned edition was of poor quality, the notes own. In some cases text was missing from that printing, they say. Corrections made to the text are listed for the reader.

A missing page was supplied from another edition for this copy. That page starts a chapter on birth, death, and existence. Two pages were switched in the printed book, the notes record. Verses missing at one place were restored from other printings. One page in the original repeated a far later page by error. The dialogue of the sage and the prince fills such chapters. Release from bondage through knowledge is their burden throughout. The notes give the English reader an honest text at last.
7113-the-land-of-midian-revisited-volume:
Burton's second Midian volume continues the march through central and eastern Midian, from chapter eleven onward. The contents list unknown lands south of the Hisma, ruins of Shuwak and Shaghab, and a road from Shaghab to Ziba with ruins of El Khandaki and Umm Amil. A turquoise mine and a return to El Muwaylah follow, with a week around and upon the Sharr mountain.

Later chapters go down south to El Wijh with notes on quarantine and the Hutaym tribe, then to a southern sulphur hill and a cruise to El Haura. The last marches pass an inland fort, ruins of gold mines at Umm el Karayat and Umm el Harab, and the road to El Bada. Only this second volume's march is traced here.
71162-the-complete-works-of-john-gower-v:
The Complete Works of John Gower, volume two, holds Gower's English works, edited from the manuscripts by G C Macaulay. The Clarendon Press printed it at Oxford in 1901, with introductions, notes, and glossaries. This volume gives the Confessio Amantis from its prologue to the middle of the fifth book. A plate shows part of the Fairfax manuscript.

Macaulay's prefatory note says the circumstances of the edition were stated in the preface to the volume of the French works. There the editor named his debts to librarians and private owners of manuscripts. The list of errata, he hopes, may be taken to show not so much carelessness as his desire to be absolutely accurate. The reproduction of this interesting text was his aim. Gower was the moral poet of Richard the Second's England, friend to Chaucer.
71249-the-yoga-vasishtha-maharamayana-of:
The Yoga Vasishtha Maharamayana of Valmiki, volume four, part two, closes the great Sanskrit dialogue. It is the latter half of the fourth and final volume of the full work. Chapter numbers run into the high hundreds in its table of contents. Rama and the sage Vasishtha hold their long talk on the nature of mind.

The world as dream, the self as pure awareness, and freedom from bondage rule these pages. Stories within stories carry the teaching through the closing books of the work. A universe that is a void nothing in one passage shows the depth of the doctrine. Long lists of textual corrections in the front matter mark a careful edition. Students of Indian philosophy meet one of its boldest texts in this final part.
713-memoirs-of-extraordinary-popular-del:
Charles Mackay devoted this second volume to four great follies that seized whole peoples. The Crusades sent armies east in the name of faith, with banners, spears, and vast loss of life. The Witch Mania then shows how fear of witchcraft led towns to hunt and burn the accused.

Two shorter studies close the book: the slow poisoners, who killed in secret for gain or hate, and haunted houses, where dread and rumour made empty rooms seem alive. Mackay's moral is plain: crowds can lose reason as fast as single minds. The volume remains a classic warning about panic, belief, and the power of a shared delusion.
7134-the-great-conspiracy-volume-2:
Logan's second part of The Great Conspiracy opens at chapter six, The Great Conspiracy Maturing, on November 6, 1860. That day came and passed, and by the seventh the conviction that Lincoln would be elected had become certainty, heralded the length and breadth of the Republic. Excitement ran unparalleled: Northern Republicans rejoiced that slavery at last stood where the people could believe it in course of ultimate extinction.

The Douglas Democracy, chagrined at their leader's defeat, filled with gloomy forebodings for the country. The Southern Democracy, or a large portion of it, openly exulted that the long wished revolt of the Slave Power and separation of Slave from Free States stood at hand. Especially in South Carolina, fire eaters led the cry. Only this second part's course is followed here.
7146-cecilia-or-memoirs-of-an-heiress-vo:
Frances Burney's Cecilia, memoirs of an heiress, continues in this second volume of three, edited by R Brimley Johnson. Book four continues with a chapter titled A Murmuring, and book five opens with a rout, a broad hint, and an accommodation. A detection, a sarcasm, and a surmise follow, with a bold stroke, a miser's mansion, and a declaration.

A gamester's conscience, a persecution, a man of business, and a solution close book five, while book six opens with a debate, a railing, and an antique mansion. A rattle, a storm, a mystery, and an anecdote lead to a conference, an attack, and a retreat. Only this second volume's course is followed here, as Cecilia's fortune entangles her in town manners and money plots.
7155-the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-2:
Part two of Twain's Prince and the Pauper opens at chapter five, Tom as a Patrician, with Tom Canty left alone in the prince's cabinet. He makes good use of his chance, turning this way and that before the great mirror and admiring his finery. Then he walks away imitating the prince's high bred carriage while watching results in the glass. Next he draws the beautiful sword, bows, and kisses the blade, laying it across his breast as he saw a noble knight salute.

That salute went to the Tower lieutenant five or six weeks before, when Norfolk and Surrey lords were delivered into captivity. Tom plays with the jewelled dagger at his thigh and examines costly ornaments. He tries each sumptuous chair, dreaming how proud he would be if the Offal Court herd could peep in. He wonders if they would believe his tale at home.
71622-the-heart-of-africa-vol-2-of-2:
Dr Georg Schweinfurth wrote The Heart of Africa, three years travels in the unexplored regions of Central Africa from eighteen sixty eight to eighteen seventy one. The hosted text is volume two of two. Ellen E Frewer translated the work. Sampson Low in London issued the set in eighteen seventy three. Maps and woodcuts aid the text. A plate shows King Munza in full dress.

Chapter thirteen treats the Niam Niam at length. Their name, general characteristics, complexion and tattooing, and time spent on hair dressing head the summary. Weapons, soldierly bearing, and a nation of hunters follow. Women agriculturists, the best beer in Africa, and cultivated plants share the pages. Cannibalism and the power of princes close the survey. Chapter fourteen treats an audience with King Munza. Exploration readers get a classic of African travel.
71643-life-in-the-forests-of-the-far-eas:
Spenser St John, formerly consul general in Borneo, wrote a two volume account of life in the forests of the far east, printed at London in 1862 with many illustrations. A front view shows Kina Balu from the lower Tampasuk river. St John had become chargé d'affaires to Haiti when the book appeared. His preface refers readers to a short introduction for the plan.

He thanks those who assisted him and notes the help behind the volumes. Smith, Elder published the work on Cornhill. St John's Borneo years gave him rare knowledge of its peoples and forests. The book mixes travel, natural history, and colonial administration. It remains a primary source on nineteenth century Borneo.
71739-life-in-the-forests-of-the-far-eas:
Life in the Forests of the Far East, volume two of two, is a travel work by Spenser St John, published in London in eighteen sixty two. St John had been British consul general in Borneo and later served as a diplomat to Haiti, as his title page states. Numerous illustrations appear, including a plate of shooting a cataract on the Limbang River. Contents open with expeditions to explore the interior.

Those expeditions run south and south east of the capital, as the first chapter head states. Rivers, forests, peoples, and trade of Borneo fill a consul's record of years in the island. Shooting rapids in native boats gives the adventure its emblem scene. Victorian Borneo, before oil and plantations remade it, lives in these pages.
7180-handy-andy-a-tale-of-irish-life-vol:
Samuel Lover's Handy Andy continues in this second volume, opening late at night in pitch dark, where a whistle from Dick answers with wheels, hoofbeats, and the rattle of an unseen vehicle. The illustrations promise Andy's cooking, a crack shot, a challenge, a party at Killarney, and an abduction, all etched from Lover's own drawings. Volume Two carries the tale past its first half without pause.

Andy remains the well-meaning Irish servant whose blunders drive the comedy, and the new chapters keep him among masters, rivals, and festive crowds. Lover writes in a broad, good-humoured style that lets mishap follow mishap while affection for his people never fades. This volume alone holds the later turns of Andy's career.
71842-a-history-of-art-in-chald-a-assyri:
History of Art in Chaldaea and Assyria, volume two, is an art history. Georges Perrot and Charles Chipiez wrote the French original in Paris. Walter Armstrong translated and edited the English edition of the work. Chapman and Hall issued it in London in the year 1884. Four hundred fifty two engravings and fifteen plates illustrate the volume.

Chapter one treats civil and military architecture of Mesopotamia in depth. The palace of Sargon fills a long section of that first chapter. Other palaces, towns, and their defences follow in ordered survey. Chapter two turns to sculpture, its themes, materials, and conventions in turn. Students of the ancient Near East got a vast, pictured handbook here.
7194-the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-2:
Part Two opens on a tranquil Sunday morning, with Aunt Polly leading family worship. Her prayer is built of solid courses of scriptural quotation, welded with a thin mortar of originality. From that summit she delivers a grim chapter of Mosaic Law, as if from Sinai itself, before Tom girds himself to get his verses.

Sid learned his lesson days before, but Tom bends all his energy to five short verses, choosing part of the Sermon on the Mount because he can find none shorter. The comedy lies in the gap between holy duty and a boy's cunning economy of effort. This part holds the Sunday-school scene alone, bright with Twain's eye for village ritual.
72075-the-scrap-book-volume-2-no-2:
The Scrap Book for October 1906 is volume two, number two of a monthly miscellany of clippings and comment. It leads with How to Live Well, taken from a letter by George Washington to his nephew Bushrod in 1783. Washington counsels courtesy to all, intimacy with few, and charity weighed by the widow's mite.

A symposium gathers the latest viewpoints of men worth while, as the heading puts it. Lady Ward discusses how female suffrage works in New Zealand, where even Maori women vote but only men hold office. Other pieces weigh college fraternities, Esperanto, and the cost of saving a soul. Bernard Shaw calls Americans children in business, and Lord Roberts wants rifle shooting made a national sport. The editors present New Zealand as a twelve-year lesson for Americans still arguing theory against theory.
72155-travels-in-southern-abyssinia-volu:
Travels in Southern Abyssinia, through the country of Adal to the kingdom of Shoa, volume one, is a travel narrative by Charles Johnston, published by Madden at London in 1844. Johnston dedicated the volumes to his father at Birmingham, and the frontispiece shows the Mulkukuyu ford over the Hawash river.

The preface owns that, as a young author, Johnston undertook the journey by resigning a valuable medical appointment in the East and voluntarily assuming the character of an adventurer. In 1840 he held the post of surgeon aboard the iron armed steamer Phlegethon, on secret service. His friends questioned his taste and prudence at the time. Whether the results justified the sacrifice, he leaves to the reader's judgment, having prepared in London with instruments and an outfit for a road across the continent.
72340-pictorial-history-of-the-war-for-t:
Pictorial History of the War for the Union, by Ann Stephens, opens its first of two volumes in a Cincinnati printing of 1863. A front plate groups Lincoln with his cabinet: Seward, Chase, Welles, Stanton, Bates, Hamlin, and Blair. Stephens promises a complete and reliable history of the war from its start to its close, with more than two hundred pictures.

The title page boasts graphic accounts of encounters, hairbreadth escapes, desperate charges, and personal anecdotes. All were gleaned, it says, from eyewitnesses and men who took part. A full chronological analysis of the war is added. The introduction owns the hard task of writing history while events still rage. Stephens wrote for a Northern public hungry for the war as story and picture, while the war itself still ran.
7243-a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur:
Part Two of Mark Twain's Connecticut Yankee finds the hero second personage in the kingdom for political power, dressed in silks, velvets, and cloth of gold that prove showy and most uncomfortable. He takes the choicest suite in the castle after the king's, aglow with loud-coloured hangings. Yet the stone floors hold only misfit rushes for carpet, and proper conveniences, he notes, simply do not exist.

Merlin's tower gives the part its centre, as magic and modern cunning face each other across a court of silk and stone. Twain mines the gap between splendour and squalor for comedy, letting the Yankee's plain talk puncture courtly pride. This part holds the rise to power and its gaudy, draughty rooms.
72465-mirror-for-magistrates-volume-2-pa:
Mirror for Magistrates, volume two, part two, is a 1815 London edition of the old Tudor verse lives. Joseph Haslewood edited the set, printed for Lackington, Allen and Company. Baldwin's preface and a reader's address from the 1610 edition open the part.

The contents list the legends from the Conquest onward, each a fall to warn rulers. The fall of Robert Tresilian, chief justice in 1388, leads the run, by Ferrers. Two Mortimers follow, then Thomas of Woodstock, murdered in 1397. Mowbray, raised to a dukedom and then banished, comes next in a piece by Chaloner. Richard the Second, deposed and murdered in prison, fills the following legend. Owen Glendour, Owen the Welsh rebel, starves in the mountains in a tale by Phaer.
72676-the-cotton-kingdom-volume-1-of-2:
The Cotton Kingdom, volume one of two, gathers Olmsted's observations on cotton and slavery in the American slave states. The work rests on his three earlier travel books, reshaped for English readers. It was issued in England and in this country at the same time.

The front matter lists the earlier books: the seaboard slave states, a Texas trip on the southwestern frontier, and a trip through the back country. Prices run from a dollar and a quarter to two dollars for this set. A coloured map shows the cotton kingdom and its dependencies, drawn chiefly from the United States census. Blue marks the dominant cotton districts, at two bales or more to each slave. Yellow and red mark lesser districts, and lines show where slaves outnumber freemen.
72677-the-cotton-kingdom-volume-2-of-2:
The Cotton Kingdom is Frederick Law Olmsted's account of travel through the American slave states, and this text is volume two of two. Its subtitle calls it a traveller's observations on cotton and slavery. Olmsted built the book from three earlier volumes of his journeys and investigations. Mason Brothers published it in New York.

Olmsted rode through the South in the eighteen fifties and wrote what he saw. His pages report plantations, enslaved workers, poor whites, and the economics of cotton from direct witness. The dialect of his informants is kept uncorrected in this text. The book remains one of the sharpest northern reports on slavery before the Civil War.
72881-the-irish-guards-in-the-great-war-:
The Irish Guards in the Great War, volume two, covers the Second Battalion of the regiment. Rudyard Kipling edited and compiled the history from the battalion's diaries and papers. Doubleday, Page printed it at Garden City, New York, in 1923. A map at the front traces the battalion's itinerary from August 1915 to December 1918.

The contents run by years: Loos and the first autumn in 1915; the Salient and the Somme in 1916; Rancourt to Bourlon Wood in 1917; and Arras to the end in 1918. The Second Battalion was formed in July 1915, made up from the personnel of the reserve battalion. Kipling, whose own son served and died with the regiment, shaped the record from official papers and private diaries. Appendices and an index close the volume. The history is a memorial as much as a chronicle, written in Kipling's grave and careful prose.
72996-tough-yarns-vol-1-of-2:
The Old Sailor spins Tough Yarns, a run of naval tales and sketches in two volumes, volume 1 printed in 1835. Carey and Hart of Philadelphia stand among the sellers. He gives the book to Captain Marryatt, the famed sea writer. His aim, the sub title jokes, is to please all hands.

Three tales fill this volume. Greenwich Hospital leads, then Tom Brookes, then Daddy Davy. His preface says it is no joke to keep the brains like a winch, spinning yarns all day. The first tale calls the hospital a grand store house of human fragments. It is a snug harbour for docked remnants of the sea, in his fond phrase.
732-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
Edward Gibbon devoted this second volume, with notes by H. H. Milman, to Rome's turn toward Christianity and to Constantine. A long opening section traces how Roman rulers treated Christians, from Nero's cruelty to Constantine's favour. It weighs law, persecution, and the slow growth of the church within the empire.

The volume then tells of the founding of Constantinople, Constantine's new capital, and his political system. Gibbon's irony and learning are on full show, as he links faith, power, and city-building. The book is essential for readers who want to see how an empire changed its gods and its centre, and what that change cost.
73260-travels-in-southern-abyssinia-volu:
Charles Johnston, a surgeon, wrote Travels in Southern Abyssinia, in two books put out in London in 1844. Book two is the part held here. Its full road runs through the land of Adal to the realm of Shoa. A plate shows a view of a lake from Sankarl.

The first parts tell of a stay at Farree, with fear of a raid by the Galla. Women of a train were borne off as slaves, and five Galla men were slain. Word then fails from Ankobar, and fear grows that all is not right. Johnston flees a forced stay, is chased by the men of the Wallasmah, and strikes a deal. He tells of the homes and the flour mill of Farree. Notes on the start of the Amhara folk and their build fill a part.
73287-in-two-years-time-vol-1-of-2:
In Two Years' Time is a novel by Ada Cambridge, published in two volumes by Bentley in London in 1879. This first volume opens at Narraporwidgee, an Australian station, on a stifling mail day. Father flings his hat on the sofa and demands why the boy is not back. Kitty rushes to open the house to a blessed south sea breeze.

Chapters move from pears and greengages and an Arcadia of station life to despair, a mail steamer, and English relations.
