Cambridge, who wrote much of her work in Australia, draws colonial society with an insider's ease. The novel contrasts bush freedom with the claims of Mrs Grundy and English rank. It is early evidence of her long career as one of Australia's leading novelists.
73585-introduction-to-the-science-of-lan:
Introduction to the Science of Language, volume one of two, by A H Sayce, was published by C Kegan Paul and Company of London in 1880. Sayce was Deputy Professor of Comparative Philology at the University of Oxford. The work aims to give a clear and systematic account of what the new science of language had established. It builds on his own Principles of Comparative Philology.

The preface warns that the science moves fast, too fast for the man who also carries university and college duties. Sayce hopes the book is still free of grave error, while doubting it is the last word. He asks the reader for practical phonetics: the vowels and consonants of classic languages are to be sounded as the learned pronounce them. Tables and new type carry the symbols the argument needs.
73859-short-story-masterpieces-vol-2:
J Berg Esenwein translated and introduced a second volume of French short story masterpieces, copyrighted in 1911 and issued at Springfield in 1912. A picture of Anatole France opens the volume. Esenwein edited Lippincott's Magazine and taught the writing of fiction. The Home Correspondence School published the set for students learning the craft by mail.

Like the first volume, this one pairs each story with a critical introduction to its author. Studying French masters was meant to teach compression and finish. The series treated the short story as a form with rules that could be learned. Students of the correspondence school worked through the tales as models for their own writing.
73911-belgium-vol-1-of-2:
J Emerson Tennent, a member of parliament, wrote a two volume account of Belgium, of which this is the first volume, with Belgium's motto on the title page: union makes strength. Tennent had written letters from the Aegean and a history of modern Greece. A picture shows Waterman's Hall on the Grass Quay at Ghent. Richard Bentley published the work from New Burlington Street.

Belgium was a new kingdom, born in 1830 from the Dutch union. Tennent surveys its government, industry, and arts for British readers. His Prussian League volumes were in the press at the same time. Travel and politics mix in his pages. The two volumes appeared as Belgium entered European diplomacy.
74112-the-magazine-of-history-with-notes:
The Magazine of History with Notes and Queries for February 1905 is the second issue of a new monthly from William Abbatt of New York. A year cost five dollars, and one issue cost fifty cents. The front shows portraits of Lorenzo Dow Thompson and Jonathan Moore.

Inside, Thomas Addis Emmet writes on myths of American history, and David S. Kellogg writes on early events in the Champlain Valley. Other pieces cover Captain Lincoln, side lights on Carolina history, Indian farming in Wisconsin, and old Fort George in New York City. A war letter by Walt Whitman and a letter by Lincoln stand in a part for source texts. Notes, family history, and book news close the issue.
74170-the-stone-age-in-north-america-vol:
The Stone Age in North America is a survey of the tools and arms of the first peoples of the continent. Warren K Moorehead wrote the work in two volumes. Volume one came out in 1910.

Moorehead calls the book an encyclopedia of the old crafts. It treats implements, ornaments, weapons and utensils of the tribes. More than three hundred full page plates show the finds. Four hundred figures picture over four thousand objects in all. A front plate shows fine chipped work in jasper and agate from Oregon. Scholars and collectors both used the work as a guide. Moorehead served as curator of American archaeology at Phillips Academy.
74187-pictorial-history-of-the-war-for-t:
Ann S Stephens wrote the Pictorial History of the War for the Union, and Benjamin W Hitchcock issued volume two in New York in eighteen hundred sixty seven. More than two hundred pictures fill the set. Stephens gave the work to Major-General William T Sherman. Eye witness tales feed the text throughout.

Volume two opens with the rival hosts in May eighteen hundred sixty two. The Army of the Potomac marches toward White House in Virginia. Stonewall Jackson raids the Shenandoah vales in the same weeks. Fair Oaks, the Seven Days, and Malvern Hill follow fast. Memphis falls and Cedar Mountain burns next. South Mountain and Antietam close this slice of the contents. A dated war log ends the set.
74244-the-pageant-of-parliament-vol-1-of:
The Pageant of Parliament, volume one, was written by Michael MacDonagh. Fisher Unwin issued the work in London, in two volumes. MacDonagh had written The Speaker of the House and The Reporters' Gallery. A plate at the front shows the Speaker's chair and clerks' table in the Commons. The picture comes from Benjamin Stone's photographs, held at the British Museum. A boxed advert for another man's portraits of public life faces the title page. It is a publisher's insert, not part of the text.

The title promises a parade of Parliament across the years. MacDonagh knew the building from the press gallery side. His earlier books treated its officers and its reporters. This larger work widens the lens to the institution itself, its scenes, ceremonies, and leading figures, told for general readers.
74291-seven-years-in-south-africa-volume:
Emil Holub, a doctor, wrote Seven Years in South Africa, an account of travel, study, and the hunt. Book two came out in London in 1881, in a form put into English by Ellen E Frewer. The trip ran from 1872 to 1879, from the gem fields to the Zambesi. Near two hundred plates and a map fill the two books.

Book two starts on the road from the gem fields to the Molapo stream. Tales of graves by the Harts River and a crane nest by a salt lake fill the first part. Later roads lead to Shoshong, the great salt lakes, and the falls of night hunts. Chiefs, weddings, court cases, and wild beasts crowd the pages. Holub notes plants, rock, folk ways, and game with the same close eye.
74317-scotland-under-her-early-kings-vol:
William Robertson wrote this history of Scotland under her early kings, and Edmonston and Douglas printed it at Edinburgh in 1862. The first volume runs to the close of the thirteenth century. A map of the early kingdom heads the book.

Robertson says in his preface that the work fills a gap left open. Early Scots history, above all before Malcolm Ceanmore, had been left to guessers. Old hands treated it as a debate ground for their pet schemes, he writes. They fought with feathered weapons as hotly as Pict, Scot, or Attacot ever fought with steel. His two volumes aim at a sober, full tale of the kingdom's first ages.
74390-the-stone-age-in-north-america-vol:
The Stone Age in North America, volume 2, by Warren Moorehead, curator of American archaeology at Phillips Academy, was published in Boston and New York in 1910 by Houghton Mifflin. The set calls itself an archaeological encyclopedia of the implements, ornaments, weapons, and utensils of the prehistoric tribes of North America. More than three hundred full-page plates and four hundred figures show over four thousand objects.

This volume treats ground stone: effigies, bird-stones, pipes, mortars, and pestles. Objects of shell, bone, and copper follow, with the native copper work of Wisconsin given in detail. Textiles and pottery close the survey. A plate shows grooved effigies and celts from the Bahama Islands in natural colors, from a collection at Albany. Moorehead catalogs with a collector's zeal and a museum man's order.
74675-travels-in-eastern-africa-volume-1:
Travels in Eastern Africa, volume one of two, was written by Lyons McLeod and published in London in eighteen sixty by Hurst and Blackett. McLeod had been Her Britannic Majesty's consul at Mozambique. He dedicates the work to the merchants and chambers of commerce of Great Britain and Ireland. His hope is that commerce will end slavery in Africa.

The first chapters sail with the Ireland, a wretched postal steamer, from Plymouth. A gale drives her back and ten passengers abandon ship. The Cape brings Table Mountain, Constantia wines, and the observatory. McLeod notes the discovery of coal on the Zambesi and its promise for the region. The narrative of his residence in Mozambique waits in the later chapters. His argument throughout is that trade binds nations in peace better than missions alone.
74676-travels-in-eastern-africa-volume-2:
Lyons McLeod, once the British consul at Mozambique, wrote an account of travel in eastern Africa and of his residence in that port. Volume two came out in London in 1860. McLeod writes from hard firsthand years spent facing down the slave trade and feuding with local power.

The volume opens with a governor-general removed for slave dealing and the arrival of his successor. McLeod tells of the seizure of the slaver Charles et Georges, plots by slave dealers to drive him out, and attacks that left his house cut off and his wife wounded. Later chapters turn to Mauritius, its people, trade, and labor brought from India. Readers get a consul's blunt record of empire, trade, and danger on that coast.
74980-the-best-stories-of-sarah-orne-jew:
Best Stories of Sarah Orne Jewett, volume two, is the Mayflower edition selection, dated 1925. Willa Cather selected and arranged the stories and wrote a preface for the set. Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York issued the two volume choice. Contents open with A White Heron, Jewett most loved tale of Maine woods.

The flight of Betsey Lane, the Dulham ladies, and going to Shrewsbury follow in order. The only rose, Miss Tempy watchers, and Martha lady fill the middle list. The town poor, the Hiltons holiday, and Aunt Cynthy Dallett close the volume. Cather homage fixed Jewett place in the American short story canon.
75059-the-american-in-paris-vol-1-of-2:
The first volume of a travel book in letters, published at London in 1838. Henry Colburn issued the two volumes. A preface in letter form explains the book's birth. Letters written from Paris were gathered and sold to booksellers. The author disclaims all high titles for himself. He is no critic, politician, or economist, he says. Shakespeare's phrase serves instead: a snapper-up of inconsiderate trifles.

The letters begin at Havre and Rouen. Custom houses, passports, and diligences get sharp treatment. Paris letters walk the boulevards and the Palais Royal. Taglioni at the opera, Sunday dancing, and splendid cafes follow. French dinners and gambling rooms fill later pages. The book sold American sharpness about Paris to English readers.
75060-the-american-in-paris-vol-2-of-2:
The American in Paris, volume two of two, was printed in London by Henry Colburn in 1838. The book runs as letters from a traveling American. Letter twelve treats mass at St Roch for Admiral de Rigny and the churches of Paris.

That letter takes up the Abbe Lacordaire at Notre Dame, the state of the French church, St Genevieve, and St Etienne du Mont. An American child at prayers, the miracles of St Medard, and the Madeleine follow. Letter thirteen walks Pere la Chaise cemetery, with the funeral of Bellini, grave merchants, and the tomb of Abelard and Heloise. The feast of the dead and the monument of Foy stand in it. Letter fourteen treats the Louvre and the patronage of the fine arts. Travel fans get Paris of the 1830s through sharp American eyes.
75182-an-american-tragedy-v-2:
Theodore Dreiser wrote An American Tragedy, here volume two, issued in New York by Boni and Liveright in MCMXXV. Volume two holds book two continued and book three. Chapter thirty nine stands in the hosted text. Clyde Griffiths is the hero, torn between Roberta Alden and Sondra Finchley. Chance did not aid him, the text says plainly.

Roberta presence in the factory would not let Clyde dismiss her from his mind, the tale says. If only he could persuade her to leave and live elsewhere, he might think more calmly, he feels. Her presence asked without cease what he intended to do. His love for her had cooled, which cut his sense of what was her due. He was too infatuated with Sondra, and pursued that enticing dream nightly. Novel readers get ambition, sex, and murder in Dreiser heavy prose.
75257-the-nights-of-straparola-volume-1-:
Nights of Straparola is a set of Italian tales, now first translated into English by W G Waters. Pictures by E R Hughes go with the text. The hosted copy is volume one of two, issued at London in eighteen ninety four. Only two hundred ten copies were printed on special paper, the copy notes, and this is number ninety five.

Contents open with an introduction and a proem, then the first night's fables. The first tale tells of a son who disobeys his father's will and is condemned to death. A noted robber who steals his friend's bed and horse fills the second. A priest duped once by three robbers, who dupes them thrice in return, fills the third. A prince of Salerno and his daughter fill the fourth, a darker tale.
75313-emmanuel-appadocca-or-blighted-lif:
Maxwell Philip wrote Emmanuel Appadocca, or blighted life, a tale of the freebooters, in two volumes printed in London in 1854. This is the first volume. Philip gives the book to his friend Harry Daniels. A preface tells what roused him to write. A statement of the cruel way the slave-holders of America deal with their slave-children stirred him to a high pitch of wrath.

He could not think, he says, that even slavery can hide the horror of fathering children to turn them out into the fields, to labour at the lash. So he sketched the course a high-spirited, tender person would follow, picking cotton on his own father's estate. The ground-work of the tale rests on truth, the known story of the freebooters. The rest is invention. The scenes lie chiefly in Trinidad, his native isle.
75314-emmanuel-appadocca-or-blighted-lif:
Maxwell Philip wrote a tale of the buccaneers in two volumes, here the second. Charles J Skeet issued Emmanuel Appadocca in London in the Roman year MDCCCLIV. A Greek quote from Euripides fronts the title page. Chapter Sixteen opens the hosted form with a line from Julius Caesar.

Agnes and fellow captives toss in a small cutter, beating toward land. Three days of wind and wave bring no gain by the first night. The priest fears robbery and worse among strange, close-herding sailors. Readers gain a tense sea tale of peril, faith, and a blighted life.
7532-a-book-of-old-ballads-volume-2:
Beverley Nichols's second volume of old ballads begins with an invitation. Lithe and listen, gentlemen, to the tale of the Heir of Linne, who sells his broad lands for gold and spends it all. King Cophetua and the Beggar Maid follows, with Sir Andrew Barton, May Collin, and the Blind Beggar's Daughter of Bednall Green. Thomas the Rhymer, Young Beichan, and Brave Lord Willoughbey keep the sequence moving.

The Spanish Lady's Love and The Friar of Orders Gray close the book, and color plates show King Cophetua, May Collin, Thomas the Rhymer, Young Beichan, and the Heir of Linne. The volume mixes romance, sea fighting, and fairy lore, all in the direct speech of the ballads. It is the middle book of Nichols's set, and the most varied in mood.
75403-aunt-anne-vol-1-of-2:
Aunt Anne book one is a tale by Mrs Clifford, out at London in eighteen ninety two. A Bentley house brought out the two book tale that year. Walter Hibbert and his wife of four months lead the tale start. They rest at Brighton from Friday to Tuesday to brace him for work. Press work and help on a school week sheet wore him thin.

Wed life costs much at its start in gear and gifts, he jokes. Pier rest with band tunes and a sea gaze is her plan for the last day. He moans that tunes make noise, as tunes will, in his jest plea. Beach rest would bar the down gaze to the deep that she loves. They choose the pier and sit with faces to the sea in peace.
75404-aunt-anne-vol-2-of-2:
Mrs W K Clifford wrote a novel in two volumes, here in the second part. Richard Bentley and Son issued Aunt Anne in London in 1892. Clifford had written Mrs Keith's Crime, as the title page notes. A verse from James Russell Lowell fronts the volume.

Mrs Baines arrives in town and takes small rooms in Portsea Place, Connaught Square. She tests chairs, sofas, chimneys, and draughts with a grand, firm air. Landlady Mrs Hooper yields to her awe of the spare old lady. A guinea a week seals the rooms, and a dinner guest is due that night.
75559-the-journal-of-george-fox-vol-1-of:
The Journal of George Fox, volume one of two, appears here in the eighth, bi centenary edition, printed for the Friends' Tract Association in London in 1901. Its subtitle promises an historical account of his life, travels, sufferings, and Christian experiences. A notice by the association's secretary, Norman Penney, introduces this issue.

Penney explains that the text is reprinted from stereotype plates, slightly corrected, with enlarged indexes, and that a map has been newly prepared to show the places Fox names. A commendation from Spurgeon heads the advertisements: the Journal, he says, contains ingots of gold, things to be thought on month by month before the reader gets to the bottom of them. The two volumes were sold at five shillings net, or six and sixpence with the map.
75590-the-journal-of-george-fox-vol-2-of:
The Journal of George Fox, volume two, in its eighth edition, is the Friends' Tract Association printing of the Quaker founder's historical account of his life, travels, sufferings, and Christian experiences. Spurgeon praised the journal as a rich mine whose every page seems solid gold.

The present issue was printed from the stereotype plates of the eighth, bi-centenary, edition, slightly corrected, with additional particulars of the previous editions of the journal and greatly enlarged indexes. A map, recently prepared to accompany the journal, was sold with it or separately in a case. The bookseller's notice quotes Spurgeon's judgment that modern books are spun out, while Fox's journal contains ingots of gold, things to be thought on month by month.
75616-the-british-battle-fleet-vol-1-of-:
The British Battle Fleet, volume one of two, is a fleet past by Fred Jane. Its full name runs past its birth and growth past the ages to the day. Jane was known past books on fight ships and sky craft. It came out at London in nineteen fifteen. Plates in hue past the water draws of a famed sea hand fill it, with plans and still views.

Parts treat the birth of that lands sea power, the age of the north men, and the age that bore a set fleet. The wars with the low lands and the first wars with France take parts. Two parts run past the peace of a town to the last fall of the great chief of France. The birth of new fight ship thought and the come of the iron clad close this book.
75617-the-british-battle-fleet-vol-2-of-:
Fred Jane wrote this second volume of The British Battle Fleet, its start and growth through the ages to the present day, printed in London in 1915. Plates in colour come from water-colours by Wyllie. Many plans and photographs go with them. A front plate shows dreadnoughts anchoring in 1912. Contents open with the Barnaby era.

The White era and the Watts era follow. The dreadnought era, under Watts, takes the fourth head. Boats that dive, sea flying, and the helper navies come in turn. Broad matters of the last hundred years close the book. Lists of plates name the ships shown: a cruiser turned mine-layer, battleships of the Majestic class, early destroyers, and the Dreadnought of 1906. Portraits show Barnaby, White, and Watts, the men whose names mark the eras, with Fisher and Jellicoe at the end.
75644-the-sacred-theory-of-the-earth-vol:
Sacred Theory of the Earth, by Thomas Burnet, joins Scripture with earth history. The sixth edition was printed in London in seventeen twenty six. Burnet gives an account of the origin of the earth in two volumes. This first volume holds books on the Deluge and on Paradise.

Later books treat the burning of the world and new heavens and earth. A review of the theory and its proofs, tied to Scripture, is added. Burnet defence against Warren and Keil is also bound in this edition. An ode to the author by Addison fronts the work in verse. Readers get a famed early bid to read earth past through Bible text.
75872-journal-of-the-waterloo-campaign-v:
Journal of the Waterloo Campaign, volume one of two, is the diary of General Cavalie Mercer. Mercer commanded a brigade of royal artillery through the campaign of 1815. Blackwood published the journal at Edinburgh and London in 1870. A preface by the author's son explains how the work was made.

Mercer wrote the journal in its present form some forty years after the war. He worked from rough notes set down each evening while events were fresh. His son stresses that the book is no history of the campaign's operations. It is a diary of one officer's own sights, feelings, and hardships. The tedium of quarters, the strain of the march, and the bivouac all stand recorded. Of the great battle itself, Mercer tells only the part played by his own troop of horse artillery.
75873-journal-of-the-waterloo-campaign-v:
General Cavalie Mercer kept this journal through the Waterloo campaign of 1815, and this book is the second of two volumes. Mercer commanded the 9th Brigade Royal Artillery. The set was printed at Edinburgh and London in 1870. Contents for this volume start at chapter fifteen, as the army pushes on past the field of battle.

Heads trace blocked roads, night alarms, poor fare, and plundering by allies on the march. Later heads cross the Somme, note French deserters, and record the revenge taken by Prussian troops. The army comes in sight of Montmartre and gains its first glimpse of Paris. Rumours of peace, the crowd in the streets, and the royal cortege close the march.
75876-lucius-davoren-or-publicans-and-si:
Volume two of a sensation novel by the author of Lady Audley's Secret continues the tale in an edition issued by John Maxwell and Company at London in 1873. The story runs to three volumes.

Geoffrey learns the worst in chapter fourteen. A week-old moon shines on the quiet town as he leaves his hotel at half past nine. He carries his friend's letter in his pocket. He is bound to visit a lady who had forbidden him to visit her at all. The contents promise a beginning of mystery and an unpleasant discovery. Lady Baker tells the story of the past. Lucius makes a confession. A hidden staircase, a plundered muniment chest, and the mystery of Lucille's parentage drive book three. Troubles thicken to the close.
76182-memories-volume-1-of-2:
Lord Redesdale published the first volume of his Memories in nineteen fifteen, giving the book to his wife and children. He had spent much of his life among men who made the history of their time. Their public deeds, he notes, fill the records of their lands.

What is often lost, he argues, is the private side of such men. Small traits and small details can fix a wrong view of a person. Chapters run from his cradle and family to Frankfort, Paris, and Eton. Sir Ernest Satow let him check the Japan years against private journals. Edmund Gosse gave counsel and support.
76183-memories-volume-2-of-2:
Memories, volume two, is the second half of the memoirs of Lord Redesdale, published in London by Hutchinson in 1915. A photograph of King Edward the Seventh, taken by the author at Balmoral in 1904, forms the frontispiece. Redesdale had served in Japan and in Parliament, and his life crossed the courts and camps of two centuries.

The contents of this volume range widely. Ten chapters cover Japan: an adventurous journey, the civil war, the Mikado, and the reception of the Duke of Edinburgh. Home again, the book turns to Lord Clarendon and Lord Granville, to Damascus and Richard Burton, and to Garibaldi. Westward chapters reach the Mormons and Brigham Young. Later pages treat Lord Beaconsfield, the Office of Works, Joseph Hooker, King Leopold, the French fleet's visit in 1905, and Bayreuth in 1912. Few memoirs hold so many famous names.
76362-africana-or-the-heart-of-heathen-a:
Duff Macdonald, a Church of Scotland mission man late of Blantyre in East Central Africa, wrote Africana, a study of native ways and beliefs issued in London in 1882. This first of two volumes treats customs and beliefs, as its own line states. A front quote holds that the proper study of mankind is man.

Macdonald says most of his facts are new in print, won while he worked in the mission field. He had been called home in a clash with his board over a civil rule they set up at the post, and he wrote in part to stir Christians to stronger work. He holds that lands left wholly to old faiths shrink each year as missions and Islam press in.
76428-the-history-of-the-harlequinade-vo:
Maurice Sand wrote The History of the Harlequinade, in two volumes, first put out by Secker at London in 1915. Volume one treats Harlequin, Polichinelle, the Captain, Columbine, Pierrot, Lelio, and Ruzzante. A plate of each chief figure faces its part of the text. The tale starts far back, with the first mime who leapt on a bench or table. Song, dance, and a droll tale were his whole art, made up on the spot.

In Icaria, Sand says, Susarion gave form to such clown acts, and bands bore their booths through Greek towns. Thespis then set up a stage, gave each mime a role, and smeared faces with dregs or soot. From those roots grew the masked play of Italy and France. Sand traces each stock mask with love and lore, for readers of stage past.
76625-the-little-review-june-1917-vol-4-:
The June 1917 issue of The Little Review is a monthly magazine of the arts from New York. Margaret Anderson published and edited it, with Ezra Pound as foreign editor. The issue is volume four, number two, priced at fifteen cents.

The contents mix poetry and prose. Chinese poems of Li Po appear in translations by Sasaki and Maxwell Bodenheim. William Butler Yeats contributes a group of poems, including The Wild Swans at Coole and Broken Dreams. Pound's Imaginary Letters appear, credited to Wyndham Lewis in the contents. A Reader Critic department closes the listed matter. The masthead boasts that the magazine makes no compromise with the public taste. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
76786-a-summer-in-skye-volume-1-of-2:
A Summer in Skye, volume one, is a Highland travel book by Alexander Smith. Strahan published it in London in 1865. Smith had written A Life Drama before it. Eight chapters make up this first volume. The road runs from Edinburgh to the island.

The book opens in a heat wave. Summer has leaped on Edinburgh like a tiger. Dust chokes the streets of Princes Street. The narrator longs for one hour of heavy rain. He is tired and jaded with work. Visions of vacation haunt him. Stirling and the north come next. Oban follows, then Skye at last. Later chapters treat the second sight and life in a Skye bothy.
76787-a-summer-in-skye-volume-2-of-2:
A Summer in Skye, by Alexander Smith, author of A Life Drama, fills two volumes; the second was published in London in 1865 by Strahan. Contents of this volume name The Landlord's Walk, Orbost and Dunvegan, Duntulm, John Penruddock, A Smoking Parliament, The Emigrants, and Homewards, by way of Glasgow, to Home.

The Landlord's Walk opens the volume. Walking into the interior of Skye, Smith writes, is like walking into antiquity; the present is behind you, and your face is turned toward Ossian. In the quiet wilderness, London or Edinburgh feels like a place known in a former existence. Turf-thatched huts, crooked spades, and stone piles over handfuls of bones fill the road. Smith travels as a poet among crofters, castles, and emigrant ships, in the high romantic manner of Scots letters.
76867-tough-yarns-vol-2-of-2:
Tough Yarns, volume two, is a set of naval tales and sketches by an anonymous writer who calls himself the Old Sailor. Carey and Hart published the two volumes at Philadelphia in 1835. The author had written Greenwich Hospital.

The tales promise to please all hands, from the officers down to the newest boys. Ghost Stories leads the volume, with a motto from Henry the Fourth about calling spirits from the deep. The narrator recalls a father who feared no ghost and would walk a churchyard at midnight, while his five sons trembled at every noise after dusk. Other pieces give the Frere du Diable, a fisherman's family, the red flag at the fore, a prisoner, a convict, and a burning ship. A veteran soldier closes the set.
77060-the-autobiography-of-a-seaman-volu:
Thomas, Tenth Earl of Dundonald, wrote The Autobiography of a Seaman, shown here in Volume One of the 1861 second edition. Dundonald was an Admiral of the Red and Rear Admiral of the Fleet. Richard Bentley issued the book at London. The first part is given to the electors of Westminster.

Dundonald thanks those electors for aid near half a century past. He says their help saved him from despair. He links that help to harm done by foes in public life. Those foes had struck back at his push for reform in the navy. The life that follows tells of sea service, strife at home, and a long fight for fair play.
77164-walks-and-talks-of-an-american-far:
Walks and Talks of an American Farmer in England, part one of two, was published by Putnam at New York in 1852. The volume is inscribed to George Geddes, late of the New York senate. The preface says the author spent long winter evenings reading literary tourists on England, yet never found one written by a farmer. He writes for farmers and farmers' families, asking a fireside relation with his readers.

His errand is practical: the wages, cost, and manner of living of labouring men, and the labour customs of the districts foreign writers draw their data from. He warns that his gait is a farmer's leg and a sailor's leg helped by a crooked academic sapling of a walking stick. The frontispiece shows an English school-house. The book became a noted American account of English farming, soils, rents, and rural labour.
77165-walks-and-talks-of-an-american-far:
Walks and Talks of an American Farmer in England, part two, records a walking tour of 1850 and 1851. Frederick Law Olmsted wrote the book before his fame as a park maker. Putnam published this part at New York in 1852. Olmsted dedicates the volume to the memory of Andrew Jackson Downing.

The preface calls the book a fireside talk with his readers. Young Americans walked the west and south of England, he explains. A young farmer's eye judges farms, villages, and rural customs as they pass. Sheep walks, draining, gorse, and churchyards fill the early chapters. Shrewsbury cakes and brawn get their due as well. An appendix advises readers on cheap walking tours in Europe. Olmsted's eye for landscape already shows on every page.
77310-the-mediaeval-stage-volume-2-of-2:
Chambers wrote The Mediaeval Stage, first printed at Oxford in 1903, and this second volume is a later impression of 1925. A front picture shows the Dublin Quem quaeritis from a fourteenth-century manuscript at the Bodleian. The contents list both volumes. The first treats minstrelsy, from the fall of the theatres through the minstrel life and his repertory.

Folk drama fills the rest of the first volume: village festivals, the may-game, the sword-dance, and the mummers' play. The feast of fools, the boy bishop, and masks and misrule close it. This second volume turns to religious drama, with the liturgical plays and their slow move into guild and parish hands. Moralities, puppet-plays, and pageants follow, then the interlude and its players.
77322-notes-on-the-west-indies-vol-1-of-:
George Pinckard, a London physician, wrote these Notes on the West Indies in two volumes. The second edition came out in London in 1816. Pinckard served as deputy inspector-general of hospitals. He also worked as a physician at the Bloomsbury Dispensary. His letters cover the Creole and slave society of the western colonies and the Indians of South America.

The full title promises added letters from Martinique, Jamaica, and Saint Domingo. It also promises remarks on the seasoning, or yellow fever, of hot climates. The preface says the notes began as private writing for a friend. Pinckard never meant them for print while he wrote. Friends pressed him to publish, and he did so with misgivings. The book preserves an army doctor's close look at the Caribbean world of his day.
77323-notes-on-the-west-indies-vol-2-of-:
George Pinckard wrote Notes on the West Indies, here volume two. Baldwin and Seeley at London put out this edition in 1816. Observations on the creoles and slaves fill its long title. The Indians of South America stand in that title too. Remarks on the seasoning, or yellow fever, run through it.

Additional letters from Martinique, Jamaica, and Saint Domingo were added. Favourable tidings from Grenada and Saint Vincent open the letters. An enormous snake and talk of mermaids fill the first letter. An excursion to a Dutch plantation follows in the second. Funeral rites of an officer close that letter's account. Yellow fever treatment fills the third letter. Remarks on medical life stand in the same letter. Pinckard served as a deputy inspector of hospitals in the islands. The letters give a staff surgeon's West Indies in detail.
77498-life-histories-of-north-american-s:
Life Histories of North American Shore Birds, Part Two is a Smithsonian Institution bulletin on the sandpipers, plovers, and their kin. The United States Government Printing Office first published it in 1929. It appeared as Bulletin 146 of the United States National Museum. Part One had come out in 1927 as Bulletin 142.

A Dover reprint of 1962 kept the work in circulation unabridged. The transcriber's note for this edition memorialises the proofreading project manager who chose it for preservation. The life history method treats each species in turn: nesting, eggs, migration, food, and behaviour. Shore birds travel farther than almost any creatures on earth. Their Arctic nurseries and southern winters made their records precious to science. These bulletins remain the foundation on which modern shore bird study stands, entry by patient entry.
7751-godolphin-volume-2:
Constance and Godolphin walk and ride together each day in the second volume of Lytton's Godolphin, and at evening he hangs over her chair to hear her rich, soft songs. Lady Erpingham watches with secret delight, sure a match grows between two handsome, gifted young people.

Prudence whispers they are poor, but the countess recalls a dowry saved from her jointure for Constance, which she would gladly give if Godolphin were the groom. Through rural scenes, omens, and a first shy confession, the volume traces love growing under a kind chaperone's eye.
7758-falkland-book-2:
Emily Mandeville, married to a man she cannot love, finds her feelings waking in Book Two of Lytton's Falkland. The narrator warns it is risky for women to sit still with their hearts, for pause reveals a hollow that worldly folly once hid. Her son's birth had filled that hollow with new joy.

Then Falkland comes, and no woman he wished to charm had ever resisted him. His ardor matches her tenderness, and from that meeting her life splits in two. The volume is a frank early tale of a married woman's love, told with pity for a heart caught between duty and desire.
77586-magyarland-volume-1-of-2:
Magyarland is a travel book in two volumes, and the hosted text holds the first. Its author hides his name and calls himself a fellow of a mountain club. The full title calls it a tale of travels through the high and low lands of Hungary. The book came out in London in the year eighteen eighty one.

Chapters roam the great plain, gypsy camps, ice caves, and snow peaks in turn. Towns, wells, races, and folk rites of Slovaks and Rusniaks fill the route. Prints of peasants, shepherds, and town views face the text as plates. A love of mountains frames the whole tour, with awe at each new range. This first volume ends in high peaks with a chamois hunter tale.
77660-os-lusiadas-the-lusiads-vol-1-of-2:
Os Lusiadas, the Lusiads, is Camoens' great Portuguese epic in the English version of Richard Francis Burton. His wife Isabel Burton edited the two volumes, and Bernard Quaritch published them in London in 1880. Burton dedicates the version to the Emperor Dom Pedro II of Brazil, to the man rather than the monarch.

The first volume carries cantos one to six, each with its argument and endnotes. Isabel's preface tells what editing cost her: she had shared his travels in Portugal, four years up country in Brazil, and nineteen years of the Camoens table set apart each day. Burton's own sonnet hails Camoens as the great pilgrim-poet of sea and land. The volume gives English readers the poem in a scholar traveller's dress, notes and all.
77719-yes-and-no-volume-1-of-2:
A tale of the day, Yes and No, turns on a mind torn in two. Volume one came out in London in 1828. Its author had wrote Matilda, a tale in its fourth form then. Dante and Shakespeare lines head the book's front pages. Yes and no fight in my head, the Dante line says in tongue terms.

The front words grant two charges may be laid at his door. One is that he took too much from past tales. One is that he drew too sharp from true folk he knew. He pleads pure aims on the first and care on the next. Town love and pride fill the tale at hand.
77720-yes-and-no-volume-2-of-2:
Yes and No, billed as a tale of the day, came out in London in 1828 from Henry Colburn, in two volumes. This is the second. The title page names no author, only a credit to the writer of Matilda, and it carries lines from Dante and Shakespeare as mottoes.

The volume opens in the middle of a ball. Lady Latimer, held up at her dressing table, arrives two hours late to find the room at its height. Guests roll in by coach-and-six, by farm team and family chariot, each entrance a small study in rank and pride. Readers who like novels of manners get a close, arch look at the London season, where a yes and a no can both ruin a name.
77890-the-autobiography-of-a-seaman-volu:
Thomas, tenth Earl of Dundonald, wrote the Autobiography of a Seaman. Bentley at London put out this second volume in 1861. It is the second edition, printed by Spottiswoode for the house. Dundonald was an admiral of the Red and of the fleet. Contents open at chapter twenty-four of the whole.

That chapter is called a naval study for all time in the list. Charts supplied by one government and refused by a former one fill it. Affidavits, letters to Barrow, and a singular Admiralty minute stand there. The charts were refused again, and the writer departed for Chili. Renewed application and a duke's kindness close the contents entry. Elsewhere the volume treats of courts-martial and their fallacies at length. A judge advocate's reasons are detected in error by a president. Dundonald, the famed Lord Cochrane, pleads his own sea case.
77921-knickerbocker-s-history-of-new-yor:
Volume one of Knickerbocker's History of New York, by Washington Irving, is a comic false history told by Diedrich Knickerbocker. The Van Twiller printing is dated eighteen ninety-four, with drawings by Edward Kemble. Knickerbocker claims his is the sole true account of Dutch New York, in a tale that runs from the start of the world to the end of Dutch rule.

Book one plays with wild ideas on how the world was made and peopled, and book two turns to the first Dutch towns and to Hendrick Hudson's voyage. The three Dutch chiefs are Walter the Doubter, William the Testy, and Peter the Headstrong. Irving mocks proud histories while he tells real early facts of the colony.
77951-the-memoirs-of-philip-de-commines-:
The Memoirs of Philip de Commines, Lord of Argenton is the next part of a two part set, out at London in eighteen fifty-six. Commines tells the past of two kings of France and of a duke of Burgundy. A life of the man and notes by the hand who shaped the book stand with the text. A plate of the first king heads the book.

Parts of this book treat how that king coaxed the English past the dukes death, wed deals for the dukes heir, and the take back of towns in the dukes lands. The send of the lord to a town of Italy and a fight take parts. The kings sick spells, his loss of sense and speech, and his call for a holy man to cure him fill the mid parts. His death charge to his son closes the run.
77954-the-last-punic-war-vol-2-of-2:
Last Punic War is a history of Tunis past and present, in two volumes, by A M Broadley. The hosted text is volume two, issued at Edinburgh and London in eighteen eighty two. Broadley was a barrister and a correspondent of a London paper during the war in Tunis. Its subtitle promises a narrative of the French conquest of the regency. A picture shows a governor waiting for French troops outside a city gate.

Contents of this volume run from chapter twenty five onward. A revolt in a town, the shelling of Sfax, and loot take early chapters. The French occupation of the city of Tunis follows. Fighting in the south, the taking of Kairwan, and a journey to southern Tunis fill the middle. A month of chaos and a look at the future close the list.
78015-khartoum-and-the-blue-and-white-ni:
George Melly's second volume of travels in the Sudan continues his journey up the Nile, in the second edition published by Colburn at London in 1852. The chapters move by camel and boat through Nubia: the temple at Samneh, a jackal hunt, alkaline hot springs, Arab villages, and the antiquities of Gebel Berkel. At last the party reaches Khartoum, where the governor, Latiffe Pasha, receives them with extreme civility.

Khartoum's houses, trade, schools, and mixed peoples fill several chapters, with a grand banquet for the pasha and a visit to his household. The return takes in the pyramids at Meroe, a frightened hippopotamus, and arrival at Berber. Melly writes a lively gentleman's travel diary, curious about everything from dromedary saddles to summary justice.
78451-lectures-on-ancient-ethnography-an:
Niebuhr's Lectures on Ancient Ethnography and Geography, volume one of two, came out at London in 1853 from Walton and Maberly. Leonhard Schmitz, rector of the High School of Edinburgh, translated them from Isler's German edition, with additions from Niebuhr's own manuscript notes. The lectures were delivered at Bonn in the winter of 1827-28 and first printed at Berlin in 1851. Their scope covers Greece and her colonies, Epirus, Macedonia, Illyricum, Italy, Gaul, Spain, Britain, and the north of Africa.

Schmitz's dedication to Bishop Thirlwall tells how the bishop first urged publishing the lecture notes, some fifteen years earlier. Thirlwall had done much to make Niebuhr known to British scholars. The volume treats the peoples and lands of the ancient world as Niebuhr rebuilt them from the sources. The manner is the lecture manner: discursive, learned, and full of argument about names, migrations, and frontiers.
78452-lectures-on-ancient-ethnography-an:
Niebuhr lectures on the old world in Lectures on Ancient Ethnography and Geography, volume 2, printed in London in 1853. Walton and Maberly made the book. The lectures were translated from the German edition of Isler by Leonhard Schmitz, rector of the High School of Edinburgh, with additions and corrections from his own notes.

The course comprises Greece and her colonies, Epirus, Macedonia, Illyricum, Italy, Gaul, Spain, Britain, and the north of Africa. This volume's contents open on Italy: its name, its population, its physical character, and its divisions. Latium follows at length, then the topography of Rome. The most ancient parts of the city, the Seven Hills, the regions of Augustus, and the course of the ancient walls fill the run. The Capitoline Hill and the Tarpeian Rock stand in the city walk.
7851-memoirs-of-aaron-burr-volume-2:
Matthew L Davis's Memoirs of Aaron Burr, volume two, opens with Burr's brief study of law. It gives his definition of the craft, his way of preparing cases, his maxim for sluggards, and his love of mystery and surprise against opponents. His choice of agents and his coolness in civil and military life follow.

An anecdote from the contested election of 1800 shows the same acuteness in politics, after a career begun at the Revolution's close under fair auspices. With a frontispiece of Theodosia and the motto of burying Caesar, not praising him, Davis offers a candid, close portrait of a divisive founder.
78537-from-the-hebrides-to-the-himalayas:
From the Hebrides to the Himalayas, volume one, is a travel book by Gordon Cumming. Sampson Low issued it in London in 1876. Its subtitle calls it a sketch of eighteen months of wandering. Western isles and eastern highlands bound its range. The book is dedicated to the author's sister. Her care preserved the rough notes sent home by sea. She died while the pages lay by. Her memory now receives the dedication.

A publisher's note names Isabella Bird as proof editor. Bird, a famed traveller herself, revised the sheets. The author had sailed for Fiji as printing began. Family allusions are left as they stood, the note says. The letters form a lady's grand tour of the 1870s. Scotland's isles open the wandering here. The Himalaya end gives the title its sweep. Such journals taught the home public the wide world.
78570-a-mission-to-gelele-king-of-dahome:
Captain Sir Richard F. Burton wrote this tale of his trip to the King of Dahome, in two books of which this is the first. It stands in the set of his works made in his name past his death, set in order by his wife Isabel. The set is sent forth to all who speak English and hold his name in fame. He is named there as man of war, man of tongues, man of books, man of roams, poet, and friend of science.

The full head of this book gives the cast of the land he was sent to. He went as the Queen's man to Gelele, the King. The book bears notes on the so-called Amazons, the women of war of that king.
78571-a-mission-to-gelele-king-of-dahome:
Richard Burton, a British captain and famed traveler, wrote of his mission as royal envoy to Gelele, King of Dahome in West Africa. This second of two volumes came out in a memorial set of his works in London in 1893, edited by his wife Isabel. The front art shows the king's victims, a hint of the grim rites inside.

These pages treat the king's yearly customs, with human sacrifice at their heart, and the famed women troops called Amazons. Burton also covers Dahoman faith, a water sprinkling rite, the slave trade of the day, and his own views on the place of Black peoples in nature. The trip ends with his message given, a march back to the coast, and lists of route and costs.
78576-the-lost-bride-vol-2:
Lost Bride is a novel by Georgiana, Lady Chatterton, in three volumes. The hosted text is volume two, issued at London in eighteen seventy two. The right of translation is reserved on its title page. Chapter one of this volume is called Castle Hall and Its Beautiful Ghost. The narrator drives home with her Aunt Jane as it opens.

Her aunt felt sure their hostess had something on her mind, the narrator says. She had never known the lady so reserved before. The narrator longs to ramble over the old ruins again. Haunted, uninhabited rooms draw her, she owns. Next day they return by another road through the park. They cross a bridge and climb to the old entrance of the ancient castle. There they wander for hours to their hearts' content, she says.
78675-magyarland-volume-2-of-2:
Magyarland, volume two of two, is a travel narrative through Hungary by a fellow of a Carpathian society. The author had earlier written The Indian Alps, a book on high Asia. This second volume was published in London in eighteen eighty one. Its frontispiece shows the defile of the lower Danube in full page form.

Twenty five chapters carry the tour from the Danube heights to Agram. Roman remains at Trajan's bridge and the baths at Mehadia open the route. Grosswardein offers a Good Friday in the Greek church for study. The queen of the great plain and Hermannstadt follow in the march eastward. Time with the Wallachs and the Red Tower pass lead into high Transylvania. Debreczin, the wine districts of Tokay, and the gold mines of Schemnitz close it. Many small pictures show soldiers, priests, peasants, and river scenes.
78724-six-months-in-america-vol-1-of-2:
Six Months in America, volume I, is a travel narrative by Godfrey T Vigne. Whittaker, Treacher and Co published it in London in 1832. Vigne was a barrister of Lincoln's Inn. He refused, he says, to inflict a preface on the reader. He sailed from Liverpool on the 24th of March, 1831. The packet George Canning carried him, alone, with note-book, sketch-book, gun, and fishing rod.

The passage took twenty-three days, fast for the season. Vigne sailed through the Narrows into New York bay. He describes Fort La Fayette, Fort Tomkins, and the landing place at New Utrecht. An engraving of Niagara fronts the volume. Vigne meant to see all he could of the United States in six months. He also meant, as far as an Englishman can, to travel unprejudiced. This first volume begins the record of what he saw.
78730-knickerbocker-s-history-of-new-yor:
Knickerbocker's History of New York is Washington Irving's comic history of Dutch New York, and this text is volume two of two. It is the Van Twiller edition, published by Putnam in New York in 1894. Edward Kemble drew the illustrations. The frontispiece shows colonists filing through the gate at the head of Wall Street.

Irving pretends the book is the work of Diedrich Knickerbocker, a Dutch antiquarian. Its full title promises the ponderings of Walter the Doubter and the projects of William the Testy. The chivalric achievements of Peter the Headstrong, Peter Stuyvesant, fill this volume. Irving's mock history, first printed in 1809, made his name and fixed the Dutch legend of New York.
78744-specimens-of-the-russian-poets-vol:
Specimens of the Russian Poets, volume one of two, was translated by John Bowring and printed in London in eighteen twenty-one. This is the second edition, with additions, sold by R Hunter and by Constable of Edinburgh. A Russian title, Rossiiskaya Antologiya, heads the title page. Bowring adds preliminary remarks and biographical notices.

His advertisement calls Russian poetry an unformed and infant literature, born but yesterday. The contents begin with Derzhavin and Batiushkov, then Lomonosov and Zhukovsky. Karamsin, Dmitriev, and the fabulist Krilov follow, with national songs near the end. Bowring hoped England would welcome these strangers as cordially as it had. The anthology was most English readers' first meeting with Russian verse. Its specimens are small, but the door they opened was large.
78758-six-months-in-america-vol-2-of-2:
Volume two of Six Months in America, by Godfrey Vigne, was issued at London in 1832. A plate of locks on the Rideau Canal, at Bytown on the Ottawa river, fronts the book. Vigne was a barrister of Lincoln’s Inn who toured the young republic. This volume opens as he leaves Washington behind him.

His road runs to Harper’s Ferry, in the second volume’s first pages. English travellers of that age crossed America with notebooks in hand. They judged its inns, its manners, its canals, and its politics for readers at home. Vigne gives six months of such notes in two volumes. The Canadian scenes in the plate hint at the range of his tour. The book is a sharp eyed tour of the United States of Jackson’s day.
7877-passages-from-the-english-notebooks:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Passages from the English Note-Books, volume two, opens April 4, 1856, at a Milton Club dinner on Ludgate Hill. Hawthorne dines with Bennoch at a club for dissenters and nonconformists whose ideas sit uneasily with church and state, in a large reading room full of papers.

A tall white-haired gentleman and Mr. Tupper greet each other warmly, and Hawthorne steps forward with outstretched hand before his name can be spoken unheard. Through London dinners, travel, and talk, the notebooks record an American author's daily England with candor, humor, and watchful detail.
7880-passages-from-the-french-and-italia:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Passages from the French and Italian Note-Books, volume two, continues in Florence on June 8, with a morning at the Uffizi gallery. The entrance lies through a great palace court to the Arno at one end and the Grand Ducal Piazza at the other, with Medici busts in the vestibule.

Hawthorne walks the long gallery slowly, full of sculpture and pictures, a chronological run from Giotto and Cimabue through Botticelli, Fra Angelico, and Filippo Lippi. Though pictures face away from light, he calls it the most perfect series he has seen, haunted by masters in every church.
78914-the-decline-of-the-west-volume-2:
The Decline of the West, volume two, Perspectives of World History, is Oswald Spengler's vast study of cultures and their fates. The German original came out in 1922, and the hosted copy is the authorized English version by Atkinson, issued by Alfred Knopf at New York in 1928. A translator's note explains the added references to the Encyclopaedia Britannica.

Where the first volume set out the shapes of cultures, this one walks through world history itself, stressing the Magian world of the early Middle East. Few books have stirred more argument about whether nations and cultures must age and die like living things.
79321-clare-abbey-volume-1-of-2:
Clare Abbey, or The Trials of Youth is a tale in two parts, of which this is the first. It came out at London in eighteen fifty-one. Its hand is named past a past book on the rule of life. Two poems head the tale, one on how life may have more high ends than joy, and one by an old bard on a posy made as a day ran by.

That bard tells how Time beckoned his blooms and they stole off past noon and died in his hand. His hand, then his heart, took the soft warn with no moan. The tale opens with a boy of six years who slides from his chair with a lead point in hand. He has a most set thing to say to his mother, he vows. His bold mien makes him seem past his years.
79324-clare-abbey-volume-2-of-2:
Clare Abbey, or The Trials of Youth, volume two, continues the novel by the author of The Discipline of Life. Colburn and Company of Great Marlborough Street, London, published both volumes in 1851. The second volume opens with the new year, which dawns well in Camilla's opinion because it brings a little novelty with it.

Reginald enters the drawing room earlier than usual and asks Camilla to walk with him to the white stone on the hill above the park. She laughs that she is not quite a cripple yet. Reginald answers with a slight sarcasm: Miss Vincent said yesterday that she was so very easily knocked up, and perhaps she had taught Camilla the same. The exchange sets the volume's terms: her spirits tested by those who would school them down. The Druids' stones draw her curiosity onward.
79367-the-book-of-the-boudoir-volume-1-o:
Lady Morgan published The Book of the Boudoir in London in 1829, in two volumes, and this is the first of them. She opens with a line from Montaigne that sets the tone: I do not teach, I relate. The book belongs, by her own account, to a light class of writing that the French did best.

In her note to the reader, Lady Morgan says the pages were drawn from her own manuscript volumes. She had lived at times among noted and well-known people, and she kept notes on them all. She chose what was safe to print and aimed her sharp words at ideas, not at persons. Readers get loose, chatty sketches of the society she moved in.
79368-the-book-of-the-boudoir-volume-2-o:
The Book of the Boudoir, volume two, is a set of short essays by Lady Morgan, printed at London in 1829. Morgan took her motto from Montaigne: I do not teach, I tell. The volume runs through dozens of brief heads, from fans and cats to poets' loves and the trades.

Some pieces weigh grave themes like toleration, the Catholic question, and the rights of women. Others are light notes on temper, riches, truth, and old friends. Strawberry Hill and the arts get longer treatment near the end. The mix shows a sharp, well read hostess at work, turning talk into print for readers who liked wit with their thought.
79387-maxwell-drewitt-vol-2-of-2:
Maxwell Drewitt, volume two of two, is a novel by Trafford, issued at Leipzig in 1866. It appeared in the Tauchnitz collection of British authors. That series sold English books for readers on the continent. Buyers were asked not to carry copies into England. Trafford also wrote George Geith, a well-known tale. The contents list runs to twenty-two chapters and a close.

The second volume follows Brian and Harold through fresh troubles. A funeral, a farewell, and an hour of success come early. An unfortunate likeness stirs a key misunderstanding. The tale moves through country gossip to Connemara. Brian's repentance and a sickness unto death follow. Brighter days end the closing chapters. The Tauchnitz dress marks the book's wide reach. English novels then travelled fast across Europe in this form.
79410-abeokuta-and-the-camaroons-mountai:
Volume two of Abeokuta and the Camaroons Mountains, by Richard Burton, came out in London in 1863. Tinsley Brothers put out the two-volume work of travel in West Africa. This half opens with statecraft, a leave-taking, and a return to Lagos. It then turns to the Camaroons range, with first steps and a camp at Mann's Spring. Burton tells of the first ascent of Pico Grande in full. Later climbs by Calvo, Saker, and Mann are set down too.

A final ascent and the trip back to Fernando Po close the tale. Back parts add notes on land, folk, plants, and beasts of the range. One long list names the flora of the peaks and isles nearby. Charts of heights and weather notes end the book. Burton writes as a trained lands man, keen on place and wild ground.
79527-the-pageant-of-parliament-vol-2-of:
The Pageant of Parliament, volume two, explains the ways of the British legislature from inside. Michael MacDonagh, a gallery reporter, wrote the book. Fisher Unwin published the volume at London in 1921. MacDonagh had written lives of the Speaker and of the reporters' gallery.

Twenty chapters run from the big debate to the call of who goes home. The making of an act and the royal assent come early. A night in the Lords and the Lord Chancellor's powers follow. Chapters treat the party whip's thumb and the tricks of party war. Money bills, the budget, and control of the purse fill the centre. War time changes and the Chiltern Hundreds close the book. MacDonagh writes as a lover of the old house and its ways.
79675-the-life-of-sethos-vol-1-of-2:
The Life of Sethos, printed in London in 1732, purports to be taken from private memoirs of the ancient Egyptians. Lediard translated it into English from the Paris edition, itself rendered from a Greek manuscript into French. This first of two volumes comes with a map of Egypt, and the preface explains that the library holding the supposed original must stay concealed.

The work is in truth a romance of ancient Egypt dressed as recovered history, following Sethos through the courts, temples, and mysteries of the Nile kingdom. Its preface defends history itself as the surest guide in politics and a foundation of moral instruction. Sethos became one of the most influential Egypt romances of its century, feeding the European taste for Egyptian wisdom and secret rites.
79720-china-and-the-allies-vol-1-of-2:
Savage-Landor wrote this account of China and the Allies, volume one. Heinemann printed it in London in 1901 with maps and plates. A Buddhist priest fronts the volume, the book given to his sister. Past books took him to Tibet and Corea morning calm land.

Chapter one traces the Boxers, or Volunteer United Fists, to their source. The Big Sword Society and crusade against foreign devils follow there. Reform edicts, Boxer colours, arms, and war songs fill chapter two. Roman Catholics, mistaken beliefs, and placards fill the next chapter. Assembly halls, or Loo, of the Boxers get their own passage in chapter two.
7975-memoirs-of-james-robert-hope-scott-:
Robert Ornsby, professor of Greek and Latin literature in the Catholic University of Ireland, wrote this second volume of memoirs of James Robert Hope-Scott of Abbotsford, with selections from his correspondence. The volume opens in 1841 and 1842 with Hope's pamphlet on the Jerusalem bishopric, his study of canon law. And his letters to John Henry Newman about a monastery and the Oxford Movement. Later chapters follow Pusey's consultation of Hope and the religious controversies of the time.

The memoir is built from letters, so Hope's mind and friendships emerge in his own words. Readers interested in the Oxford Movement, the road to Rome, and Victorian religious argument will find a detailed, insider account. Volume two stands on its own for the 1840s, though it gains depth read after the first.
8089-passages-from-the-american-notebook:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's second volume of passages from his American notebooks opens at Brook Farm on April 13, 1841, where he calls the snowy settlement a polar paradise. Comparing the community's stormy arrival to the Plymouth pilgrims stepping ashore on mountain snowdrifts, he insists that spring and summer will come in due season. Later extracts come from his private letters as well as his journals.

The notebooks show Hawthorne observing before he invented: landscapes, neighbours, and the daily life of the Brook Farm experiment. They are the raw material of his fiction, full of images that later grew into stories. For readers of The Scarlet Letter and The House of the Seven Gables, this volume is a revealing workshop, and a record of a writer watching America closely.
8167-gargantua-and-pantagruel-illustrate:
Book two of Rabelais's Gargantua and Pantagruel follows the giant Pantagruel, son of Gargantua, through his heroic deeds and sayings. The English text reprints Sir Thomas Urquhart of Cromarty's 1653 translation, with footnotes from the Maitland Club edition of 1838 and the translators. Urquhart's translation of book three appeared posthumously in 1693, and Peter Antony Motteux's rendering of books four and five followed in 1708. With some omitted passages restored from the 1738 edition edited by Ozell.

Rabelais's second book is a feast of learned comedy, bawdy humour, and satire on church, law, and learning. Pantagruel's Paris education and his battles remain famous. For readers new to Rabelais, this book offers his world at its most exuberant, in a translation that is itself a classic of English prose.
8459-marse-henry-an-autobiography-volume:
Volume 2 of Henry Watterson's autobiography, Marse Henry, continues the Louisville editor's story into Congress and wider circles. Contents list Charles Eames and Charles Sumner, Schurz and Lamar, and Watterson going to Congress. Stephen Foster and his songs, music and Theodore Thomas follow, then Henry Adams and his family, John Hay, and the three mousquetaires of culture, with Paris scenes.

Watterson writes as a man who knew the makers of post-Civil War America, and the volume mixes politics with music, letters, and friendship. Readers get a firsthand account of Washington and Louisville life, witty and partisan. It pairs with volume 1, and stands alone as a memoir of an editor among statesmen.
8461-memoirs-of-henry-hunt-esq-volume-2:
Henry Hunt wrote these memoirs himself, in His Majesty's jail at Ilchester, in Somerset, and volume 2 continues his story. Hunt, the radical orator known as Orator Hunt, was jailed after the Peterloo era. His memoirs mix self-defense, political argument, and prison life, with Pope's lines on faultless pieces as his epigraph.

Readers meet a leading voice of early nineteenth-century radicalism, writing from a cell about reform, crowds, and his own career. Hunt's memoirs are partisan and vivid, and they show how radicals told their own stories when the press attacked them. The volume suits readers of British political history, and of prison writing.
8472-life-on-the-mississippi-part-2:
Part 2 of Life on the Mississippi opens with chapter 6, A Cub-pilot's Experience, aboard the poor old Paul Jones. Delayed four days on rocks at Louisville, plus other delays, the boat fools away about two weeks going from Cincinnati to New Orleans. The young Twain gets acquainted with a pilot who teaches him to steer, deepening the fascination of river life.

This section shows the cub pilot's schooling, with steering lessons, river lore, and the slow growth of skill. Readers get Twain's apprenticeship in full, after the geography of part 1. It is the book's training montage, told with humor about a young man's eagerness to master a dangerous trade.
8512-the-three-cities-trilogy-lourdes-vo:
Émile Zola's Lourdes, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, continues in volume 2 with the second day of the pilgrimage. The train arrives at twenty minutes past three by the Lourdes station clock, its dial lit by a reflector. Shadowy forms move under the slanting roof of the platform, resignedly going to and fro, pilgrims and patients seeking a cure.

Zola, the naturalist novelist, studied Lourdes as a social phenomenon: faith, sickness, hope, and commerce around the grotto. Volume 2 follows Pierre and Marie through the second day's devotions and disappointments. Readers get a novel that is also reportage, skeptical and compassionate, about why crowds still come to Lourdes.
8527-eve-s-diary-part-2:
Part 2 of Mark Twain's Eve's Diary, illustrated by Lester Ralph, opens on Sunday, pleasant again, though heavy days came before. Eve writes that she tried to get Adam some of those apples, but cannot learn to throw straight, and failed, though she thinks the good intention pleased him. The apples are forbidden, Adam says she shall come to harm, but she is not so sure.

This middle part follows Eve's Eden life as she learns the garden, its creatures, and Adam's gruff ways. Readers get Twain's Eve in full curiosity, testing rules and charming her companion. The part suits readers following the diary in order, and those who want Eve's voice at its most playful.
8533-the-literary-remains-of-samuel-tayl:
Volume 2 of the Literary Remains of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, collected and edited by Henry Nelson Coleridge, continues the poet's unpublished writings. Contents open with an extract from a letter of February 1818 to a gentleman who attended Coleridge's spring lectures, and a letter to J. Britton, before moving into Shakespeare criticism and other remains.

Readers meet Coleridge as lecturer and critic, thinking aloud about Shakespeare and poetry in letters and fragments. The volume, like its companion, preserves what Coleridge's nephew judged worth saving from a vast, unfinished mind. For Coleridge students, it is a primary source; for general readers, a glimpse of Romantic criticism in the making.
8540-the-life-of-the-rt-hon-sir-charles-:
Stephen Gwynn began this life of Sir Charles W. Dilke, and Gertrude M. Tuckwell, Dilke's literary executrix, completed and edited it, in two volumes with portraits. Volume 2 opens with chapter 34, Home Affairs from October 1883 to December 1884. Egypt in 1884, and franchise and redistribution, follow, tracing Dilke's career through the great questions of late Victorian politics.

Dilke, a radical Liberal minister, fell from power over a divorce scandal, and the biography treats his later life with care. Readers get a political life from inside the Liberal Party, with documents and recollection. The volume suits readers of Victorian politics, and of reputations made and broken.
8552-the-seaboard-parish-volume-2:
George MacDonald continues The Seaboard Parish in volume 2, with contents including Another Sunday Evening, Niceboots, The Blacksmith, The Life-Boat, Mr. Percivale, The Shadow of Death, At the Farm, The Keeve, The Walk to Church, and The Old Castle, with Joe and his trouble and a small adventure.

MacDonald, the Scottish minister and fantasist who influenced C. S. Lewis, writes a parish novel as a series of sermons, stories, and seaside scenes. The narrator, a minister, reflects on his people, his family, and the shore. Readers get Victorian religious fiction at its gentlest, where sermons and daily life braid together by the sea.
8583-roughing-it-part-2:
Chapter 11 begins the second part of Mark Twain's Roughing It, published in 1880, by turning to frontier justice in Montana. There, local vigilantes hanged Slade, a notorious figure who had relocated to the territory from Rocky Ridge. Twain retells the episode using Dimsdale's history The Vigilantes of Montana as his source.

This section follows Twain's western years through the Slade story and frontier justice, with humor and horror mixed. Readers get the West as Twain lived it, where law was improvised and violence common. Part 2 suits readers following Roughing It in order, and those who want Twain's frontier at its rawest.
8594-normandy-the-scenery-romance-of-its:
This second part of Gordon Home's illustrated tour of Normandy opens at chapter four, in the cathedral city of Evreux at evening. The great bell tolls over cobbled streets, yellow light washes painted house fronts, and laurels in the courtyard of the Hotel du Grand Cerf catch the last sun. Home insists Evreux needs no fine evening to please, and the chapter sets out to prove it street by street.

From Evreux the road runs to Bernay and on through the towns covered in this middle stretch of the book, with Home's drawings and notes on churches, inns, and country roads. The pace stays slow and observant, built for a traveller on foot or by carriage rather than a hurried tourist. Readers get the companion volume to parts one and three, filling the map between Rouen and the western coast.
8674-charles-o-malley-the-irish-dragoon-:
Charles Lever continues the adventures of Charles O'Malley, the Irish dragoon, in this second volume, illustrated by Phiz. The Peninsular War provides the ground: skirmishes, the lines of Ciudad Rodrigo, the Coa, night marches, Lisbon, and the retreat of the French. Between battles come dinners, masquerades, villas, letters, confessions, and the hero's charger, Maurice, all told with Lever's high spirits.

Later chapters reach Fuentes d'Onoro, Almeida, and a night on the Azava, mixing real campaign history with comic scrapes and romantic entanglements. O'Malley's servant Mike and the regimental doctor add broad humour to the soldiering. The volume stands as a classic of Irish military fiction, best read after volume one, and still enjoyable for its pace, its jokes, and its picture of Wellington's army from inside.
8702-the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-2:
Gustave Dore's Bible illustrations reach their second volume with the patriarchs and the early judges. The text pairs each engraving with its Bible passage, beginning with the trial of Abraham's faith on Mount Moriah. Then the burial of Sarah, Eliezer finding Rebekah, Isaac blessing Jacob, and Jacob tending Laban's flocks. Joseph's story follows, from his sale into Egypt to his dreams for Pharaoh and his reunion with his brothers.

Moses in the bulrushes closes the patriarchal arc, before the volume turns to war against Gibeon and Jael slaying Sisera. Dore's dramatic engravings, all shadow, scale, and gesture, made the Bible visible for millions who could not afford the grand original edition. Readers can enjoy the pictures in the mind's eye through the passages, and follow a sweep of Genesis and Judges in short, powerful scenes.
8722-the-three-cities-trilogy-rome-volum:
Emile Zola's Rome, in Ernest A. Vizetelly's translation, follows Abbe Pierre Froment through the Eternal City in this second volume, which is Part II of the novel. Pierre, having leisure one afternoon, begins his wanderings with a visit he has set his heart on. Prompted by a letter from old Count Orlando Prada, hero of Italian independence and reunion. Prada wrote spontaneously after a hasty reading of Pierre's book New Rome, and his letter blazes with patriotic faith, accusing the priest of errors about Italy.

From that meeting, the volume opens Rome's two worlds: the Romans of the new Italy, the Pradas and Saccos, the Corso and the Pincio. The ancient city of palaces, forums, and catacombs. Zola piles up street life, art, and church politics as Pierre seeks a hearing for his book. Readers get the middle movement of a great naturalist novel about faith, Rome, and modern Italy.
8791-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
This second part of Dante's Purgatory, in Cary's translation, covers cantos five through ten. Canto five opens with Dante leaving spirits behind and following his conductor. When a soul points and cries out that light does not shine from Dante's left hand, since he, a living man, blocks it. The shades gaze in wonder, first at the marvel and then at Dante himself, until Virgil urges him on like a tower, unmoved by babbling crowds.

Later cantos climb the mountain's lower slopes, meeting the late repentant, the negligent rulers, and souls who sing as they wait. The mood softens from Hell's terror to hope: punishment here cleanses rather than merely torments. Readers moving from the Inferno will feel the change at once, in lighter air, music, and the promise that these souls will, in time, ascend. The part makes a gentle entry to Purgatory's middle cantos.
8797-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
Cary's Paradise continues in this second part, covering cantos fifteen through twenty-one, where Dante climbs through the heavens of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. Canto fifteen opens with true love showing itself clear in kindness, as sacred chords fall silent before righteous prayer, and a sudden trail of fire glides through the still, pure evening air. The imagery of light grows ever more intense as Dante meets his ancestor Cacciaguida.

Warriors of faith, just rulers formed into an eagle of light, and contemplatives on a golden ladder fill these cantos, testing Dante's understanding of history, justice, and prayer. Beatrice guides and explains, while Dante's questions grow bolder. Readers in the middle of Paradise will find its most political heavens here, where earthly fame and heavenly order are weighed against each other in shining, difficult poetry.
8824-poems-in-two-volumes-volume-2:
William Wordsworth's second volume of Poems in Two Volumes turns to Scotland and to moods of his own mind. Poems written during a tour in Scotland open with Rob Roy's Grave, The Solitary Reaper, Stepping Westward, Glen-Almain, the Matron of Jedborough, To a Highland Girl. An address to the sons of Burns after visiting their father's grave on August 14, 1803. Yarrow unvisited closes the Scottish group in the contents shown.

Moods of My Own Mind follows. To a Butterfly, Written in March while resting on the bridge at the foot of Brother's Water, The Small Celandine, and The Sparrow's Nest. The volume shows Wordsworth at his most intimate and musical, finding large feeling in small encounters. Readers who love the famous Reaper will find its companions here, and a book that rewards quiet, repeated reading.
891-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
In this second volume of Gibbon's history, Rome's story turns from emperors to faith and to a new capital. The opening chapters follow the Roman state's dealings with Christians, from Nero's reign to Constantine's favour, tracing persecution, growth, and the church's slow rise within the empire.

Gibbon then tells how Constantine founded Constantinople and remade the empire's government around it. Milman's notes guide the reader through the sources. The volume matters because it shows an empire changing its gods and its centre, a change that would shape Europe and the Near East for a thousand years.
8912-lyrical-ballads-with-other-poems-18:
William Wordsworth issued this second volume of Lyrical Ballads in 1800, the book that helped launch English Romantic poetry. It gathers short poems on farm folk, children, lost love, and quiet country scenes, told in plain speech rather than grand, high-flown verse. Wordsworth held that true feeling could live in simple words.

Here readers meet Lucy Gray, the shepherd boys of Dungeon-Gill, Ruth, and the boy who listens to owls, among many others. The poems prize memory, nature, and the inner life of plain people. For students of poetry, this volume is a key text, showing a new style at the very start of its life.
8929-adela-cathcart-volume-2:
George MacDonald's Adela Cathcart continues in this second volume with song, the curate and his wife. The shadows, an evening at the curate's, Percy and his mother, the broken swords, and my uncle Peter. The narrator confesses slight dismay at the solemn turn the club-stories have taken, lasting only a moment. Adela is deeply interested, again wearing the look of abstracted thought and feeling. He tells himself this mental fare differs greatly from what she is used to, yet she can mark, learn, and inwardly digest it.

Adela, an invalid young woman, is healed in part by stories told by a circle of friends, in MacDonald's frame-tale design. Fairy tales, parables, and sermons in story form do the work of medicine and ministry together. Readers who enjoy MacDonald's fantasy and his theology will find volume two deepening the first.
9095-the-life-and-letters-of-maria-edgew:
Augustus J. C. Hare edited this second volume of the life and letters of Maria Edgeworth, the Irish novelist. The letters, such as one from Coppet in September 1820, follow Edgeworth and her father through Switzerland, in low carriages over mountain roads, past glaciers, cascades, and the fair valley of Lauterbrunn. Her eye is quick and amused.

Through her own words, readers meet the Europe of her day, its writers, hosts, and scenes, and see how a working novelist watched the world she later wrote about. Hare's editing lets Edgeworth speak for herself. The volume is a delight for those who love letters as a form of travel and talk.
9165-the-three-cities-trilogy-paris-volu:
Émile Zola wrote Paris as the third book of his Three Cities trilogy, translated by Ernest Vizetelly. This volume holds Book Two of the novel. Its hero, Abbé Pierre Froment, a priest who has lost his faith, shelters his wounded brother Guillaume in a quiet house at Neuilly. Revolution brews in the streets outside.

Pierre tends Guillaume in silence, torn between love for his brother and dread of the plot around him. Zola sets private anguish against public strife. The volume carries the trilogy toward its close, where faith, reason, and life fight for Pierre's soul.
920-ethics-part-2:
Baruch Spinoza's Ethics continues in Part Two, on the nature and origin of the mind, translated by R. H. M. Elwes. Spinoza now explains the results that must follow from the essence of God, the eternal and infinite being, though not all of them, for the mind itself becomes his subject.

He argues that mind and body are one substance seen in two ways, and that ideas follow from God as surely as bodies do. His geometric method stays strict, with definitions, axioms, and proofs. Part Two is the bridge from God to man in Spinoza's system, and it is vital for readers following his argument whole.
9316-a-doctor-of-the-old-school-volume-2:
Ian Maclaren wrote this Scots tale of Dr. MacLure, the doctor of Drumtochty, in Book Two, Through the Flood. MacLure gives no grand speech from the hearthrug, as town doctors might.
