Speeches in a working tongue are rendered into the other. Speeches in the other three official tongues are rendered into both. A delegate may also speak in any other tongue, at the cost of providing the rendering. The Assembly urges all other UN bodies to adopt the same rules, and asks for a study of phone-based live translation.
un-ga-res-a-69-2:
Heads of state and chiefs from across the world met at UN headquarters in New York on 22 and 23 September 2014 for the World Conference on Indigenous Peoples. Resolution A/69/2 adopts the outcome text of that meeting. The assembled chiefs pledge fresh fealty to the aims of the Charter, in a spirit of joint work with the native peoples of the world.

The text welcomes the ground work of the native peoples themselves, above all the world meet at Alta, in Norway, in June 2013. It states fresh backing for the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. The UN's role in guarding those rights, the chiefs hold, stays both weighty and lasting.
un-ga-res-es-11-2:
War's human toll in Ukraine fills Resolution ES-11/2, passed by the General Assembly in emergency session on 24 March 2022. The text backs Ukraine's freedom, unity, and land in full, out to its waters. Russia's attack inside Ukraine, it says, has brought a scale of suffering Europe has not seen in decades. The Secretary-General's plea that Russia halt its attack is backed in plain terms.

Aid must reach all who need it, the vote holds, and civilians must be shielded from harm. States near Ukraine that took in crowds of the fleeing are praised. The text was the Assembly's second vote of the emergency session, after the call for Russia to pull out. It passed by 140 votes to five.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 2, adopted on 1 February 1946, set the language rules of the United Nations. The annexed rules made Chinese, French, English, Russian, and Spanish the official languages, with English and French as the working languages used day to day.

Under the rules, speeches in one working language were interpreted into the other, and speeches in the other official languages into both. Word-for-word records were kept in the working languages, short records in all official ones, and all resolutions were issued in the official languages. The Assembly also urged the other organs to adopt like rules, and asked for study of telephone interpretation systems.

General Assembly resolution 69/2 adopts the outcome document of the World Conference on Indigenous Peoples, the Assembly's high-level meeting held in New York on 22 and 23 September 2014. Governments meeting there recommit to the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted in 2007.

The outcome document commits states to consult and cooperate with indigenous peoples through their own institutions. It commits them to seek free, prior, and informed consent before measures that affect them. It commits them to build national action plans to carry out the Declaration. It promises better data, equal access to education and health care, and protection for indigenous women and children. It promises respect for rights over lands, territories, and resources. It also asks for a system-wide United Nations action plan. The conference turned the Declaration from a statement of rights into a program of national follow-through.

Resolution ES-11/2 of the General Assembly, adopted at the eleventh emergency special session in 2022, deals with the humanitarian consequences of the aggression against Ukraine. It follows resolution ES-11/1 of 2 March 2022. That resolution's demand for the complete withdrawal of Russian forces is repeated here. The text responds to a humanitarian crisis it describes as unseen in Europe for decades.

The Assembly demands an immediate end to the hostilities by the Russian Federation, above all attacks on civilians and civilian objects. It demands that sieges of cities, in particular Mariupol, be lifted. It calls for safe humanitarian access. It calls for protection of medical and aid workers, hospitals and supplies. It calls for respect for international humanitarian law. It asks member states to fund the United Nations humanitarian and refugee response plans in full. The plans are for Ukraine and its neighbours.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: UN Security Council Resolution 2 — the 1946 resolution urging Iran and the Soviet Union to negotiate over the troop presence. It stands among the Council’s earliest formal acts, from its founding year. The founding-year negotiation is the earliest: the 1946 Soviet-Iran talks urged.
un-un-res-united-nations-human-rights-co: UN Human Rights Council Resolution 32/2 — the Council's 2016 vote numbered 32/2. It put the 2016 stance on record. The 32/2 vote is the 2016 mark: the Council's line that year on file, filed here in full session today.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s10-2:
Section 10.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers the scope and sources of the Presidential Papers publication. It sits in Part 10, on presidential papers. Part (a) states what the text of the publication is made of. It is made of oral statements by the President or of writing signed by the President. The matter is chosen from transcripts or texts issued by the Office of the White House Press Secretary.

The kinds of matter named are six in the part of the text shown. They are communications to Congress, public addresses and remarks, and news conferences and interviews. They are also public messages and letters, statements put out on other subjects, and formal executive documents issued under law. Part (b) of the section adds further matter. The text is drawn from the eCFR as of October 2026.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s11-2:
Section 11.2 of Title 1 of the federal rules sets prices for the Federal Register. The daily paper is the daily Federal Register sold by subscription. A full year of the paper form costs a set sum in the rule. A joint subscription adds the monthly index and a monthly list.

That list names the rule book sections touched by new rules each month. The joint paper subscription costs a set higher sum per year. Six-month subscriptions are sold at one half of the yearly rate. Postage is not in the prices and is charged by delivery mode. A single copy of the daily paper costs by its page count. Three page bands carry three set prices in the rule text. The online form of the Register is free on government sites.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s12-2:
Section 12.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations deals with copies of the Code in paper form. It sits in Part 12, on the spread of the Code in the federal state. Copies in paper form are to be given with no charge to a set of bodies. The first body named is the committees of Congress. Each committee of the Senate and of the House is to be given the count of copies it needs for use in public work.

The count for a committee is set by a written call. That call is to come from the chair of the committee, or from a man the chair names for the end, to the Director of the Federal Register. A second body named is the Supreme Court.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s15-2: Section 15.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers information services of the Office of the Federal Register. It sits in Part 15, on services to federal agencies. The Director of the Federal Register is to provide for the answering of each fit inquiry. Inquiries may be made in person, by phone, or in writing. Each piece of writing and each matter that touches the Administrative Committee is to be sent to a named address. That address is the Director in Washington, DC.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s16-2:
Section 16.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations lists the duties of agency liaison officers. It sits in Part 16, on agency representatives, in the title on general provisions. Each such officer serves as the agency's link to the Office of the Federal Register.

The officer speaks for the agency in all matters on sending documents to that office and on compliance with the chapter. The officer must see that Federal Register guidance on drafting and on publication help is spread and used in the agency. The officer must also push the agency's share in the training that guidance backs. Last, the officer must be on hand to talk over filed documents with the Register's editors.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s17-2:
Section 17.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets the procedure and timing for the regular schedule of Federal Register filing and publication. It comes from the Administrative Committee of the Federal Register and sits in the part on filing for public inspection and publication schedules.

A document is filed for public inspection only after it has been received, processed, and given a publication date. Documents received by the daily 2:00 deadline that meet the chapter's rules go on the regular schedule, while later arrivals move to the next working day. Meeting notices under the Government in the Sunshine Act go on immediate public inspection instead, with timing set by when they arrive.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s18-2:
Section 18.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations is a short bar on mixed files in the Federal Register. The rule sits in Part 18, which deals with how documents are made and sent in for filing and print. The text here is the web text as of October 23, and that web text is not the formal yearly book.

The Director of the Federal Register will not accept a document that mixes material from more than one class. For example, one file may not hold both rulemaking material and a notice of proposed rulemaking. The bar is on the mix in a single file, not on links between files. If two linked documents are to run in the same issue, the agency may put a cross-reference in each one.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s19-2:
Section 19.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations deals with the path of drafts of orders of the President. It sits in Part 19, on Executive orders and proclamations of the President. A draft of such an order is first to be sent to the Director of the Office of Management and Budget. Seven copies of the draft are to go with it. A letter is to go with the draft as well. That letter must be signed by the head of the agency where the draft was born, or by an officer with the right to sign.

The letter is to set out the kind, the aim, the past, and the force of the draft. It is also to set out the tie of the draft, if any, to laws that bear on it and to orders of the past.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s2-2:
Section 2.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations describes the Administrative Committee of the Federal Register. The rule sits in a part on general information under Title 1. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. That committee oversees the federal rulemaking journal system.

The committee is established by a section of Title 44 of the United States Code, the rule states. Its membership is then listed by office. The Archivist of the United States, or the Acting Archivist, serves as chairman. An officer of the Department of Justice is named next. A small cross agency board thus steers the Register and the Code.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s20-2:
Section 20.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers preparation of agency statements for a federal manual. The manual is the United States Government Manual. The rule sits in the part on handling statements for that manual. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six.

In line with schedules set under a linked section, each agency must submit an official draft for the manual. That draft must carry the facts required by the manual's own rules and by this part. A single short sentence carries the whole duty. Read with the deadline rule nearby, it forms the filing duty that keeps the manual complete and on time.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s22-2: Section 22.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations tells agencies how to cite their authority in a notice. It sits in the part on preparing notices and proposed rules. The whole regulation is one sentence. The authority under which an agency issues a notice must be cited in narrative form within the text. Or it may be given in parentheses on a separate line following the text.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s3-2:
Section 3.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers public inspection of documents filed with the Federal Register. The rule sits in a part on services to the public under Title 1. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. Filed documents can be seen before they are published.

Documents filed with the Office of the Federal Register under law are available for public inspection, the rule states. A street address in Washington and the office hours are given for that inspection. There are no formal inspection procedures or requirements, as the rule goes on to note. Walk in access to pending federal actions is thus kept deliberately simple.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s301-2:
Section 301.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations states the purposes of the Administrative Conference of the United States. The first purpose is cooperative study. Federal agencies, helped by outside experts, may study mutual problems together, swap information, and frame recommendations for action.

The ends named are the full protection of private rights and the speedy, public-spirited conduct of federal duties. Further purposes follow in a list. They are to promote public participation and efficiency in rulemaking. They are to reduce needless litigation in the regulatory process. They are to improve the use of science in that process. And they are to improve the effectiveness of the laws that govern regulation. The section sits in Part 301 of Title 1, on the organization and purpose of the Conference. The hosted text is from the electronic Code as of late October 2026.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s304-2:
Section 304.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets out proactive disclosure duties for one small agency. The agency is the Administrative Conference of the United States, called ACUS in the text. Part 304 covers how that agency discloses its records and information.

The Freedom of Information Act requires some records to be open for public inspection in electronic form. The rule says those records may be reached through the agency's website. Covered records include ones requested three or more times by the public. Records once released that seem likely to be asked for again also qualify. So do records that appear to be of general interest. A subject index of such records may also be posted, and it is to be kept updated. The rule also covers information the agency routinely gives out in its regular work, such as press releases and adopted recommendations.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s425-2:
Section 425.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations, in the part for the President's Commission on White House Fellowships, tells people how to ask whether records about them exist. The Commission's system of records, as defined in the Privacy Act of 1974, is listed each year in the Federal Register. A person may appear in person at a stated room in Washington, on work days in set hours. Or the person may write to the Commission's Administrative Officer.

Written requests are recommended. A requester who is not the person the record concerns must state their relationship to that person. The part notes that requests are honored under the Privacy Act only when made by the person concerned, or by that person's legal guardian where the person cannot act.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s5-2:
Section 5.2 of Title 1 of the federal rules lists documents that must be filed and printed. They must be filed for public view with the Office of the Federal Register. They must also be printed in the Federal Register itself for all. Three classes of document are named in the body of the rule.

The first class is Presidential proclamations and executive orders in the numbered series. Any other document the President sends for printing joins that class. The second class is each document Congress has said must be printed. The third class is each document of general reach and legal force. The rule is a gate that tells agencies what they must file.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s6-2:
Section 6.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations orders subject indexes for the Federal Register. The rule comes from the Administrative Committee of the Federal Register. It sits in Part 6, on indexes and ancillaries. Title 1 covers general provisions. The text is taken from the eCFR as of October 23, 2026, and the official edition is the annual Code of Federal Regulations.

Analytical subject indexes covering the contents of the Federal Register shall be published. They are to appear as currently as practicable, keeping pace with new issues as closely as can be done. The indexes shall be cumulated and separately published at least once each calendar year. That yearly cumulated issue gives readers a single gathered index for the year.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s601-2:
Section 601.2 of Title 1 of the federal rules lists the policies of a planning body. The body is the National Capital Planning Commission for the capital. Its work must follow the national environment law and its rules. The body must give those who apply clear help with the rules.

That help is to make sure plans and projects meet the law in full. The body must fold the environment review into its choices as early as it can. It must run that review at the same time as other checks. Checks under the law on old and prized sites are named there. The review must spot and weigh sound paths that harm the setting less. Those paths must spare the quality of life in the capital region. The list goes on to guard the setting by all means that can be used.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s602-2: Section 602.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations states the open-records policy of the National Capital Planning Commission, in its Freedom of Information Act rules. The policy is to make information as widely available as possible, chiefly through the Commission's website and handouts of material not online. Staff must help the public get information, both through the formal steps and in informal ways that fit them. The Commission must release agency records of interest to the public that are fit for disclosure.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s603-2:
Section 603.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations defines the terms of the National Capital Planning Commission's privacy rules. Definitions govern how every later duty in the part is read. The longest definition in the opening text is adverse determination.

An adverse determination is a decision to withhold a requested record, in whole or in part. It also covers a decision that the record does not exist or cannot be located. A ruling that requested information is not a record under the Privacy Act counts as well. So does a decision that a record needs no amendment or correction. Refusing an accounting of disclosures, or denying a fee waiver, falls under the same term. The definition also reaches challenges to the commission's own handling, as the text continues. Naming every kind of no in one term lets the part attach rights of appeal to all of them.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s8-2:
Section 8.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations deals with the growth of the Code in good order. It sits in Part 8, on the Code of Federal Regulations. The aim of the rule is to keep the growth of the Code on sound lines. To that end, the Director of the Federal Register may make new titles in the Code. The Director may also move the titles and the parts that are in place.

A bar is set on that power. Before the Director takes such a step, the Director must talk with each agency that the change would touch in a direct way. The rule thus joins a wide power of shape with a duty to hear the bodies that would feel the change. It is a short rule, and it turns on the sense of order in the book of laws.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s9-2:
Section 9.2 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations states the scope of the United States Government Manual. The Manual contains appropriate information about the three branches of the Federal Government. For the major executive agencies, that information takes three forms listed in the text.

It includes descriptions of each agency's legal authorities, public purposes, programs, and functions. It includes the established places and methods by which the public may obtain information and make submittals or requests. And it includes lists of the officials heading major operating units. The Manual also carries brief information about quasi-official agencies. Supplemental information is included where the Director judges it of enough public interest to warrant a place. The section sits in Part 9 of Title 1. The hosted text is from the electronic Code of late October 2026.
vedanta-sutras-thibaut-vol-2:
Thibaut's second Vedanta Sutras volume appeared in 1896 with Ramanuja's commentary instead. Ramanuja, the great rival interpreter, read the same sutras very differently. The volume formed part thirty-eight of the Sacred Books of the East.

Ramanuja answers Sankara with a God of love and devotion. Reality stays one, yet holds souls and matter within itself as God's body. Salvation comes through loving surrender rather than knowledge alone. Devotion meets metaphysics on every page of his commentary. Reading both volumes lets students weigh the rivals directly. The debate between these commentators shaped Hindu theology for a thousand years.
visuddhimagga-pe-maung-tin-vol-2:
Part two of Pe Maung Tin's Path of Purity, issued in 1929, continues Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga from part one of 1923. The great fifth-century manual of Theravada practice presses on from concentration toward wisdom. The translation was made for the Pali Text Society.

The reader moves through the higher reaches of meditation: the formless attainments, the divine eye and ear, and the recollection of past lives. Then the ground shifts to wisdom, the analysis of mind and matter, and the stages of insight. Buddhaghosa's method is exact and cumulative, step laid on step. With part one, it gives English readers the fullest classic map of Buddhist meditation.
vittoria-volume-2: Volume two of George Meredith's Vittoria stands here behind an old Project Gutenberg header, which names it number 42 in the series of Meredith's works. Nothing beyond that header is present in these pages: no chapter heads, no contents, and no lines of the novel itself. The header speaks of free plain vanilla electronic texts, readable by humans and computers since 1971, and asks for donations to the archive foundation. The tale of Vittoria herself must be sought in the companion records of the set.
voltaire-age-of-louis-xiv-1753-vol-2:
Volume two completes the 1753 English translation of Voltaire's Age of Louis XIV, first published in French in 1751. Voltaire treated the reign of the Sun King as a whole civilization, not a mere line of battles. The two English volumes of 1753 carried that new kind of history to British readers at once.

In this second volume the age unfolds in its courts, churches, arts, and wars, all weighed by one sharp mind. Voltaire praises the glory and notes the cost, especially where pride drove France to ruin. His method, history as the story of a whole society, founded a school. The Age of Louis XIV remains his most durable work of history.
vyse-operations-gizeh-vol-2:
Volume Two of Howard Vyse's Operations continues the 1837 work at Gizeh. The colonel's crews kept digging, hauling, and recording through the season. More tombs, stones, and finds pass through his journal.

Vyse logs labor, costs, and quarrels with the same care as finds. He describes shafts and chambers as his men cleared them. The detail lets later scholars retrace work long since altered. The tone stays brisk and sure. For readers of the first volume, this record deepens the picture of how Egypt's greatest sites were first explored. Sweat and stone fill every dated page.
wacousta-a-tale-of-the-pontiac-conspirac:
Volume two of John Richardson's Wacousta, or The Prophecy, opens on the evening of the sad day that filled the first volume. For the third time since the siege began, the drawbridge of Detroit is lowered. This time no rattling chains give the garrison away. The bridge drops with a care that speaks of deep secrecy. No armed party stands ready within the walls.

Most of the troops, worn out by the day's harassing duties, have gone to their rest. A few guards pace their posts, less to fight off sleep than to watch what goes on by torchlight in the barrack square. There an anxious knot of officers stands close around two figures. The two figures wear clothes with nothing of the bright soldier about them. Richardson slows the scene to a held breath, before a night errand steals out of the fort.
waverley-or-tis-sixty-years-since-volume:
Volume two of Sir Walter Scott's Waverley, in the same Caledonian series as its first volume, opens at chapter thirty-six, titled An Incident. The scene is an autumn afternoon. Dinner then came at two o'clock. By four, Mr. Gilfillan, a stern Covenanter, begins his march. He hopes to reach Stirling, eighteen miles off, by borrowing an hour or two of the night.

Gilfillan marches stoutly at the head of his followers. He eyes his prisoner from time to time, as if he longs to draw him into argument. At last he drops back beside Waverley's horse. After a few silent steps, he asks who the man in the black coat and powdered head was, that stood with the Laird of Cairnvreckan. Waverley's answer, a Presbyterian clergyman, draws a contemptuous snort. Scott lets the march carry a whole debate of Scotland's churches in its stride.
welles-diary-vol-2:
Volume Two of Gideon Welles's diary runs from 1864 into the troubled peace that followed the Civil War. Welles stayed on as navy secretary under Andrew Johnson. The 1911 edition completes the published diary.

The war's end, Lincoln's reelection, and then his assassination shake these pages. Welles describes the cabinet's grief and the turn to Johnson with growing alarm. His break with the president over Reconstruction deepens entry by entry. The diary closes as a record of a government strained by victory, murder, and a feud that led toward impeachment. Later editors filled gaps with notes on the men he names.
what-i-remember-volume-2: Here only the title page and chapter list are shown, so the memoir text itself is missing. Thomas Adolphus Trollope published What I Remember in two volumes in 1887, and this record covers volume two. The contents begin in the north of England and on a journey in Brittany. Later chapters return to Paris, go to Ireland, and settle in Florence. Named chapters honor Charles Dickens and Elizabeth Barrett Browning. A final listed chapter joins the Garrows, science meetings, and his first marriage.
what-s-mine-s-mine-volume-2:
Volume two of George MacDonald's What's Mine's Mine opens with a tale told by Ian. He tells of a widow left poor with a large family when her well-off husband died. Work was hard to find, hard to do, and poor in pay. Yet she trusted God through each want.

The contents of this volume name Rob of the Angels, a new house, and two pairs of lovers. A great stag, a lesson, and a granny's anger fill the middle chapters. One chapter takes place in a tomb. MacDonald mixes Highland scenes, love, and faith in this middle part. The story Ian tells sets the tone of trust under loss.
wieland-geschichte-des-agathon-teil-2:
Agathon's education continues in Part Two of Wieland's pioneering German novel, presented in the original German. The young hero passes through fresh love, political turmoil, and long philosophical debate. Experience slowly tempers the dreamer of the first part into a wiser man.

Part One asked how a young idealist survives a world that laughs at ideals. Part Two shows him learning to live in that world without surrendering his soul. Wieland balances story and reflection with a master's ease, pausing the plot for conversations that earn their place. The two parts together founded a genre German literature would own for two centuries. The novel of formation starts here, fully formed in outline.
wild-youth-volume-2:
Volume two of Gilbert Parker's Wild Youth opens at chapter ten, The Moon Was Not Alone. Orlando has fought his life's first great battle out on the prairie under the stars. He won, Parker says, since struggles of the soul allow no drawn battles. Yet he fears no one will believe the truth the next day.

Louise, at daybreak, is glad of the win, though trouble looms in her eyes. She must face Tralee with no proof of her innocence. Joel Mazarine, who trusts no man or woman, will judge her hard. A breakfast of two biscuits left from bronco work cheers them a little. Love and honor face a grim homecoming.
yoga-vasistha-mitra-vol-2:
Volume two of Vihari-Lala Mitra's Yoga-Vasistha, from his four-volume English translation of the 1890s, carries Vasistha's teaching of Prince Rama onward. The frame stays the same: the sage answers the young prince's despair with doctrine and tale. The subject is liberation from the wheel of birth.

The book now stresses practice: self-effort over fate, the calming of thought, and the vision of the world as mind alone. Long inset stories show sages and kings waking from the dream of separate selfhood. Mitra's translation, dated in style, remains the only complete English version of the whole epic. Readers come for the stories and stay for the philosophy.
zibeline-volume-2: Philippe de Massa wrote this French romance, shown here as volume two of three. Pages present here hold only a publisher's header giving the title, his name, and an April 2003 release note. No chapter text or contents list appears in these pages. The header again names the French Immortals series. The middle volume's share of the story cannot be described from a header alone, so nothing further is claimed here.
